1.html:
Why start here

Before calculating anything, you need to know which question you are answering. Corporate finance is not a collection of formulas: it is a way of making decisions with money when the future is uncertain. Every formula you will see in this course serves to answer three questions, and only three.

The central idea: creating value

A company receives money (from its shareholders, from its banks), uses it to buy machines, hire people, produce, sell, and hopes to get back more money than it put in. If it manages that, it creates value. If not, it destroys value, even if it reports an accounting profit.

Remember this nuance from now on, we will come back to it often: a profit is not necessarily value creation. If your shareholders could have earned 8% by investing their money elsewhere at the same risk, and your company only returns 5% to them, you have made a profit but you have destroyed value. This is the notion of opportunity cost, and it is the heart of finance.

The three big questions

1. Where to invest? (the investment decision)

Which projects should the company launch? Opening a factory, buying a competitor, launching a product, developing software... Each project costs money today and promises money tomorrow. The question is: is what I will receive tomorrow worth more than what I spend today?

This is the left-hand side of the balance sheet (assets): what the company owns and uses.

2. How to finance it? (the financing decision)

Once you know what to do, you have to find the money. Two main sources:

  • Equity: shareholders' money. They become owners, they are not repaid on a fixed date, but they demand a high return because they take the most risk (they are paid last).
  • Debt: lenders' money (banks, bond investors). It must be repaid with interest, whatever happens, but it is generally cheaper.

This is the right-hand side of the balance sheet (liabilities and equity): where the money comes from.

3. How to manage day-to-day? (cash management)

A profitable company can go bankrupt if it runs out of cash at the wrong moment. Customers pay at 60 days, suppliers want to be paid at 30, salaries are due at the end of the month... Managing these timing gaps is the management of working capital requirement and cash. People often say: "revenue is vanity, profit is sanity, cash is reality."

The diagram that sums it all up

          INVESTORS                       COMPANY                      REAL ASSETS
  (shareholders, banks)                                       (factories, inventory, patents...)

     1. provide the money   ───────►  [ Chief      ]  ───────►  2. invests in assets
                                      [ financial  ]
     5. receive dividends   ◄───────  [ officer    ]  ◄───────  3. the assets generate cash
        and interest                   4. reinvests a part

The finance director (the CFO, Chief Financial Officer) stands in the middle: they collect money from investors, put it into the best projects, and pass back what those projects earn. Their goal: that the cash coming back (arrow 3) is worth more than the cash that went out (arrow 1).

Who does what in the finance function

  • The management controller (contrôleur de gestion) tracks costs, budgets and the gaps between forecast and actual.
  • The accountant records transactions and produces the financial statements (balance sheet, income statement).
  • The treasurer manages cash day to day, the relationships with banks and short-term investments.
  • The CFO coordinates all of this and takes the strategic decisions: major investments, fundraising, acquisitions.

Outside the company, market finance (investment banks, funds, asset management) links those who have money with those who need it. We will talk about it in module 5.

The principle that guides every decision

The classic objective of corporate finance is to maximise the value of the company for its shareholders. Not revenue, not this year's profit: value, that is, the sum of all the cash the company will generate in the future, brought back to today.

This "brought back to today" is crucial: €1 today is worth more than €1 in a year. Why? Because with €1 today you can invest it and have more than €1 in a year. And because the future is uncertain. That is exactly the subject of tomorrow's lesson: the time value of money.

(Note: today there is also a lot of talk about other stakeholders, employees, customers, the environment, through CSR and ESG criteria. These topics do not replace the logic of value creation, they enrich it.)

Key takeaways

  • Finance answers three questions: where to invest, how to finance, how to manage cash.
  • Investing = the asset side of the balance sheet; financing = the liabilities side.
  • Creating value means earning more than the opportunity cost of the money used, not just making a profit.
  • Shareholders take more risk than lenders, so they demand a higher return.
  • €1 today is worth more than €1 tomorrow.

Exercise

For each situation, say whether it is an investment decision, a financing decision or a cash management decision:

  1. Decathlon decides to open 15 new stores in India.
  2. A start-up raises €3m from a venture capital fund.
  3. An SME negotiates with its customers to be paid at 30 days instead of 60.
  4. LVMH issues 10-year bonds for €2bn.
  5. A company buys a competitor.
  6. Your company has €500,000 sitting idle in its current account and decides to put it in a 3-month term deposit.

Bonus question: a company makes a profit of €1m with €20m of equity. Its shareholders could get 9% a year elsewhere, at comparable risk. Has it created value?

Answers (try first!)
  1. Investment: money is committed today to assets (stores) for future cash flows.
  2. Financing: equity.
  3. Cash management: you reduce the gap between sales and cash receipts (working capital requirement).
  4. Financing: debt.
  5. Investment: an acquisition is a big investment project.
  6. Cash management: short-term investment of surplus cash.

Bonus: return for shareholders = 1 / 20 = 5%. They require 9%. The company made a profit but destroyed value: it would have needed a profit of at least 20 × 9% = €1.8m simply to meet their expectations.

Next lesson: the time value of money, simple interest and compound interest.

2.html:
Why this is the basic building block

Yesterday we finished on one sentence: €1 today is worth more than €1 in a year. Today we turn that intuition into numbers. The whole rest of the course (loans, NPV, company valuation, bonds) rests on what we see this morning. If this lesson is clear, half of finance becomes logical.

Three reasons why money has a time value

  1. Opportunity cost: €1 available today can be invested and earn interest. Waiting means giving up that gain.
  2. Inflation: over time prices rise, so €1 buys fewer things tomorrow than today.
  3. Risk: a promise of future payment may never be honoured. A certain euro in your pocket is worth more than a promised euro.

The interest rate is the price of waiting. It is what you must be given to accept parting with your money for a certain time.

Simple interest

With simple interest, interest is calculated only on the starting capital, the same amount every year.

Final value = Capital × (1 + rate × number of years)

VF = C × (1 + i × n) (VF = valeur finale, the final or future value)

Example: you invest €1,000 at 5% a year with simple interest for 3 years. Each year you earn 1,000 × 5% = €50. After 3 years: 1,000 × (1 + 0.05 × 3) = €1,150.

Simple interest is mainly used for short periods (less than a year): cash investments of a few months, discounting of trade bills, bank overdrafts.

Compound interest

With compound interest, each year's interest is added to the capital and in turn earns interest. We say the interest is compounded (capitalisé). It is interest on interest.

Final value = Capital × (1 + rate)^(number of years)

VF = C × (1 + i)^n

Same example: €1,000 at 5% for 3 years, with compound interest.

YearCapital at start of yearInterest for the yearCapital at end of year
1€1,000.00€50.00€1,050.00
2€1,050.00€52.50€1,102.50
3€1,102.50€55.13€1,157.63

Look at the interest column: it grows every year. In year 2 you receive €50 on your starting capital, plus €2.50 of interest on the €50 of interest from year 1. Check with the formula: 1,000 × 1.05³ = €1,157.63.

Over 3 years, the difference from simple interest is tiny (€7.63). But wait until you see what happens over a long period.

The (mathematical) magic of time

Still €1,000 at 5%:

PeriodSimple interestCompound interestDifference
3 years€1,150€1,158+ €8
10 years€1,500€1,629+ €129
30 years€2,500€4,322+ €1,822

With simple interest, growth is linear (a straight line). With compound interest, it is exponential (a curve that takes off). The longer the period, the more the gap explodes.

The story always told in class: in 1626, Dutch settlers are said to have bought the island of Manhattan for the equivalent of 24 dollars. A bad deal for the sellers? If those $24 had been invested at 7% a year for 400 years, they would be worth more than 13,000 billion dollars today. Compound interest over a very long period produces dizzying numbers.

A version closer to home: Léa invests €2,000 just once at age 20, at 7% a year. Tom invests the same amount at the same rate, but at 30. At 60:

  • Léa has 2,000 × 1.07⁴⁰ ≈ €29,950
  • Tom has 2,000 × 1.07³⁰ ≈ €15,225

A ten-year head start almost doubled the result, with exactly the same effort. In finance, time is your best ally.

The rule of 72: mental arithmetic

To find out how many years it takes an investment to double, divide 72 by the rate (in %):

Years to double ≈ 72 / rate

  • At 5%: 72 / 5 ≈ 14.4 years (exact calculation: 14.2 years)
  • At 6%: 72 / 6 = 12 years (check: 1.06¹² = 2.01)
  • At 8%: 72 / 8 = 9 years

It also works the other way round: with 3% inflation a year, prices double in 72 / 3 = 24 years. Your purchasing power is halved in a generation.

It is a valuable tool in an interview or a meeting, when you have no calculator.

Vocabulary to master

  • Capital (C): the sum invested at the start. It is also called present value (VA in French, or PV for present value).
  • Future value / accumulated value (VF, or FV): what the capital is worth at the end of the investment.
  • Interest rate (i): always expressed per period (usually per year). Careful: an annual rate is used with a number of years, a monthly rate with a number of months.
  • Compounding (capitalisation): calculating a future value by making an amount "grow" into the future. That is exactly what the formula C × (1 + i)^n does.

Tomorrow we will go the other way: start from a future sum and find out what it is worth today. That is discounting, and it is the most widely used tool in all of finance.

Key takeaways

  • The interest rate is the price of time: it pays for opportunity cost, inflation and risk.
  • Simple interest: VF = C × (1 + i × n), interest is only on the starting capital. Used for the short term.
  • Compound interest: VF = C × (1 + i)^n, interest itself earns interest. This is the default rule in finance.
  • Over a long period, the gap between the two becomes huge: compound growth is exponential.
  • Rule of 72: an investment doubles in about 72 / rate years.
  • Starting early often matters more than investing a lot.

Exercise

  1. You invest €5,000 at 3% a year for 4 years with simple interest. How much do you have at the end?
  2. Same investment, but with compound interest. How much do you have at the end?
  3. Using the rule of 72, how long does it take a sum invested at 6% to double?
  4. Your bank offers you two investments of €10,000 over 10 years. A: 4% a year simple interest. B: 3.5% a year compound interest. Which do you choose?
  5. Food for thought: a start-up tells you its revenue "grows by 10% a year". Why is this compound growth and not simple growth?
Answers (try first!)
  1. 5,000 × (1 + 0.03 × 4) = 5,000 × 1.12 = €5,600.
  2. 5,000 × 1.03⁴ = 5,000 × 1.1255 = €5,627.54. That is €27.54 more thanks to interest on interest.
  3. 72 / 6 = 12 years. Check: 1.06¹² = 2.012, so the sum has indeed (slightly more than) doubled.
  4. A: 10,000 × (1 + 0.04 × 10) = €14,000. B: 10,000 × 1.035¹⁰ = €14,105.99. B is better, even though its rate is lower! Over 10 years, compounding more than makes up for the half point less in rate. Moral: never compare two rates without knowing how they are calculated.
  5. Because the 10% applies each year to the previous year's revenue, which has already grown. Revenue of €1m becomes €1.1m, then €1.21m, then €1.331m... That is the formula (1 + i)^n. Using the rule of 72, revenue doubles in a little over 7 years.

Next lesson: discounting and compounding, or how to work out what a sum you will receive in the future is worth today.

3.html:
The way back

Yesterday you learnt how to make a sum grow over time: €1,000 invested at 5% becomes €1,157.63 in 3 years. That is compounding: you start from today and look towards the future.

Today we go the other way. You are promised a sum in the future: what is it worth today? That is discounting. And it is probably the most widely used tool in all of finance: valuing a project, a company, a bond, a footballer's contract... everything goes through it.

Compounding and discounting: two sides of the same formula

We start again from yesterday's formula:

Compounding: VF = VA × (1 + i)^n

You just have to turn it round:

Discounting: VA = VF / (1 + i)^n

  • VA (valeur actuelle, or present value): what the sum is worth today.
  • VF (valeur future, or future value): the sum received in the future.
  • i: the discount rate, per period.
  • n: the number of periods.
     TODAY                                        IN n YEARS

      VA   ──────── compound : × (1 + i)^n ───────►   VF
      VA   ◄─────── discount : ÷ (1 + i)^n ────────   VF

The number 1 / (1 + i)^n is called the discount factor. It is always less than 1 (as soon as the rate is positive): a future sum is always worth less today.

First example

Your grandmother promises you €10,000 for your 25th birthday, in 5 years. You could invest your money risk-free at 4% a year. What is her promise worth today?

VA = 10,000 / 1.04⁵ = 10,000 × 0.8219 = €8,219.27

Interpretation: if you invested €8,219.27 today at 4%, you would have exactly €10,000 in 5 years. The two are therefore equivalent. Receiving €10,000 in 5 years or €8,219.27 today is the same thing (for equal risk).

The discount rate changes everything

Which rate should you use? It is the return you could get elsewhere for the same level of risk. In other words, the opportunity cost seen in lesson 1. The riskier a future cash flow, the higher the rate used to discount it, and the less it is worth today.

The same €10,000 in 5 years, discounted at different rates:

Discount ratePresent valueTypical situation
2%€9,057Virtually risk-free investment
5%€7,835Large, solid company
10%€6,209Risky project, established start-up

At a 10% rate, the promise loses nearly 40% of its value. That is why venture capital investors, who demand very high returns, value a start-up's distant profits so harshly.

Remember the inverse relationship: when the rate goes up, present value goes down. You will see in module 5 that this is exactly why bond prices fall when central banks raise their rates, as in 2022-2023.

Comparing sums received at different dates

Golden rule of finance: never compare euros from different dates. First bring them back to the same date, usually today.

Example: you win a game. Option A: €50,000 right now. Option B: €60,000 in 4 years. Your opportunity rate is 5%.

VA of B = 60,000 / 1.05⁴ = €49,362

€49,362 < €50,000: you take A, even though 60,000 looks bigger. With a lower rate (say 3%), the answer would flip. The right choice always depends on the rate.

Discounting several cash flows

In real life, you often receive money in several instalments. The method is simple: discount each cash flow separately, then add them up.

Example: a football club sells a player for €30m, payable in three instalments of €10m at the end of each year. The club borrows at 8%. What is the sale really worth today?

InstalmentAmountCalculationPresent value
End of year 1€10m10 / 1.08€9.26m
End of year 2€10m10 / 1.08²€8.57m
End of year 3€10m10 / 1.08³€7.94m
Total€30m€25.77m

The "€30m" transfer is in reality worth only €25.8m today. That is why clubs negotiate payment schedules so fiercely: paying later means paying less. This technique (adding up discounted cash flows) is the basis of NPV, which you will see in module 4, and of company valuation in module 7.

Finding a rate or a duration

The formula has four variables (VA, VF, i, n). If you know three, you can find the fourth.

Finding the rate: i = (VF / VA)^(1/n) − 1

Example: a flat bought for €200,000 is sold for €260,000 six years later. What annual return? i = (260,000 / 200,000)^(1/6) − 1 = 1.3^(1/6) − 1 = 4.47% a year. That looks less spectacular than "+30%", and that is normal: the gain is spread over six years. Always bring a performance back to an annual rate so you can compare it.

Finding the duration: yesterday's rule of 72 gives a quick order of magnitude. For an exact calculation, use logarithms: n = ln(VF / VA) / ln(1 + i).

In Excel

In companies, nobody does these calculations by hand. In French-language Excel (English Excel names in brackets, with commas instead of semicolons):

  • =VA(4%;5;0;-10000) gives 8,219.27 (the present value; =PV(4%,5,0,-10000) in English Excel)
  • =VC(4%;5;0;-8219,27) gives 10,000 (the future value, "valeur capitalisée"; =FV(...))
  • =TAUX(6;0;-200000;260000) gives 4.47% (=RATE(...))

The minus sign is an Excel convention: money leaving your pocket is negative, money coming in is positive. If you get a negative result, it is almost always a sign issue.

Key takeaways

  • Compound: VF = VA × (1 + i)^n. Discount: VA = VF / (1 + i)^n. It is the same formula in both directions.
  • A future sum is always worth less today (the discount factor is less than 1).
  • The discount rate reflects opportunity cost and risk. Higher rate = lower present value.
  • Never compare euros from different dates: bring them all back to today.
  • For several cash flows: discount each one then add them up.
  • Always compare a performance as an annual rate: i = (VF / VA)^(1/n) − 1.

Exercise

  1. What is the present value of €15,000 received in 3 years, at a rate of 5%?
  2. What is the future value of €8,000 invested for 6 years at 3%?
  3. Your future employer offers you a bonus: €20,000 when you join, or €23,000 in 3 years if you stay. What do you choose at a rate of 4%? And at 6%?
  4. You invested €5,000 and get back €6,500 after 5 years. What was your annual return?
  5. What is the present value of three payments of €2,000 received at the end of each of the next three years, at a rate of 10%?
Answers (try first!)
  1. 15,000 / 1.05³ = 15,000 / 1.157625 = €12,957.56.
  2. 8,000 × 1.03⁶ = 8,000 × 1.1941 = €9,552.42.
  3. At 4%: 23,000 / 1.04³ = €20,446.92 > €20,000, so you take the bonus in 3 years. At 6%: 23,000 / 1.06³ = €19,311.24 < €20,000, so you take the bonus right away. Same offer, opposite decision: it all depends on the rate. (And in reality, the future bonus is also riskier, since you have to stay three years: one more argument for a high rate.)
  4. i = (6,500 / 5,000)^(1/5) − 1 = 1.3^0.2 − 1 = 5.39% a year.
  5. 2,000 / 1.1 + 2,000 / 1.1² + 2,000 / 1.1³ = 1,818.18 + 1,652.89 + 1,502.63 = €4,973.70. The €6,000 promised is not quite worth €5,000 today.

Next lesson: nominal rate, effective rate, inflation and real rate. Why a "3%" is not always a 3%.

4.titre: Nominal, effectif, réel : lire un taux
4.html:
A "3%" is not always a 3%

For two days we have been handling rates as if it were simple: "5% a year". In real life, a rate often hides two traps.

  1. The rhythm of interest: interest paid every month does not earn the same as interest paid once a year, even with the same advertised rate.
  2. Inflation: earning 3% when prices rise by 5% means getting poorer.

Today you learn to see through these two traps. It is what separates someone who reads a loan offer from someone who understands it.

First trap: the compounding frequency

Nominal rate and effective rate

A bank quotes you a nominal rate of 12% a year, with interest calculated every month. In practice, it applies 12% / 12 = 1% a month.

But remember lesson 2: each month, interest is added to the capital and in turn earns interest. Over a year, €1,000 becomes:

1,000 × 1.01¹² = €1,126.83

That is 12.68% over the year, not 12%. This 12.68% is the effective rate (or actuarial rate): what you really earn or pay over a year.

Effective annual rate = (1 + nominal rate / m)^m − 1

where m is the number of compounding periods per year (12 for monthly, 4 for quarterly, 365 for daily).

  • The nominal rate is a "headline" rate. It does not let you compare two offers that have different compounding frequencies.
  • The effective rate is the true measure. It is always the one you compare.

The more frequent the compounding, the bigger the gap. At 4% nominal: quarterly gives 4.06%, daily gives 4.08%. The gap is small at low rates, much more visible at high rates.

Proportional rate and equivalent rate

The reverse problem: you know an annual rate and you need a monthly rate (for a repayment schedule, for example).

  • Proportional rate: you simply divide. 6% a year gives 6 / 12 = 0.5% a month. Simple, but over a year that gives back more than 6%.
  • Equivalent rate: the monthly rate which, compounded 12 times, gives back exactly 6%. (1.06)^(1/12) − 1 = 0.487% a month.

Equivalent rate = (1 + annual rate)^(1/m) − 1

In France, banks often use the proportional rate for mortgages, which makes the effective rate slightly higher than the advertised rate. It is not a scam, it is a convention, but you need to know it.

The TAEG: the law requires the effective rate

To protect borrowers, French law (like EU law) requires lenders to display the TAEG, the taux annuel effectif global (the French equivalent of the APR, the annual percentage rate of charge). It includes not only interest but also all compulsory fees: arrangement fees, required insurance, guarantee fees.

Typical example: a car loan advertised at "4.5%" can have a TAEG of 5.3% once arrangement fees and insurance are included. To compare two loans, compare the TAEGs, never the nominal rates.

The case of revolving credit: some store cards or "revolving" credit lines display a monthly rate. 1.5% a month seems small. As an effective rate: 1.015¹² − 1 = 19.56% a year. That is why this kind of credit is so dangerous.

Second trap: inflation

Nominal rate and real rate

Here the word "nominal" has another meaning (a classic vocabulary trap in exams):

  • The nominal rate is the rate expressed in current euros, the one you see on your statement.
  • The real rate is what you gain in purchasing power, once inflation is removed.

The exact relationship is called the Fisher equation (after the economist Irving Fisher):

(1 + nominal rate) = (1 + real rate) × (1 + inflation)

so real rate = (1 + nominal rate) / (1 + inflation) − 1

And the approximation, valid when rates are low:

Real rate ≈ nominal rate − inflation

Example: your savings account pays 3% and inflation is 2%. Exact: 1.03 / 1.02 − 1 = 0.98%. Approximation: 3 − 2 = 1%. Your purchasing power has increased by about 1%.

What happened in 2022

In 2022, inflation in France exceeded 5% over the year, while the Livret A (France's regulated, tax-free savings account) paid between 0.5% and 2%. Savers saw their balance rise in euros, but their real rate was roughly between −3% and −4.5%: they could buy fewer things with their savings than a year earlier. Making money in euros does not mean getting richer.

The same logic applies to salaries. A 3% rise with 5% inflation is a fall in purchasing power: 1.03 / 1.05 − 1 = −1.9%. When you negotiate your first salary and then your pay rises, always think in real terms.

Inflation and discounting

One last point, important for the rest of the course: when you discount future cash flows (lesson 3), you must be consistent.

  • Cash flows in current euros (which include inflation) → discount with a nominal rate.
  • Cash flows in constant euros (without inflation) → discount with a real rate.

Mixing the two is one of the most frequent mistakes in case studies. We will come back to it in module 4 with NPV.

Key takeaways

  • Two rates with different compounding frequencies cannot be compared directly: convert them to an effective annual rate, (1 + i/m)^m − 1.
  • Proportional rate = annual rate / m. Equivalent rate = (1 + annual rate)^(1/m) − 1.
  • To compare loans, compare the TAEGs (APRs), which include interest and compulsory fees.
  • Real rate ≈ nominal rate − inflation (exactly: (1 + nominal) / (1 + inflation) − 1).
  • An investment or a pay rise is judged in real terms.
  • Discount nominal cash flows with a nominal rate, and real cash flows with a real rate.

Exercise

  1. Bank A: 6% nominal, interest compounded monthly. Bank B: 6.15% a year, compounded once a year. Where do you put your money?
  2. What monthly rate is equivalent to an annual rate of 5%?
  3. An investment pays 4% a year, inflation is 2.5%. What is the real rate (exact calculation and approximation)?
  4. Your salary goes from €30,000 to €31,000 gross a year. Inflation is 4%. Have you gained purchasing power?
  5. Food for thought: why does a bank that lends prefer to display a monthly nominal rate, and a bank that pays interest on your savings prefer to display an effective rate?
Answers (try first!)
  1. Effective rate of A: 1.005¹² − 1 = 6.17%. B: 6.15%. A is (slightly) better, even though its advertised rate is lower. Always compare effective rates.
  2. 1.05^(1/12) − 1 = 0.407% a month (and not 5 / 12 = 0.417%).
  3. Exact: 1.04 / 1.025 − 1 = 1.46%. Approximation: 4 − 2.5 = 1.5%. Very close, because rates are low.
  4. Nominal rise: 31,000 / 30,000 − 1 = 3.33%. Real rate: 1.0333 / 1.04 − 1 = −0.64%. No: despite €1,000 more on your payslip, your purchasing power has fallen slightly.
  5. Because each one displays the figure that suits it. For a loan, the nominal rate is lower than the effective rate: the credit looks cheaper. For savings, the effective rate is higher than the nominal: the investment looks more rewarding. That is exactly why the law requires the TAEG for loans.

Next lesson: annuities, or how to calculate the monthly repayment on a loan.

5.html:
The formula behind every loan

One day (maybe soon), you will sign a loan: for a car, for a flat, to fund your studies. The bank will tell you: "it will be €1,170 a month for 20 years". Where does that figure come from? It is not magic, it is the direct application of what you have learnt over the past three days.

Today we study annuities: a series of identical payments made at regular intervals. Loan repayments, rents, retirement pensions, regular savings plans, bond coupons: all of these are annuities. And a company handles them every day, when it borrows to buy a machine or rents its offices.

What exactly is an annuity?

An annuity is a series of n equal cash flows, written a, paid each period, at a rate i per period. The word "annuity" comes from "year" (annus), but it is also used for monthly payments (in French these are called mensualités, monthly instalments).

By convention, unless stated otherwise, payments are made at the end of the period: that is the case for a loan, whose first monthly payment falls one month after the funds are released. This is called an ordinary annuity (payments in arrears).

Remember the last exercise of lesson 3: three payments of €2,000 at 10%. You discounted each cash flow, then added them up, to get €4,973.70. It works, but imagine doing that for 240 monthly payments... Luckily, there is a formula that does the whole sum in one go.

The present value of an annuity

VA = a × [1 − (1 + i)^(−n)] / i

where a is the payment per period, i the rate per period and n the number of payments.

The term in square brackets divided by i is called the annuity factor. It tells you what a series of n payments of €1 is worth today.

Check with the lesson 3 exercise: a = €2,000, i = 10%, n = 3.

VA = 2,000 × (1 − 1.1⁻³) / 0.1 = 2,000 × 2.4869 = €4,973.70. Exactly the same result, in a single line.

Concrete example: you can put €900 a month towards a mortgage. The bank lends to you at 3.6% a year (proportional rate of 0.3% a month, as we saw in lesson 4). How much can you borrow?

TermNumber of monthly paymentsAmount you can borrow
20 years240€153,817
25 years300€177,865

Five more years let you borrow about €24,000 more... but you will also pay 60 more monthly instalments. This is exactly the calculation your bank adviser does when talking about your "borrowing capacity".

The monthly repayment on a loan

The most common case is the reverse: you know the amount borrowed (the capital C) and you are looking for the monthly payment. You just turn the formula round:

a = C × i / [1 − (1 + i)^(−n)]

The underlying idea is simple: the capital lent today equals the present value of all the future repayments, discounted at the loan rate. The bank is not giving you a present, nor is it robbing you: it swaps €200,000 today for a series of monthly payments worth exactly €200,000 today, at its rate.

Example: a mortgage

Camille borrows €200,000 over 20 years at 3.6% a year, repayable monthly (a fictional example, but realistic for France in 2024-2025; rates change, so always check current conditions).

  • Monthly rate: 3.6% / 12 = 0.3% = 0.003
  • Number of monthly payments: 20 × 12 = 240
  • a = 200,000 × 0.003 / (1 − 1.003⁻²⁴⁰) = €1,170.22 a month (excluding insurance)

Over 20 years, Camille will pay 1,170.22 × 240 = €280,853.50. The total cost of the loan (the interest) is therefore 280,853.50 − 200,000 = €80,853.50. She repays €1.40 for every euro borrowed.

The impact of rate and term

Same €200,000 loan, with different rates and terms:

Annual rateMonthly payment over 20 yearsMonthly payment over 25 years
3.0%€1,109.20€948.42
3.6%€1,170.22€1,012.01
4.0%€1,211.96€1,055.67
4.5%€1,265.30€1,111.66

One and a half points more on the rate means about €156 more every month over 20 years. That is why the rise in rates in 2022-2023 caused the number of mortgages granted in France to plunge: for the same monthly payment, households could borrow much less.

An example from the company side

A (fictional) SME buys a machine for €15,000 and finances it with a 4-year loan at 5% a year, repaid monthly. Monthly rate: 5% / 12. Monthly payment: 15,000 × (0.05/12) / (1 − (1 + 0.05/12)⁻⁴⁸) = €345.44. Total interest cost: 345.44 × 48 − 15,000 ≈ €1,581. The CFO compares this cost with what the machine will bring in: that is the start of the investment decision (module 4).

The future value of an annuity: regular saving

You can also ask what a series of regular payments will be worth at the end. That is the case for a regular savings plan.

VF = a × [(1 + i)^n − 1] / i

Example: you pay €100 a month for 10 years into an investment at 3% a year (0.25% a month). After 120 payments:

VF = 100 × (1.0025¹²⁰ − 1) / 0.0025 = €13,974.14

You paid in €12,000; compound interest added nearly €2,000 more. The longer the period, the bigger this share of interest becomes (lesson 2, again and always).

A limiting case: the perpetuity

What if the payments never stopped? When n becomes very large, (1 + i)^(−n) tends to 0, and the formula becomes surprisingly simple:

Perpetuity: VA = a / i

An income of €1,000 a year forever, at a rate of 4%, is worth 1,000 / 0.04 = €25,000. It looks theoretical, but it is a key idea: you will meet it again in module 5 to value shares (the Gordon-Shapiro model) and in module 7 to calculate a company's terminal value in a DCF.

In Excel

  • =VPM(3,6%/12;240;-200000) gives 1,170.22 (the monthly payment, "valeur de paiement"; =PMT(3.6%/12,240,-200000) in English Excel)
  • =VA(3,6%/12;240;-900) gives 153,816.85 (the amount you can borrow; =PV(...))
  • =VC(3%/12;120;-100) gives 13,974.14 (the accumulated savings; =FV(...))

The classic trap: rate and term must be expressed in the same unit. Monthly payments? Monthly rate and number of months. If you enter 3.6% with 240, Excel thinks you pay 3.6% a month for 240 months, and the result is absurd.

Key takeaways

  • An annuity is a series of equal, regular payments: loans, rents, savings, pensions.
  • Present value: VA = a × [1 − (1 + i)^(−n)] / i.
  • Loan repayment: a = C × i / [1 − (1 + i)^(−n)]. The capital lent equals the present value of the repayments.
  • Future value of regular saving: VF = a × [(1 + i)^n − 1] / i.
  • Perpetuity: VA = a / i.
  • The cost of the loan = total repayments − capital borrowed. It rises sharply with rate and term.
  • Always use a rate and a number of periods in the same unit.

Exercise

  1. You borrow €10,000 at 6% a year over 5 years, repaid by constant annuities (one payment a year). What is the annual payment?
  2. A couple borrows €180,000 over 20 years at 3.6% a year (proportional monthly rate). What is the monthly payment, excluding insurance? What is the total cost of the loan?
  3. You can repay €500 a month for 10 years. The rate is 4% a year (proportional monthly rate). How much can you borrow?
  4. You save €200 a month for 20 years at 3% a year (0.25% a month). How much will you have at the end? What share comes from interest?
  5. Food for thought: extending a loan from 20 to 25 years lowers the monthly payment. Why is that both good news and bad news for the borrower?
Answers (try first!)
  1. a = 10,000 × 0.06 / (1 − 1.06⁻⁵) = 10,000 × 0.06 / 0.25274 = €2,373.96 a year. Over 5 years, you repay €11,869.82, i.e. €1,869.82 of interest.
  2. Monthly rate: 0.3%, n = 240. a = 180,000 × 0.003 / (1 − 1.003⁻²⁴⁰) = €1,053.20 a month. Total paid: 1,053.20 × 240 = €252,768.15. Cost of the loan: €72,768.15 (exactly 90% of Camille's figures, since the capital is 90% of €200,000).
  3. VA = 500 × (1 − (1 + 0.04/12)⁻¹²⁰) / (0.04/12) = €49,385.09. You will repay €60,000 in total for about €49,400 borrowed.
  4. VF = 200 × (1.0025²⁴⁰ − 1) / 0.0025 = €65,660.40. You paid in 200 × 240 = €48,000, so €17,660.40 comes from interest, more than a quarter of the total.
  5. Good news: the monthly payment falls (for €200,000 at 3.6%, from €1,170 to €1,012), which eases the monthly budget and sometimes lets you borrow more. Bad news: you pay for longer, so the total cost climbs (1,012.01 × 300 − 200,000 ≈ €103,600 of interest, against about €80,900 over 20 years). In practice, rates offered over 25 years are also often a little higher. It is all a trade-off between cash comfort today and total cost.

Next lesson: building an amortisation schedule, or how each monthly payment is split between interest and repayment of capital.

6.html:
Where does your monthly payment really go?

Yesterday you calculated Camille's monthly payment: €1,170.22 a month for 20 years for €200,000 borrowed at 3.6%. But one question remains open: each month, how much of that €1,170.22 actually pays off the debt, and how much goes on interest?

The answer surprises almost everyone. And you can read it in a document the bank must hand over with the loan offer: the amortisation schedule (repayment table). Knowing how to build and read it is useful for you (renegotiating a loan, repaying early) and essential in a company, where every loan shows up in the balance sheet and the income statement, as you will see from module 2.

The principle: interest first, capital next

Each instalment (annual or monthly) breaks down into two pieces:

  • Interest: the bank's payment for the period. It is calculated on the outstanding capital (what you still owe) at the start of the period.
  • Amortisation: the part that actually repays the capital. Careful: in finance, "amortising a loan" means "repaying the capital", nothing to do with depreciating a machine in accounting.

Interest for the period = outstanding capital at start of period × rate

Instalment = interest + amortisation

Outstanding capital at end of period = capital at start of period − amortisation

These three lines are enough to build any amortisation schedule. You apply them period after period, until the outstanding capital falls to zero.

Method 1: constant annuities

This is the lesson 5 method, and the one used for almost all personal loans: the instalment is the same from start to finish.

Example: a (fictional) SME borrows €10,000 at 6% a year over 4 years, repaid in constant annuities. Annual payment: a = 10,000 × 0.06 / (1 − 1.06⁻⁴) = €2,885.91.

YearOpening capitalInterest (6%)AmortisationAnnual paymentClosing capital
110,000.00600.002,285.912,885.917,714.09
27,714.09462.852,423.072,885.915,291.02
35,291.02317.462,568.452,885.912,722.56
42,722.56163.352,722.562,885.910.00
Total1,543.6610,000.0011,543.66

(Amounts are rounded to the cent, hence sometimes a one-cent difference in the totals.)

How to fill in row 1: interest = 10,000 × 6% = €600. Amortisation = 2,885.91 − 600 = €2,285.91. Closing capital = 10,000 − 2,285.91 = €7,714.09. And you start again with €7,714.09 in row 2.

Look at the columns: interest decreases (outstanding capital falls) and amortisation increases by the same amount, since the annual payment does not move. The two checks to always do: the sum of amortisation equals the capital borrowed, and the outstanding capital ends at zero.

The mortgage shock

Back to Camille (€200,000 at 3.6% over 240 months, monthly payment €1,170.22, monthly rate 0.3%):

MonthOpening capitalInterestAmortisationClosing capital
1200,000.00600.00570.22199,429.78
2199,429.78598.29571.93198,857.84
3198,857.84596.57573.65198,284.19
...............
120118,596.43355.79814.43117,781.99
...............
2401,166.723.501,166.720.00

In the first month, more than half of the payment goes on interest. Over the first year, Camille pays about €7,086 of interest and only repays about €6,957 of capital. And after 10 years, half the term, she still owes €117,782, nearly 59% of the starting capital. It is mechanical: at the start the outstanding capital is high, so the interest is too.

Finding the outstanding capital without the whole table

Tip: the outstanding capital after k instalments is the present value of the remaining instalments (lesson 5).

Outstanding capital after k instalments = a × [1 − (1 + i)^(−(n − k))] / i

For Camille after 120 months: 1,170.22 × (1 − 1.003⁻¹²⁰) / 0.003 = €117,781.99. The same figure as the table, without 120 rows of calculation. It is the amount to repay if she sells her flat at that point.

Method 2: constant amortisation

Here it is the share of capital repaid that is fixed: capital / number of periods. Interest falls, so the instalment decreases over time. A common method for business loans.

Same loan: €10,000 at 6% over 4 years, amortisation of 10,000 / 4 = €2,500 a year.

YearOpening capitalInterestAmortisationAnnual paymentClosing capital
110,0006002,5003,1007,500
27,5004502,5002,9505,000
35,0003002,5002,8002,500
42,5001502,5002,6500
Total1,50010,00011,500

Total interest: €1,500, a little less than with constant annuities (€1,543.66), because capital is repaid faster at the start. On the other hand, the first instalment is heavier (€3,100 against €2,885.91): you need the cash to pay it.

Method 3: bullet repayment (in fine)

You pay only interest for the whole term, and repay all the capital at the end.

YearOpening capitalInterestAmortisationAnnual payment
110,0006000600
210,0006000600
310,0006000600
410,00060010,00010,600

Total interest: 4 × 600 = €2,400, the highest of the three, because the full capital remains owed to the very end. Why choose it? Because the intermediate instalments are very light. It is exactly the logic of bonds: when a large company such as TotalEnergies or LVMH borrows on the markets, it pays a coupon each year and repays the capital at maturity. Often, it refinances this repayment with a new issue. We will come back to this in module 5.

What this changes in practice

  • Repaying early is all the more worthwhile the earlier you do it: interest weighs most at the start of a loan. Careful, the bank may charge early repayment penalties (in France these are capped by law; check the contract and the rules in force).
  • Borrower insurance is added to the monthly payment. Depending on the contract, it is calculated on the initial capital (fixed amount) or on the outstanding capital (decreasing amount). For example, a (fictional) insurance at 0.30% a year of the initial capital costs €50 a month, i.e. €12,000 over 20 years for Camille. It is included in the TAEG (APR, lesson 4).
  • In accounting, only the "interest" part is an expense (a cost that reduces profit). Repayment of capital reduces a debt on the balance sheet. Keep this distinction in mind: you will meet it again from lesson 7.

Key takeaways

  • Each instalment = interest (outstanding capital × rate) + amortisation (repayment of capital).
  • Constant annuities: fixed instalment, decreasing interest, increasing amortisation. Standard for personal loans.
  • Constant amortisation: fixed capital repayment, decreasing instalments, slightly less interest in total.
  • Bullet (in fine): interest only, then all the capital at the end. The most expensive in interest, the lightest on cash. It is the bond model.
  • Outstanding capital = present value of the remaining instalments.
  • Checks: sum of amortisation = capital borrowed, and outstanding capital ends at zero.

Exercise

  1. Build the amortisation schedule for a loan of €6,000 at 5% a year over 3 years, with constant annuities. What is the total interest?
  2. Same loan, with constant amortisation. Build the table and calculate the total interest.
  3. Same loan, repaid as a bullet. How much interest in total?
  4. A loan of €20,000 at 4% a year over 5 years is repaid in constant annuities. What is the outstanding capital just after the 2nd annual payment?
  5. Food for thought: why would a start-up that has just launched its product prefer a bullet repayment, even though it is the option that costs the most interest?
Answers (try first!)
  1. Annual payment: 6,000 × 0.05 / (1 − 1.05⁻³) = €2,203.25. Year 1: interest 300.00, amortisation 1,903.25, closing capital 4,096.75. Year 2: interest 204.84, amortisation 1,998.41, closing capital 2,098.33. Year 3: interest 104.92, amortisation 2,098.33, closing capital 0. Total interest: €609.75 (check: 3 × 2,203.25 − 6,000 = 609.75).
  2. Amortisation: €2,000 a year. Year 1: interest 300, payment 2,300. Year 2: interest 200, payment 2,200. Year 3: interest 100, payment 2,100. Total interest: €600.
  3. 3 × 6,000 × 5% = €900 of interest, plus €6,000 of capital to repay at the end of year 3 (last instalment: €6,300).
  4. Annual payment: 20,000 × 0.04 / (1 − 1.04⁻⁵) = €4,492.54. After 2 payments, 3 remain: 4,492.54 × (1 − 1.04⁻³) / 0.04 = €12,467.21. (You can check by building the first two rows of the table: you get the same figure.)
  5. Because at the start, the start-up generates little or no cash: it needs to keep its cash to develop its business. A bullet lets it pay only interest during this phase, and repay the capital later, once the business has taken off (or by refinancing). It pays more interest, but it buys time and cash. The risk: if the business does not take off, the final instalment may become impossible to pay. This is the cost / cash trade-off from lesson 5 again.

Next lesson: we open module 2 with the three financial statements (balance sheet, income statement, cash flow statement) and how they fit together.

7.html:
Learning to read the language of companies

So far we have talked about rates, discounting and loans: the mathematical tools. With this second module, we change ground. We are going to learn to read a company's accounts, the way a doctor reads a blood test.

Every year, every company publishes (or at least produces) three main documents: the balance sheet (bilan), the income statement (compte de résultat, also called the profit and loss account) and the cash flow statement (tableau des flux de trésorerie). Taken separately, each tells part of the story. Together, they tell it all. Above all, they are linked to each other in precise ways: that is what we will see today, before going through them one by one in lessons 8 to 12.

The three financial statements in one sentence each

1. The balance sheet: the snapshot

The balance sheet shows what the company owns (its assets) and how this is financed (its liabilities: equity and debts), at a given date, usually 31 December. It is a snapshot: it describes a situation, a stock, at a precise moment.

Assets = Equity + Debts

Remember lesson 1: assets are the investment decision (where the money goes); liabilities are the financing decision (where the money comes from).

2. The income statement: the film of performance

The income statement traces what the company has earned (its income, first of all revenue) and what it has consumed (its expenses) during the year. The difference is the result: profit or loss.

Net profit = Income − Expenses

It is a film: it tells a flow, what happened between two snapshots.

3. The cash flow statement: the film of cash

It explains how cash (the money actually available in the bank) moved from its level at the start of the year to its level at the end, distinguishing three sources: operating activities, investing and financing.

Change in cash = Operating cash flow + Investing cash flow + Financing cash flow

It is also a film, but shot with a different camera: it is only interested in the euros that really go into and out of the bank account.

How they fit together

Here is the picture to keep in mind: two snapshots (the opening balance sheet and the closing balance sheet), and two films that explain what happened in between.

LinkWhat happens
Income statement → balance sheetThe year's net profit is added to equity. Closing equity = opening equity + net profit − dividends paid.
Cash flows → balance sheetYear-end cash (in the balance sheet) = opening cash + change calculated in the cash flow statement.
Income statement → cash flowsThe cash flow statement often starts from net profit, then adjusts it for everything that is not cash (depreciation, payment timing differences).

These links are no coincidence: they follow from double-entry bookkeeping, where every transaction is recorded twice (where it comes from, where it goes). Practical consequence: if in an exercise your closing balance sheet does not balance, one of the links has been forgotten.

A complete example: Atelier Lumen

Atelier Lumen (a fictional company) makes lamps in Brittany. Let's follow a complete year.

Starting snapshot: the balance sheet at 31/12/Y−1

AssetsAmountLiabilitiesAmount
Machines€50,000Equity€50,000
Inventory€10,000Bank loan€20,000
Trade receivables€5,000Trade payables€10,000
Cash€15,000
Total€80,000Total€80,000

The film of performance: the income statement for year Y

ItemAmount
Revenue€120,000
Materials consumed− €60,000
Wages and social charges− €30,000
Other expenses (rent, energy...)− €8,000
Depreciation charge− €10,000
Loan interest− €1,000
Profit before tax€11,000
Corporation tax (25%)− €2,750
Net profit€8,250

The depreciation charge (dotation aux amortissements) reflects the wear on the machines: they lose €10,000 of value during the year. It is an expense, but not a single euro leaves the bank account to pay it. Keep that in mind. (The 25% corporation tax rate (IS) is in line with the standard rate in France in recent years; there is a reduced rate for small businesses, and these rates change.)

During the year, other things also happened that do not affect profit: Lumen bought a new machine for €15,000, repaid €5,000 of loan capital (lesson 6: repaying loan capital is not an expense) and paid €3,000 in dividends. Its inventory rose to €12,000, its trade receivables to €9,000 (some customers pay late) and its trade payables to €11,000.

The film of cash: the cash flow statement

FlowAmount
Net profit€8,250
+ Depreciation (expense with no cash outflow)+ €10,000
− Increase in inventory− €2,000
− Increase in trade receivables− €4,000
+ Increase in trade payables+ €1,000
Operating cash flow€13,250
Purchase of the machine− €15,000
Investing cash flow− €15,000
Loan repayment− €5,000
Dividends paid− €3,000
Financing cash flow− €8,000
Change in cash− €9,750

Don't worry if not every line is clear yet: we will take this table apart in lesson 11. For now, remember the result: Lumen earned €8,250 but its cash fell by €9,750.

Closing snapshot: the balance sheet at 31/12/Y

AssetsAmountLiabilitiesAmount
Machines (50,000 + 15,000 − 10,000)€55,000Equity (50,000 + 8,250 − 3,000)€55,250
Inventory€12,000Bank loan (20,000 − 5,000)€15,000
Trade receivables€9,000Trade payables€11,000
Cash (15,000 − 9,750)€5,250
Total€81,250Total€81,250

The balance sheet balances. And you can see every link at work: net profit has fed equity, the change in cash explains the new bank balance, depreciation has reduced the value of the machines.

Where to find these documents?

  • Listed companies (such as those in the CAC 40, the Paris stock market's flagship index) publish their consolidated accounts (the whole group, subsidiaries included) under the international IFRS standards, in their annual report or universal registration document, available on their website.
  • French SMEs prepare their accounts under the Plan comptable général (PCG, the French general chart of accounts) and must in principle file them with the commercial court registry (greffe du tribunal de commerce). Some small companies can ask for all or part of their accounts to be kept confidential.

Presentations vary a little depending on the standards (IFRS uses the terms balance sheet, income statement and cash flow statement), but the logic of the three statements and their links is universal.

Key takeaways

  • Balance sheet = snapshot at a date: what the company owns (assets) and how it is financed (liabilities). Assets = equity + debts.
  • Income statement = film of the year: income − expenses = net profit.
  • Cash flow statement = film of cash: operating + investing + financing = change in cash.
  • Net profit (minus dividends) increases equity.
  • The change in cash links the cash in the opening balance sheet to the cash in the closing one.
  • A company can be profitable and lose cash (and vice versa): profit and cash are two different things.

Exercise

  1. In which financial statement do you mainly find each of these items? a) revenue; b) inventory at 31 December; c) the purchase of a lorry paid in cash; d) the amount of the loan still outstanding; e) the year's wages.
  2. A company has €100,000 of equity on 1 January. It makes a net profit of €12,000 and pays €5,000 in dividends. What is its equity at 31 December?
  3. A company's cash is €20,000 on 1 January. Operating cash flow: + €30,000. Investing cash flow: − €45,000. Financing cash flow: + €10,000. What is cash at 31 December?
  4. Go back to Atelier Lumen. Imagine customers had paid as quickly as last year, so that trade receivables stay at €5,000. What happens to operating cash flow and year-end cash? Does net profit change?
  5. Food for thought: why could an investor who only looked at the income statement be wrong about a company's health?
Answers (try first!)
  1. a) Income statement. b) Balance sheet (assets). c) Cash flow statement (investing cash flow), and the lorry then appears in the balance sheet assets. d) Balance sheet (liabilities, debts). e) Income statement (expenses).
  2. 100,000 + 12,000 − 5,000 = €107,000.
  3. 20,000 + 30,000 − 45,000 + 10,000 = €15,000.
  4. The increase in receivables disappears: operating cash flow becomes 8,250 + 10,000 − 2,000 + 1,000 = €17,250. Change in cash: 17,250 − 15,000 − 8,000 = − €5,750, so closing cash = €9,250 (instead of €5,250). Net profit does not change (€8,250): the sales are the same, only the date of payment has changed. Four thousand euros of late customer payments means four thousand euros less cash.
  5. Because profit does not tell you whether the money has actually come in, nor what the company had to spend to invest or repay its debts. A company can be profitable on paper but short of cash (customers paying late, big investments, heavy debt), and a company short of cash can go bankrupt even with profits. You have to read the three statements together: the income statement (profitability), the balance sheet (assets and debt) and the cash flows (cash).

Next lesson: the balance sheet in detail, assets, liabilities and equity.

8.html:
The company's family photo

Yesterday you saw that the balance sheet is a snapshot: what the company owns and how it financed it, at a precise date. Today we zoom in on that snapshot. When a banker decides to lend, when an investor looks at an SME to buy, when a supplier wonders whether they will be paid, the balance sheet is often the first thing they open.

Good news: the logic fits in one line, and you already know it.

Assets = Liabilities, in other words Uses = Sources

On the left, what the company has done with the money. On the right, where that money comes from.

The two sides are always equal, by construction: every euro used somewhere (in assets) must have been provided by someone (in liabilities).

Assets: what the company owns

In the French presentation (Plan comptable général), assets are listed in order of increasing liquidity: first what stays in the company for a long time, then what turns into cash quickly, and cash itself at the very bottom.

Fixed assets: what stays

These are assets intended to be used long term, more than a year.

  • Intangible assets: what you cannot touch. Patents, software, purchased brands, goodwill (fonds de commerce).
  • Tangible assets: land, buildings, machines, vehicles, computers.
  • Financial assets: stakes in other companies, loans granted, guarantee deposits (for example the deposit paid to rent offices).

Current assets: what circulates

These are items linked to the operating cycle, constantly renewed.

  • Inventory: raw materials, work in progress, finished goods, merchandise.
  • Trade receivables: what customers still owe (sales made but not yet collected).
  • Other receivables: for example VAT to be recovered.
  • Marketable securities: short-term cash investments.
  • Cash at bank and in hand (disponibilités): the money in the bank and in the till. This is cash.

Gross, depreciation, net

A machine wears out. Each year, accounting records this wear as depreciation (an expense, as you saw with Atelier Lumen). The balance sheet therefore shows three columns:

Net value = Gross value (purchase price) − Accumulated depreciation

Example: a machine bought for €60,000 and depreciated on a straight-line basis over 5 years loses 60,000 / 5 = €12,000 a year. After 3 years, it appears on the balance sheet at 60,000 − 3 × 12,000 = €24,000 net. Careful: that is not necessarily its resale price. It is a book value, based on historical cost.

Inventory and receivables can also be written down (impaired): stock that can no longer be sold, a bankrupt customer who will never pay. The principle is the same: show the realistic value.

Liabilities: where the money comes from

Liabilities are listed in order of increasing urgency (how soon they fall due): first the money that never has to be repaid on a fixed date, then debts, from the most distant to the most urgent.

Equity: the owners' money

  • Share capital: what the shareholders (or partners) contributed when the company was set up and in capital increases.
  • Reserves: past years' profits that the company kept instead of distributing them.
  • Retained earnings carried forward (report à nouveau): a small holding account for profits (or losses) not yet allocated.
  • Profit for the year: the year's profit (or loss), which comes from the income statement (link seen yesterday).

Equity is also what would be left for the shareholders if all the assets were sold at book value and all the debts repaid:

Equity = Total assets − Debts (also called net assets)

Provisions

Provisions for risks and charges correspond to expenses that are probable but whose amount or timing is uncertain: an ongoing lawsuit, warranties given to customers, an announced restructuring. The prudence principle requires them to be recorded as soon as they are probable.

Debts

  • Financial debts: bank loans, bonds, overdrafts. They cost interest.
  • Trade payables: purchases received but not yet paid for.
  • Tax and social security liabilities: VAT to pay over, corporation tax, wages and social contributions (paid to URSSAF, the French social security collection body) owed.

Trade, tax and social liabilities do not cost interest: they are free credit arising from the business. We will see in lesson 12 that they play a key role in financing day-to-day operations.

A complete balance sheet

Here is the simplified balance sheet of Biscuiterie du Mont-Blanc, a fictional SME, at 31 December:

AssetsGrossDepr.Net
Intangible assets20,0008,00012,000
Tangible assets400,000150,000250,000
Financial assets18,000018,000
Fixed assets280,000
Inventory60,000
Trade receivables90,000
Other receivables10,000
Cash40,000
Current assets200,000
Total assets480,000
LiabilitiesAmount
Share capital100,000
Reserves120,000
Profit for the year30,000
Equity250,000
Provisions for risks and charges10,000
Bank loans120,000
Trade payables70,000
Tax and social security liabilities30,000
Total liabilities480,000

(Amounts in euros.)

What you can already draw from it, at a glance:

  • Equity finances about 52% of assets (250,000 / 480,000). The company is fairly solid, not over-indebted.
  • The machines and buildings are 37.5% depreciated (150,000 / 400,000): they are not new, so investment will be needed in the coming years.
  • Customers owe €90,000, more than the cash available: keep an eye on payment terms (lesson 16).

You will learn to turn these intuitions into precise ratios in module 3.

The limits of the snapshot

  • It is a snapshot of a single day. A balance sheet at 31 December can be flattering (low inventory after Christmas, inflated cash). You need to compare several years.
  • Historical cost: land bought 30 years ago appears at its purchase price, not at its current value.
  • Invisible assets: an internally created brand, reputation, the talent of the teams do not appear (or barely) on the balance sheet. That is why a luxury or technology company is often worth much more on the stock market than its book equity.
  • Equity can become negative if accumulated losses exceed contributions: debts then exceed the book value of assets. It is a serious warning sign (French law actually requires specific steps when equity falls below half of share capital).

Key takeaways

  • Assets = Liabilities: what the company has done with the money = where it comes from.
  • Assets are split into fixed assets (long term: intangible, tangible, financial) and current assets (inventory, receivables, cash).
  • Liabilities include equity (capital, reserves, profit), provisions and debts (financial and operating).
  • Net value = gross value − depreciation (or impairment).
  • Equity = Assets − Debts: it is the book value belonging to the shareholders.
  • The balance sheet is a book, historical value, not a market value.

Exercise

  1. Put each item on the assets or liabilities side, and specify the heading: a) a purchased patent; b) the stock of flour; c) contributions owed to URSSAF; d) share capital; e) a 5-year bank loan; f) a customer invoice not yet paid.
  2. A lorry is bought for €45,000 and depreciated on a straight-line basis over 5 years. What is its net book value after 2 years?
  3. A company shows: net fixed assets €150,000, inventory €30,000, trade receivables €25,000, cash €15,000, loans €80,000, trade payables €35,000, tax and social liabilities €15,000. Calculate total assets and equity. If share capital is €50,000 and reserves €28,000, what is the profit for the year?
  4. A company has total assets of €500,000 and €560,000 of debts. What are its net assets worth? What does that mean?
  5. Food for thought: why can a large French luxury house be worth several times its book equity on the stock market?
Answers (try first!)
  1. a) Assets, intangible assets. b) Assets, current assets (inventory). c) Liabilities, tax and social security liabilities. d) Liabilities, equity. e) Liabilities, financial debts. f) Assets, current assets (trade receivables).
  2. Annual depreciation: 45,000 / 5 = €9,000. After 2 years: 45,000 − 2 × 9,000 = €27,000.
  3. Total assets: 150,000 + 30,000 + 25,000 + 15,000 = €220,000. Debts: 80,000 + 35,000 + 15,000 = €130,000. Equity: 220,000 − 130,000 = €90,000. Profit for the year: 90,000 − 50,000 − 28,000 = €12,000.
  4. Net assets = 500,000 − 560,000 = − €60,000. Equity is negative: even by selling all the assets at book value, the company could not repay all its debts. Past losses have "eaten up" the shareholders' contribution. Lenders are exposed, and the shareholders will probably have to put money back in (recapitalise) for the company to carry on.
  5. Because the balance sheet records assets at historical cost and ignores most internally created assets: the brand, built over decades, the craftspeople's know-how, the loyal customer base, the power to set high prices. Investors, however, pay for the future cash flows these invisible assets will generate (lesson 3: value is discounted future cash flows). Market value looks to the future, book value to the past.

Next lesson: the income statement, from revenue to net profit.

9.html:
How much did the company really earn?

"Revenue grew by 8%", "the operating margin is down", "net profit attributable to the group is up": when a company publishes its accounts, the business press talks of nothing else. All these figures come from a single document, the income statement.

Yesterday, the balance sheet was the snapshot. Today we watch the film of the year: everything the company sold, everything it consumed to get there, and what is left at the end for the shareholders. We are going to go down this document line by line, from the top (revenue) to the bottom (net profit). That is why English speakers talk about the top line and the bottom line.

Income and expenses: two words to understand properly

  • Income (produit) is an enrichment of the company during the year: mainly sales (revenue), but also interest received, a grant, the sale price of an old machine.
  • An expense (charge) is an impoverishment linked to the year's activity: materials consumed, wages, rent, wear on machines (depreciation), interest paid, taxes.

Net profit = Total income − Total expenses

The key point: income and expenses are not money coming in and going out. Accounting attaches each item of income and each expense to the year it relates to, whenever the money moves. This is the accruals principle (indépendance des exercices). A few examples:

  • A sale invoiced on 20 December and paid in February counts in December's revenue.
  • A machine bought for €60,000 is not an expense in the year of purchase: it is an investment (on the balance sheet). Only its annual wear, depreciation, is expensed.
  • Repaying the capital of a loan is not an expense (lesson 6). Only the interest is.
  • Dividends are not an expense: they are a distribution of profit, after the fact.

One last detail: revenue is always excluding tax. The VAT collected from customers belongs to the State; the company merely collects it.

The three tiers of the income statement

The Plan comptable général classifies income and expenses into three categories, giving three "sub-results".

1. Operating: the core business

Everything that belongs to normal activity: selling, producing, paying staff, running the machines.

Operating profit = Operating income − Operating expenses

This is the figure that tells you whether the company's business is profitable, regardless of how it is financed. In English it is called operating income or, with a few nuances, EBIT (earnings before interest and taxes).

2. Financial: the cost of money

Interest paid on loans (financial expenses), interest received on investments (financial income), foreign exchange gains or losses.

Profit on ordinary activities before tax (RCAI) = Operating profit + Financial result

3. Exceptional: what does not recur

Under French standards, unusual transactions are isolated: the sale of a building, a fine, an insured loss, a litigation settlement. They are set apart so that they do not cloud the reading of normal performance. (Under IFRS, used by listed groups, this "exceptional" heading does not formally exist, but companies often present a "recurring" or "adjusted" result in the same spirit.)

Finally, corporation tax (and, where applicable, employee profit-sharing) is deducted to get net profit.

Example: Biscuiterie du Mont-Blanc

Let's go back to the fictional SME from lesson 8. Its balance sheet showed a profit for the year of €30,000. Here is where it comes from:

ItemAmount (€)
Revenue (biscuit sales)900,000
Change in finished goods inventory (biscuits made, not yet sold)5,000
Operating income905,000
Materials consumed (flour, butter, sugar, packaging)− 300,000
Other purchases and external expenses (energy, rent, transport, advertising)− 150,000
Taxes and duties (excluding corporation tax)− 15,000
Wages− 250,000
Social charges− 100,000
Depreciation and provisions− 47,000
Operating profit43,000
Financial income1,000
Financial expenses (loan interest)− 6,000
Financial result− 5,000
Profit on ordinary activities before tax38,000
Proceeds from the sale of an old machine6,000
Net book value of the machine sold− 4,000
Exceptional result2,000
Corporation tax (25% of 40,000)− 10,000
Net profit30,000

To keep things simple, a single rate of 25% has been applied, in line with the standard rate in France in recent years. In reality, SMEs benefit from a reduced rate on a first slice of profit, and rates and thresholds change: always check the rules in force.

What you can read in this table

  • The business is profitable, but with thin margins: operating profit represents 43,000 / 900,000 = 4.8% of revenue. Out of €100 of biscuits sold, €4.80 is left after paying for materials, staff, expenses and wear on the machines.
  • Staff is the biggest item: €350,000 (wages + social charges), nearly 39% of revenue. Typical of a manufacturing business.
  • Debt costs little: €6,000 of interest for €120,000 of loans on the balance sheet, about 5%.
  • Net margin is 30,000 / 900,000 = 3.3%.

Net margin = Net profit / Revenue

A 3% net margin can be very respectable in food manufacturing or mass retail, and disappointing in luxury goods or software, where the best companies post much higher margins. Always compare a margin with others in the same sector.

Two possible presentations

The presentation above is called by nature: expenses are classified according to what they are (purchases, wages, depreciation). It is the standard for statutory accounts in France.

Many large listed groups present their income statement by function: cost of sales, selling expenses, administrative expenses, research and development expenses. Wages are then spread across these functions (a factory worker in cost of sales, a salesperson in selling expenses). The final profit is the same; only the presentation changes. When you open the annual report of a CAC 40 company (lesson 18), you will often come across this presentation.

Key takeaways

  • The income statement measures the year's performance: income − expenses = net profit.
  • Income and expenses are not cash receipts and payments: they are attached to the year they relate to.
  • Not expenses: buying a fixed asset, repaying loan capital, dividends.
  • Three tiers: operating (the business), financial (the cost of debt), exceptional (non-recurring), then tax.
  • Revenue is always excluding tax.
  • Net margin = net profit / revenue, to be compared within the same sector.

Exercise

  1. For each transaction, say whether it is an expense of the year and, if so, of which type (operating, financial, exceptional): a) buying a machine for €50,000; b) December's rent, paid in January; c) the depreciation charge on the computers; d) repaying €10,000 of loan capital; e) €3,000 of interest on that loan; f) paying dividends.
  2. A company shows: revenue €500,000; materials consumed €200,000; external expenses €80,000; taxes and duties €10,000; staff costs €150,000; depreciation €20,000; financial income €2,000; financial expenses €12,000. No exceptional items. Corporation tax: 25%. Calculate operating profit, RCAI (profit before tax), tax, net profit and net margin.
  3. A company sends a customer an invoice for €12,000 including tax, with 20% VAT. How much does it add to its revenue?
  4. A lorry bought a few years ago has a net book value of €18,000. The company sells it for €15,000. What is the impact on the exceptional result?
  5. Food for thought: why is an analyst more interested in operating profit than net profit when judging the quality of a company?
Answers (try first!)
  1. a) Not an expense: it is an investment, recorded in balance sheet assets. b) Operating expense of the year (December), even though it is paid in January. c) Operating expense (depreciation charge). d) Not an expense: a debt on the balance sheet is reduced. e) Financial expense. f) Not an expense: it is a distribution of profit to shareholders.
  2. Operating profit: 500,000 − 200,000 − 80,000 − 10,000 − 150,000 − 20,000 = €40,000. Financial result: 2,000 − 12,000 = − €10,000. RCAI: €30,000. Tax: 25% × 30,000 = €7,500. Net profit: €22,500. Net margin: 22,500 / 500,000 = 4.5%.
  3. 12,000 / 1.20 = €10,000 of revenue. The €2,000 of VAT will be paid over to the State.
  4. 15,000 − 18,000 = − €3,000: it is a capital loss, which reduces the exceptional result (and therefore net profit). Yet the company received €15,000 in cash: another gap between profit and cash.
  5. Because operating profit measures the profitability of the business itself. Net profit is influenced by things that have nothing to do with the quality of the activity: how the company is financed (more debt = more interest), one-off events (sale of a building, litigation) and taxation. To compare two companies or follow a trend, you want a recurring, comparable figure. That is also the idea behind the intermediate management balances in the next lesson.

Next lesson: the intermediate management balances (soldes intermédiaires de gestion): trading margin, value added, EBE and EBITDA.

10.html:
Reading the income statement as a cascade

Yesterday you went down the income statement in three tiers: operating, financial, exceptional. That is useful, but still a bit rough. Between revenue and operating profit, a lot happens, and an analyst wants to know where the company makes (or loses) money.

In France, the tool for this is the intermediate management balances (soldes intermédiaires de gestion, SIG): a cascade of subtotals that starts from sales and ends at net profit, stopping at each important step. Among them are two stars you will hear about everywhere, on internships as in interviews: value added and EBE (excédent brut d'exploitation, gross operating surplus), the French cousin of EBITDA.

The SIG cascade

Here are the steps, from top to bottom. Each balance is calculated from the previous one.

BalanceCalculationWhat it measures
Trading marginSales of goods for resale − cost of goods soldWhat the resale activity brings in
Production for the yearProduction sold + stored + capitalisedWhat the company has made
Value addedTrading margin + production − purchases from third partiesThe wealth created by the company itself
EBEValue added + operating grants − taxes and duties − staff costsThe gross economic performance of the business
Operating profitEBE − depreciation and provisions (+ write-backs and other income − other expenses)The business, after wear on equipment
RCAIOperating profit + financial resultThe business, after the cost of debt
Net profitRCAI + exceptional result − employee profit-sharing − corporation taxWhat belongs to the shareholders

You have known the last three balances since yesterday. Let's focus on the first three and on EBE.

Trading margin: for resale activities

It only concerns goods for resale: what the company buys to resell as is (a bookshop, a supermarket, a wholesaler).

Trading margin = Sales of goods − Cost of goods sold

with cost of goods sold = purchases + opening stock − closing stock

Example: a (fictional) bookshop sells €400,000 worth of books. It bought €260,000 worth during the year. Its stock rose from €50,000 to €60,000: some of the purchases are still sitting on the shelves. Cost of books sold: 260,000 + 50,000 − 60,000 = €250,000. Trading margin: 400,000 − 250,000 = €150,000.

Watch out for two percentages that are often confused:

  • Markup rate (taux de marge) = margin / purchase cost = 150,000 / 250,000 = 60%.
  • Margin rate (taux de marque) = margin / selling price = 150,000 / 400,000 = 37.5%.

Same margin, two different figures depending on the base. Always ask "as a percentage of what?".

Value added: the wealth created

A company buys things from others (materials, energy, transport, subcontracting, rent), transforms them, and sells the result. The difference between what it produces and what it consumes from outside is the wealth that it has created.

Value added = Trading margin + Production for the year − Purchases from third parties

Purchases from third parties = materials consumed + other purchases and external expenses.

A small detail that matters: the sum of the value added of all the companies in a country is at the heart of the calculation of GDP. When people say the French economy "creates wealth", it is value added they are talking about.

Sharing out value added

Value added is a cake shared by everyone who contributed: employees (wages and social charges), the State (taxes and duties, corporation tax), lenders (interest), shareholders (dividends) and the company itself (what it keeps to replace its machines and grow). The debate on "sharing value" in companies, regularly in the news in France, is about exactly this cake.

EBE: analysts' favourite figure

EBE = Value added + Operating grants − Taxes and duties − Staff costs

The excédent brut d'exploitation (gross operating surplus) measures what the business brings in before three things:

  • depreciation (which depends on investment choices and accounting rules);
  • the cost of debt (which depends on how the company is financed);
  • corporation tax (which depends on the country and its tax system).

Result: it is a highly comparable indicator from one company to another, and fairly close to the cash generated by the business (we will see this tomorrow). Bankers love it: "how many years of EBE does it take to repay the debt?" is one of their favourite questions (net debt / EBE ratio, module 3).

And EBITDA?

EBITDA (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation) is the English-speaking equivalent. It is often calculated from the bottom up:

EBITDA ≈ Operating profit + Depreciation (and often provisions)

EBE and EBITDA are very close but not always identical: the treatment of certain provisions, "other income and expenses" or leases (under IFRS, most lease payments are restated, which inflates EBITDA) can create differences. And EBITDA is not defined by accounting standards: each company publishes its own, sometimes "adjusted". Always read the note explaining how it is calculated.

Application: Biscuiterie du Mont-Blanc

Let's go back to yesterday's fictional income statement. The biscuit maker makes everything it sells itself: no goods for resale, so no trading margin.

BalanceCalculationAmount (€)% of revenue
Production for the year900,000 + 5,000905,000
− Purchases from third parties300,000 + 150,000− 450,000
Value added455,00050.6%
− Taxes and duties− 15,000
− Staff costs250,000 + 100,000− 350,000
EBE90,00010.0%
− Depreciation and provisions− 47,000
Operating profit43,0004.8%

We land back on yesterday's operating profit. What the cascade tells us in addition:

  • The biscuit maker itself creates about half the value of what it sells (value added rate of 50.6%).
  • Staff absorb about 77% of value added (350,000 / 455,000). It is the main share of the cake.
  • EBE is 10% of revenue, but more than half of that EBE (47,000 out of 90,000) goes on depreciation: the business is machine-hungry. Here, with no other items, EBITDA (43,000 + 47,000) equals EBE.

Key takeaways

  • The SIG break the income statement into a cascade of balances, from revenue to net profit.
  • Trading margin = sales of goods − cost of goods sold (purchases + opening stock − closing stock).
  • Value added = production + trading margin − purchases from third parties: the wealth created by the company, shared between employees, State, lenders, shareholders and the company.
  • EBE = value added + grants − taxes and duties − staff: the performance of the business before depreciation, cost of debt and tax.
  • EBITDA ≈ operating profit + depreciation: close to EBE, but its definition varies from company to company.
  • Markup rate (on cost) ≠ margin rate (on selling price).

Exercise

  1. A (fictional) bike shop makes €250,000 of sales of goods. Its purchases for the year amount to €160,000, its opening stock to €20,000 and its closing stock to €30,000. Calculate the trading margin, the markup rate and the margin rate.
  2. A manufacturing company shows: production sold €800,000; change in finished goods stock − €10,000 (it drew on its stock of finished goods); materials consumed €320,000; external expenses €140,000; operating grants €5,000; taxes and duties €12,000; staff costs €230,000; depreciation €50,000. Calculate production for the year, value added, EBE and operating profit.
  3. For the company in question 2, what is the EBE rate (EBE / revenue, taking production sold as revenue)?
  4. Two companies A and B each have EBE of €100,000. A has €20,000 of depreciation, B has €70,000. Calculate their operating profits. What does the difference reveal?
  5. Food for thought: why should you be wary of a heavily indebted, investment-hungry company that mainly highlights its EBITDA in its communications?
Answers (try first!)
  1. Cost of goods sold: 160,000 + 20,000 − 30,000 = €150,000. Trading margin: 250,000 − 150,000 = €100,000. Markup rate: 100,000 / 150,000 = 66.7%. Margin rate: 100,000 / 250,000 = 40%.
  2. Production: 800,000 − 10,000 = €790,000. Value added: 790,000 − 320,000 − 140,000 = €330,000. EBE: 330,000 + 5,000 − 12,000 − 230,000 = €93,000. Operating profit: 93,000 − 50,000 = €43,000.
  3. 93,000 / 800,000 = 11.6%.
  4. A: 100,000 − 20,000 = €80,000. B: 100,000 − 70,000 = €30,000. Same EBE, but B wears out much more equipment: its business is more capital-intensive. To keep going, B will regularly have to replace its machines, which will eat up a large part of its EBE. For equal EBE, A is more profitable.
  5. Because EBITDA stops before exactly what weighs most on this type of company: depreciation (the cost of its heavy investments, which will need renewing) and interest (the cost of its debt). A flattering EBITDA can hide a negative net profit and melting cash. What's more, EBITDA is not standardised, and "adjusted" versions sometimes exclude very real expenses.
