Always go all the way down to net profit and look at cash flows, which is what we do tomorrow.

Next lesson: the cash flow statement, or why profit and cash are not the same thing.

11.titre: Profit et cash : les flux de trésorerie
11.html:
"Profit is an opinion, cash is a fact"

This saying does the rounds in every finance department, and you have already seen why. In lesson 7, Atelier Lumen earned €8,250 but saw its cash fall by €9,750. In lesson 9, a €3,000 capital loss came with a €15,000 cash receipt. Accounting profit and the money in the account tell two different stories.

Yet a company does not go bankrupt because its profit is negative: it goes bankrupt when it can no longer pay its employees, its suppliers or its bank. In France, a large share of business failures are linked to cash problems, including in companies that had customers and orders. Today we learn to read the document that tracks cash: the cash flow statement.

Four reasons why profit ≠ cash

  1. Expenses that do not take money out. Depreciation and provisions reduce profit, but not a single euro leaves the bank account (lesson 9).
  2. Payment timing differences. A sale counts in revenue as soon as it is invoiced, but the customer sometimes pays 60 days later. Conversely, you pay your suppliers with a delay. And inventory ties up money before it is even sold.
  3. Investments that are not expenses. A €100,000 machine takes €100,000 of cash out in one go, but only appears in profit little by little, through depreciation.
  4. Financing transactions. Borrowing brings cash in without being income; repaying capital or paying dividends takes cash out without being an expense (lessons 6 and 9).

The cash flow statement corrects precisely these four gaps.

The three families of cash flows

Change in cash = Operating cash flows + Investing cash flows + Financing cash flows

1. Operating cash flows

The cash generated by the business itself. Most companies calculate it using the indirect method: you start from net profit and adjust it.

Operating cash flow = Net profit + Depreciation and provisions (net of write-backs) − Change in WCR

The first two terms form what is called in France the capacité d'autofinancement (CAF, self-financing capacity, here in a simplified version, without gains or losses on disposals): the cash the business would generate if all customers and suppliers paid immediately.

The third term, the change in WCR (working capital requirement, BFR in French, which we will look at in depth tomorrow), captures the payment timing differences:

  • Inventory or trade receivables go up? Money is tied up: less cash.
  • Trade payables (or tax and social liabilities) go up? You pay later: more cash for now.

Simple rule: a current asset that rises consumes cash; an operating liability that rises brings cash in.

2. Investing cash flows

Purchases of fixed assets (machines, buildings, software, buying a company) as negatives; sales of fixed assets as positives. In English, investments are called capex (capital expenditure).

3. Financing cash flows

What comes from or goes back to the providers of funds: new loan (+), loan repayment (−), capital increase (+), dividends paid (−), share buybacks (−).

The direct method, to understand

You can also list cash receipts and payments directly. For example, a year's receipts from customers are found as follows:

Cash received from customers = Revenue − Increase in trade receivables

If revenue is €500,000 and trade receivables go from €40,000 to €100,000, the company has only collected 500,000 − 60,000 = €440,000. Both methods give the same total; the indirect method is simply more practical starting from published accounts.

Example: growth that drains cash

Héliotrope (a fictional company) installs solar panels for households and SMEs. Last year, demand exploded: revenue up sharply, net profit of €40,000. The boss is delighted... until he looks at his bank account.

FlowAmount (€)
Net profit40,000
+ Depreciation+ 25,000
= CAF (simplified)65,000
− Increase in inventory (panels awaiting installation)− 30,000
− Increase in trade receivables− 60,000
+ Increase in trade payables+ 20,000
Operating cash flow− 5,000
Purchase of vans and tools− 50,000
Investing cash flow− 50,000
New bank loan+ 40,000
Loan repayments− 10,000
Dividends paid− 10,000
Financing cash flow+ 20,000
Change in cash− 35,000

Cash goes from €45,000 to €10,000. What happened?

  • The business is profitable (CAF of €65,000), but growth inflated the WCR by €70,000 (30,000 + 60,000 − 20,000): more jobs in progress, more stock, more customers owing money. Result: instead of producing cash, the business consumed €5,000.
  • To keep up with demand, Héliotrope invested €50,000. It had to borrow to hold on.
  • Paying €10,000 in dividends in this context was questionable.

This is the classic trap of poorly financed growth (overtrading): the more the company sells, the more cash it needs to finance the gap between what it pays and what it collects. If the bank refuses the next loan, a profitable company can find itself insolvent (en cessation de paiements).

Free cash flow: the cash truly available

One indicator sums all this up and will become central in module 7:

Free cash flow ≈ Operating cash flow − Investments

It is the cash left once the company has financed its operations and its investments, and which is therefore available to repay lenders and reward shareholders. For Héliotrope: − 5,000 − 50,000 = − €55,000. A negative free cash flow is not necessarily serious for a growing company that is investing (many start-ups are in this situation for years), but it must be financed, and it cannot last for ever. Precise definitions vary (before or after interest, for example): we will refine them in lesson 34.

How to read a cash flow statement in 30 seconds

  • Positive, stable operating cash flow: a good sign, the business generates cash. Compare it with net profit: if it is persistently well below, ask yourself why (WCR getting out of hand?).
  • Investing cash flow: generally negative (the company invests). Compare it with depreciation: investing less than the wear means ageing.
  • Financing cash flow: positive if the company raises money, negative if it repays or rewards its shareholders. A mature company financing its dividends with debt deserves a close look.

Key takeaways

  • Profit ≠ cash: non-cash expenses, payment timing, investment and financing widen the gap.
  • Change in cash = operating + investing + financing cash flows.
  • Indirect method: operating cash flow = net profit + depreciation − change in WCR.
  • A current asset that rises (inventory, receivables) consumes cash; an operating liability that rises brings cash in.
  • Free cash flow ≈ operating cash flow − investments: the cash available for lenders and shareholders.
  • A profitable company can go bankrupt if its growth is not financed.

Exercise

  1. For each event, say whether it increases, decreases or does not change the year's cash: a) inventory increases; b) trade payables increase; c) a depreciation charge is recorded; d) an old building is sold; e) a loan is repaid; f) trade receivables decrease.
  2. A company reports net profit of €50,000 and €30,000 of depreciation. Its inventory increased by €10,000, its trade receivables decreased by €5,000 and its trade payables increased by €8,000. Calculate its operating cash flow.
  3. The same company invested €100,000 in a new production line, borrowed €60,000 and paid €20,000 in dividends. Calculate the change in cash and the free cash flow.
  4. A company makes €1,200,000 of revenue. Its trade receivables go from €150,000 to €200,000 during the year. How much did it actually collect from its customers?
  5. Food for thought: a friend starts a company whose sales double every year. He tells you: "we're profitable, the cash will follow". What do you say to him?
Answers (try first!)
  1. a) Decreases (money is tied up in stock). b) Increases (you pay later). c) No change (an expense with no cash outflow; it only reduces profit). d) Increases (positive investing cash flow). e) Decreases (negative financing cash flow). f) Increases (customers have paid part of what they owed).
  2. 50,000 + 30,000 − 10,000 + 5,000 + 8,000 = €83,000.
  3. Change in cash: 83,000 − 100,000 + 60,000 − 20,000 = + €23,000. Free cash flow: 83,000 − 100,000 = − €17,000. Cash rises only thanks to the loan: operations and investments together consumed cash.
  4. 1,200,000 − (200,000 − 150,000) = €1,150,000. €50,000 is missing compared with revenue.
  5. That profitability is not enough: when sales double, inventory and trade receivables tend to double too, and they have to be financed before being paid. WCR grows with activity and consumes cash, not to mention the investment needed to keep up. So he must forecast his cash month by month, negotiate his customer and supplier payment terms, and secure financing (loan, fundraising) before he needs it. Otherwise, he risks going bankrupt in the middle of commercial success. That is Héliotrope's story.

Next lesson: the functional balance sheet, working capital, WCR and net cash, to understand how a company finances its operating cycle.

12.html:
Three figures to judge a company's balance

Yesterday, Héliotrope found out the hard way that a profitable company can run short of cash, because its growth was inflating its WCR. Today we take this acronym seriously. We are going to reread the balance sheet from lesson 8 through different glasses, those of the functional balance sheet, to answer a simple question: is the company financing its needs with the right resources?

Three indicators are enough: working capital (fonds de roulement, FR), the working capital requirement (besoin en fonds de roulement, BFR, written WCR here) and net cash (trésorerie nette, TN). They are among the first figures a banker looks at in an SME, and this is one of the big questions from lesson 1: how to manage day-to-day operations?

Rereading the balance sheet by cycles

The accounting balance sheet (lesson 8) is ordered by liquidity and by how soon items fall due. The functional balance sheet arranges the same items according to their function in the company, in three cycles:

  • The investment and long-term financing cycle (the top of the balance sheet): stable uses (fixed assets) and the stable resources that finance them.
  • The operating cycle (the middle): inventory, trade receivables, trade payables, tax and social liabilities. It turns constantly with the rhythm of business.
  • Cash (the bottom): money available, and bank overdrafts.

Two adjustments to know:

  • Fixed assets are taken at gross value, and accumulated depreciation moves to the stable resources side. The idea: depreciation corresponds to cash the company has "set aside" through its profits (remember yesterday's CAF) to renew its equipment.
  • Bank overdrafts come out of financial debts: they are very short-term cash resources, not stable resources.

Working capital (FR or FRNG)

Working capital = Stable resources − Stable uses

Stable resources = equity + accumulated depreciation and impairment + provisions + medium- and long-term financial debts.
Stable uses = gross fixed assets.

Working capital (also called FRNG, fonds de roulement net global) is the surplus of long-term resources once investments have been financed. This surplus is available to finance the operating cycle.

The golden rule, known as the rule of financial balance: stable uses must be financed by stable resources. You don't finance a factory that will be used for 20 years with an overdraft that can be withdrawn within a month. Positive working capital means the rule is respected, with a safety margin.

The working capital requirement (WCR, BFR)

WCR = Inventory + Operating receivables − Operating liabilities

Operating liabilities = trade payables + tax and social liabilities.

WCR measures the money tied up in the operating cycle. A manufacturing company buys materials, stores them, makes things, stores them again, sells, then waits for its customer to pay. All that time, it has had to advance the money. Its suppliers, which it pays with a delay, finance part of it; the rest is the WCR.

It depends on three levers, which you will study in detail in lesson 16:

  • the storage period (the longer stock sits idle, the higher the WCR);
  • the payment period of customers (the later they pay, the higher the WCR);
  • the payment period to suppliers (the later you pay them, the lower the WCR).

In France, payment terms between businesses are in principle capped by law (around 60 days after the invoice in the general case); rules and exceptions change, so check those in force.

WCR can be negative. The typical case is mass retail: customers pay immediately at the till, stock turns over quickly, and suppliers are paid several weeks later. A (fictional) supermarket with €3,650,000 of annual revenue (€10,000 a day) and a WCR of −30 days of sales permanently has about €300,000 financed by its suppliers. The operating cycle brings in cash instead of consuming it.

Net cash (TN)

This is where everything fits together:

Net cash = Working capital − WCR

and also: Net cash = Cash assets (cash at bank, short-term investments) − Cash liabilities (overdrafts)

The two calculations must give the same result, since the balance sheet balances. It is an excellent check.

The logic: working capital is a "cushion" of long-term resources; WCR is the need it must cover. If some is left over, cash is positive. If not enough is left, the company must top up with overdrafts: net cash is negative.

SituationReading
FR > 0, WCR > 0, FR > WCR (TN > 0)Healthy situation: long-term resources finance the investments and the whole operating cycle.
FR > 0, WCR > 0, FR < WCR (TN < 0)The operating cycle is partly financed by the bank in the short term. Watch out: dependence on the banker.
FR < 0 (TN < 0 if WCR > 0)Long-term investments are financed by short-term resources. A fragile situation.
WCR < 0 (TN often > 0)The operating cycle generates resources (mass retail, some services paid in advance).

Application: Biscuiterie du Mont-Blanc

Let's go back to the fictional balance sheet from lesson 8 (amounts in euros).

UsesAmountResourcesAmount
Gross fixed assets (20,000 + 400,000 + 18,000)438,000Equity250,000
Accumulated depreciation (8,000 + 150,000)158,000
Provisions10,000
Bank loans120,000
Stable uses438,000Stable resources538,000
Inventory60,000Trade payables70,000
Trade and other receivables100,000Tax and social liabilities30,000
Cash at bank40,000Bank overdrafts0
Total638,000Total638,000
  • Working capital = 538,000 − 438,000 = €100,000.
  • WCR = (60,000 + 100,000) − (70,000 + 30,000) = €60,000.
  • Net cash = 100,000 − 60,000 = €40,000. Check: cash at bank 40,000 − overdrafts 0 = €40,000. It balances.

(The total, €638,000, is higher than in the accounting balance sheet, €480,000, because fixed assets have been put back at gross value and the €158,000 of depreciation moved to liabilities. Strictly speaking, other items such as the tax portion of liabilities should also be restated; we are simplifying here.)

The biscuit maker is in the healthy situation: its long-term resources finance its fixed assets and its WCR, with €40,000 of cash to spare. Its WCR represents about 60,000 / 900,000 × 365 ≈ 24 days of revenue. Expressing WCR in days of revenue lets you compare from one year to the next, and forecast: if revenue rises by 10%, WCR should rise by roughly as much, which will consume cash (that is the "change in WCR" in yesterday's cash flow statement).

Key takeaways

  • The functional balance sheet classifies items by cycle: investment and long-term financing, operations, cash.
  • Working capital = stable resources − stable uses: the surplus of long-term financing.
  • WCR = inventory + operating receivables − operating liabilities: the money tied up in the operating cycle.
  • Net cash = FR − WCR = cash assets − cash liabilities.
  • Rule of financial balance: finance the long term with long-term resources.
  • WCR grows with activity; it can be negative when customers pay before suppliers are paid (mass retail).

Exercise

A (fictional) SME shows the following: gross fixed assets €300,000; accumulated depreciation €100,000; equity €150,000; provisions €10,000; long-term loans €90,000; inventory €60,000; trade receivables €80,000; trade payables €60,000; tax and social liabilities €20,000; cash at bank €5,000; bank overdraft €15,000.

  1. Calculate stable resources, stable uses and working capital.
  2. Calculate WCR, then net cash using both methods.
  3. This SME makes €730,000 of revenue. Express its WCR in days of revenue. How do you interpret its situation?
  4. Another company has a WCR equal to 25% of its revenue. Its revenue goes from €2m to €2.5m. By how much does its WCR increase? What is the effect on its net cash if its working capital does not change?
  5. Food for thought: a company finances the purchase of a €200,000 machine (useful life: 10 years) with its bank overdraft, "because it's quicker than a loan". Why is this dangerous?
Answers (try first!)
  1. Stable resources: 150,000 + 100,000 + 10,000 + 90,000 = €350,000. Stable uses: €300,000. Working capital: 350,000 − 300,000 = €50,000.
  2. WCR: (60,000 + 80,000) − (60,000 + 20,000) = €60,000. Net cash: 50,000 − 60,000 = − €10,000. Check: 5,000 − 15,000 = − €10,000.
  3. 60,000 / 730,000 × 365 = 30 days of revenue. Working capital is positive (the rule of financial balance is respected), but it does not cover all the WCR: the SME depends on its overdraft to finance part of its operations. Options: reduce WCR (stock, customer payment terms), or strengthen working capital (capital contribution, medium-term loan, retaining profits).
  4. WCR before: 25% × €2m = €500,000. After: 25% × €2.5m = €625,000. Increase: €125,000. If working capital does not change, net cash falls by €125,000. That is Héliotrope's mechanism: growth is paid for in cash.
  5. Because a long-term use (a machine that will be used for 10 years) is being financed with a short-term, revocable resource: the bank can reduce or cancel the overdraft at any time, and its rate is generally high. The machine, meanwhile, will only generate the cash needed to pay for itself over several years. The company risks having to repay quickly a sum it does not have. This is exactly what the rule of financial balance seeks to avoid: a medium-term loan, repaid in annual instalments (lessons 5 and 6) over the life of the machine, would be appropriate.

Next lesson: we open module 3 with profitability ratios, ROE, ROA and ROCE.

13.html:
A profit, yes, but relative to what?

Two (fictional) bakeries publish their accounts. The first, in Lyon, makes €90,000 of net profit. The second, in Bordeaux, makes €180,000. Which is the better business?

Gut answer: Bordeaux, it earns twice as much. But a piece of information is missing: how much had to be invested to obtain that profit? If the Lyon partners put in €600,000 and the Bordeaux ones €1,500,000, the calculation changes completely:

  • Lyon: 90,000 / 600,000 = 15% a year.
  • Bordeaux: 180,000 / 1,500,000 = 12% a year.

Each euro entrusted to the Lyon bakery earns more. That is the whole idea of a profitability ratio: relating a result to the resources used to obtain it. A profit on its own says nothing; a profit relative to capital becomes comparable from one company to another, from one year to the next, and with the cost of money (remember opportunity cost from lesson 1).

With this module 3, we move from reading the accounts (module 2) to analysing them. Today, the three profitability ratios every analyst calculates first: ROE, ROA and ROCE.

Our running example: Atelier Boréal

Throughout this module, we follow the same fictional company: Atelier Boréal, an SME in Lyon that makes electric bikes. Here are its simplified accounts (in millions of euros).

Income statement

Item€m
Revenue (excl. VAT)50
EBE (EBITDA)7.5
Depreciation− 2.5
Operating profit (EBIT)5
Net financial expenses− 0.5
Profit before tax4.5
Corporation tax (25%)− 1.125
Net profit3.375

Balance sheet

Assets€mLiabilities€m
Net fixed assets22Equity20
Inventory6Financial debts12
Trade receivables8Trade payables5
Cash2Other operating liabilities1
Total38Total38

You recognise the documents from lessons 8 and 9, and EBE from lesson 10. The 25% tax rate is in line with the standard rate of corporation tax in France in recent years (it changes, so always check the current rate).

ROE: profitability for the shareholder

ROE (return on equity, rentabilité des capitaux propres) = Net profit / Equity

For Atelier Boréal: 3.375 / 20 = 16.9%.

Reading: each euro the shareholders have left in the company earned them about 17 cents of profit this year. It is the ratio shareholders look at first, because it measures their profitability, after everyone else has been paid: suppliers, employees, banks, the State.

How do you judge it? Compare it with what shareholders require for the risk they take. As an order of magnitude, shareholders of a listed company often require between 8% and 12% a year (you will see how this is calculated in module 5 with the CAPM). An ROE of 17% is therefore comfortable. An ROE of 4% over a long period is a warning sign: shareholders would earn more by investing their money elsewhere, at comparable risk.

Practical note: you often use the year's average equity (opening + closing, divided by 2), especially when it has moved a lot. And in a group, you take net profit attributable to the group over equity attributable to the group, to stay consistent.

ROA: profitability of all the assets

ROA (return on assets, rentabilité des actifs) = Net profit / Total assets

For Atelier Boréal: 3.375 / 38 = 8.9%.

ROA answers the question: "with everything the company owns, how much does it earn?". It is widely used in banking, where assets are huge relative to equity: a bank ROA of around 0.5% to 1% is considered decent, whereas it would be disastrous for a manufacturer.

Its flaw: it mixes a numerator that is after interest has been paid (net profit) with a denominator that includes all assets, also financed by debt. Some analysts correct this by using EBIT in the numerator (5 / 38 = 13.2%). There is no single definition: when you read an ROA, always check how it is calculated.

ROCE: profitability of the economic engine

ROCE is financial analysts' favourite ratio, because it measures the performance of the business, regardless of how the company is financed.

ROCE (return on capital employed, rentabilité des capitaux employés) = Operating profit after tax / Capital employed

with Capital employed = Net fixed assets + WCR = Equity + Net debt

You recognise the functional balance sheet from lesson 12: capital employed is the money tied up in the production base (factories, machines) and in the operating cycle (the WCR).

For Atelier Boréal:

  • WCR = inventory + receivables − payables − other operating liabilities = 6 + 8 − 5 − 1 = 8
  • Capital employed = 22 + 8 = 30
  • Check via financing: net debt = 12 − 2 = 10, and 20 + 10 = 30. Both sides match.
  • Operating profit after tax = 5 × (1 − 0.25) = 3.75
  • ROCE = 3.75 / 30 = 12.5%

Why EBIT after tax? Because we want to know what the business really earns for all the providers of finance (shareholders and lenders), as if the company had no debt. This result is also called NOPAT (net operating profit after tax). You will meet it again in module 7 to calculate free cash flows. Some people calculate a pre-tax ROCE (here 5 / 30 = 16.7%): that is allowed, but you must say so.

The value creation test

Here is the great benefit of ROCE: you can compare it with the weighted average cost of capital (the WACC, CMPC in French, which you will calculate in lesson 31), that is, the average return required by shareholders and lenders together.

ROCE > cost of capital: the company creates value. ROCE < cost of capital: it destroys value, even if it is profitable.

If Atelier Boréal's cost of capital is 9%, its ROCE of 12.5% means it creates value: each euro invested in the business earns more than it costs. This is exactly the sentence from lesson 1 ("a profit is not necessarily value creation"), at last translated into numbers.

Comparing the three ratios

RatioFormulaPoint of viewAtelier Boréal
ROENet profit / EquityShareholders16.9%
ROANet profit / Total assetsAll assets8.9%
ROCEEBIT × (1 − t) / Capital employedThe business, all providers of finance together12.5%

Notice that ROE (16.9%) is higher than ROCE (12.5%). It is no accident: the company borrows at an after-tax cost lower than what its business earns, and the difference benefits shareholders. That is the leverage effect, and you will take it apart in lesson 17. Remember the flip side right away: a high ROE can come from an excellent business... or simply from a lot of debt. That is why you never look at ROE alone.

Classic traps

  • Comparing different sectors: a software publisher has few assets and posts very high ROCEs; an electricity producer has costly power stations and more modest ROCEs. Compare a company first with its direct competitors.
  • A single year: an exceptionally good or bad year (asset sale, impairment) distorts everything. Look at a trend over 3 to 5 years.
  • Very low or negative equity: ROE becomes huge or meaningless. This happens after big losses or massive share buybacks (lesson 33).

Key takeaways

  • A profit can only be judged by relating it to the capital used to obtain it.
  • ROE = Net profit / Equity: profitability for the shareholder, to compare with their required return.
  • ROA = Net profit / Total assets: useful for comparing asset-heavy companies such as banks. Its definition varies.
  • ROCE = EBIT × (1 − t) / (Net fixed assets + WCR): profitability of the business, independent of financing.
  • ROCE > cost of capital: value creation.
  • A high ROE can hide heavy debt: always read it alongside ROCE and debt levels.

Exercise

Pâtisseries Margaux (fictional): revenue €12m, operating profit €1.2m, financial expenses €0.2m, tax at 25%. Equity €5m, net debt €3m, total assets €11m.

  1. Calculate net profit, then ROE.
  2. Calculate ROA (net profit / total assets version).
  3. Calculate capital employed and ROCE (after tax).
  4. The company's cost of capital is estimated at 8%. Does it create value? And if its operating profit fell to €0.8m?
  5. Food for thought: a CEO is paid according to the company's ROE. What decisions could they take to push this ratio up without the company's business improving?
Answers (try first!)
  1. Profit before tax = 1.2 − 0.2 = €1.0m. Tax = €0.25m. Net profit = €0.75m. ROE = 0.75 / 5 = 15%.
  2. ROA = 0.75 / 11 = 6.8%.
  3. Capital employed = equity + net debt = 5 + 3 = €8m. NOPAT = 1.2 × 0.75 = €0.9m. ROCE = 0.9 / 8 = 11.25%.
  4. 11.25% > 8%: yes, it creates value. With operating profit of €0.8m: NOPAT = €0.6m, ROCE = 0.6 / 8 = 7.5% < 8%. The company would still be profitable (net profit of €0.45m), but it would destroy value.
  5. They could take on more debt (leverage, lesson 17), buy back shares or pay a big special dividend to reduce equity (the denominator falls), or under-invest (less depreciation in the short term, but the future is sacrificed). None of these decisions improves the business, and some increase risk. That is why boards often combine several indicators, including ROCE.

Next lesson: the DuPont decomposition. Where does shareholder profitability really come from: margins, asset turnover or debt?

14.html:
Why it matters

Yesterday you calculated Atelier Boréal's ROE: 16.9%. Very good. But a figure on its own does not say where this profitability comes from. Does the company sell its bikes with big margins? Does it generate a lot of sales from few assets? Or does it borrow heavily?

Three companies can show exactly the same ROE for completely different reasons, and with completely different risks. The DuPont decomposition is the tool that separates these three engines. It is named after the American chemicals group DuPont, where it was developed in the 1910s-1920s to steer the performance of the different divisions. A century later, it is still an analyst's first reflex when faced with an ROE.

The three-factor formula

The trick is mathematically very simple: you multiply and divide by the same quantities, revenue and total assets.

ROE = (Net profit / Revenue) × (Revenue / Total assets) × (Total assets / Equity)

ROE = Net margin × Asset turnover × Equity multiplier (accounting leverage)

If you simplify, revenue and total assets cancel out and you are left with Net profit / Equity: that is indeed ROE. But each piece tells a different story.

  • Net margin (Net profit / Revenue): how much profit on each euro sold. This is the question of prices and costs: brand power, cost control, positioning.
  • Asset turnover (Revenue / Total assets): how many euros of sales each euro of assets generates. This is the question of efficiency: well-utilised factories, fast-moving stock, few useless assets.
  • Accounting leverage (Total assets / Equity): how many assets for each euro of the shareholders'. This is the question of financing: the higher it is, the more the company uses other people's money (financial debts, but also suppliers).

Note: the product of the first two factors, margin × turnover, gives Net profit / Total assets, i.e. yesterday's ROA. So ROE = ROA × leverage. The decomposition shows in one line how debt turns the return on assets into a return for shareholders.

Application to Atelier Boréal

We take yesterday's accounts (in €m): revenue 50, net profit 3.375, total assets 38, equity 20.

FactorCalculationResult
Net margin3.375 / 506.75%
Asset turnover50 / 381.32
Accounting leverage38 / 201.9
ROE6.75% × 1.32 × 1.916.9%

Reading: Atelier Boréal earns a little under 7 cents per euro sold, makes €1.32 of sales per euro of assets, and its assets are financed roughly half by shareholders (leverage of 1.9). The profile is balanced: no extreme factor.

Comparing with a competitor

A competitor, Cycles Garonne (also fictional), sells entry-level bikes in large quantities. Its figures: revenue €80m, net profit €2.4m, total assets €32m, equity €12m.

Atelier BoréalCycles Garonne
Net margin6.75%3.0%
Asset turnover1.322.5
Accounting leverage1.92.67
ROE16.9%20.0%

Cycles Garonne has a better ROE. But look at how: a margin half as large, offset by turnover almost twice as fast and higher leverage. Its model is fragile: with a 3% margin, a small rise in battery prices or a price war can wipe out profit, and the heavier debt will amplify the shock. Atelier Boréal, on the other hand, has a safety margin.

And if Atelier Boréal raised its net margin to 8%, without changing anything else? 8% × 1.32 × 1.9 = 20%. The same ROE as Garonne, with a much sounder profile. DuPont tells you which lever to pull.

The main sector profiles

Each sector has its DuPont "signature", dictated by its business model. Here are typical profiles, as rough orders of magnitude:

SectorNet marginTurnoverLeverageMain engine
Luxury, cosmeticsHigh (often 10 to 20%)Low (less than 1)ModerateMargin, thanks to brand power
Mass retailVery low (1 to 3%)High (often 1.5 to 2.5)HighTurnover: selling huge volumes
Heavy industry, energyMediumLowMedium to highA balance, with lots of assets
BankingVariableVery low (less than 0.1)Very high (often 15 to 20)Leverage

The lesson: a 2% margin is not necessarily bad, and a turnover of 0.5 is not necessarily a problem. It all depends on the sector. A supermarket with a 2% margin, turnover of 1.875 and leverage of 4 gets 2% × 1.875 × 4 = 15% ROE, just like a luxury house with a 15% margin, turnover of 0.8 and leverage of 1.25. Two worlds, same result.

The five-factor version

Analysts often go one step further by splitting net margin into three, to isolate tax and the cost of debt:

ROE = (NP / PBT) × (PBT / EBIT) × (EBIT / Revenue) × (Revenue / Assets) × (Assets / Equity)

(NP = net profit, RN; PBT = profit before tax, RAI; equity = CP)

  • NP / PBT: the "tax burden" (1 − effective tax rate). The closer to 1, the less tax weighs.
  • PBT / EBIT: the "interest burden". If it equals 1, no interest; the lower it gets, the more debt costs.
  • EBIT / Revenue: the operating margin, the true performance of the business.

For Atelier Boréal: 3.375 / 4.5 = 0.75; 4.5 / 5 = 0.9; 5 / 50 = 10%. So ROE = 0.75 × 0.9 × 10% × 1.32 × 1.9 = 16.9%. We land on our feet, with a finer diagnosis: operating margin of 10%, interest "eats" 10% of EBIT, tax 25% of profit before tax.

Using DuPont to diagnose a change

Where DuPont is most useful is in explaining why an ROE moves from one year to the next. The reflex: calculate the three factors over two or three years, and spot the one that has changed. A fall in margin points to prices, costs, competition. A fall in turnover points to investments not yet profitable or swelling stock (lesson 16). A rise in leverage points to increased debt: ROE goes up, but so does risk (lessons 15 and 17).

A limitation to keep in mind: DuPont's "accounting" leverage (Assets / Equity) counts all debts, including suppliers. It is not exactly financial debt. For a detailed analysis of the role of debt, in lesson 17 we will use another formula, built from ROCE.

Key takeaways

  • ROE = Net margin × Asset turnover × Accounting leverage.
  • Margin measures pricing power and cost control, turnover asset efficiency, leverage the weight of external financing.
  • ROE = ROA × leverage: debt amplifies the return on assets.
  • The same ROE can hide very different risk profiles: always look at all three factors.
  • Each sector has its signature: compare a company with its direct competitors.
  • The five-factor version isolates tax, interest and operating margin.

Exercise

Société Lumen (fictional), in €m. Year 1: revenue 200, net profit 10, total assets 125, equity 50. Year 2: revenue 220, net profit 8.8, total assets 125, equity 55.

  1. Calculate the three DuPont factors and ROE for year 1.
  2. Same for year 2.
  3. Which factor mainly explains the fall in ROE? Which other factors moved?
  4. In year 2, what net margin would have been needed to keep an ROE of 20%?
  5. Food for thought: a bank shows an ROE of 10% with an ROA of 0.5%. What is its leverage? Why do regulators watch this figure closely?
Answers (try first!)
  1. Margin = 10 / 200 = 5%. Turnover = 200 / 125 = 1.6. Leverage = 125 / 50 = 2.5. ROE = 5% × 1.6 × 2.5 = 20% (check: 10 / 50 = 20%).
  2. Margin = 8.8 / 220 = 4%. Turnover = 220 / 125 = 1.76. Leverage = 125 / 55 = 2.27. ROE = 4% × 1.76 × 2.27 = 16% (check: 8.8 / 55 = 16%).
  3. Net margin fell clearly (from 5% to 4%): the company sells more but earns less on each euro (lower prices or higher costs). Turnover improved (more sales with the same assets), and leverage fell (stronger equity, so less risk). ROE falls, but the balance sheet is sounder: it is not all negative.
  4. Turnover × leverage = 1.76 × 2.27 = 4. So a margin of 20% / 4 = 5% is needed, i.e. the year 1 level.
  5. ROE = ROA × leverage, so leverage = 10% / 0.5% = 20: €20 of assets for €1 of equity. Equity represents only 5% of the balance sheet: a 5% loss on assets would be enough to wipe it out. That is why regulators impose minimum capital requirements on banks (the so-called "Basel" rules): excessive leverage makes a bank very vulnerable, and its failure can contaminate the whole system.

Next lesson: liquidity and solvency ratios. Being profitable is good; being able to pay your debts on time is vital.

15.html:
Profitable... and yet bankrupt

For two lessons we have been measuring profitability. But a company almost never dies because it is "not profitable enough". It dies because one day it cannot pay: a salary, a supplier, a loan instalment. In France, that is the very definition of cessation des paiements (insolvency): the company can no longer meet its debts as they fall due with its available assets. Remember the sentence from lesson 1: a profitable company can go bankrupt if it runs out of cash at the wrong moment.

Today, two families of ratios, two horizons:

  • Liquidity (short term): can the company pay what it owes in the coming months?
  • Solvency (long term): can the company repay all its debts, and is its level of debt reasonable?

These are the ratios your banker looks at before lending to you, and the ones they monitor afterwards.

Liquidity ratios

Back to Atelier Boréal, our fictional electric bike maker (in €m). One detail: of its €12m of financial debts, €2m must be repaid within the year (short-term debt) and €10m later.

Current assets€mCurrent liabilities (due within one year)€m
Inventory6Trade payables5
Trade receivables8Other operating liabilities1
Cash2Portion of loans due within one year2
Total16Total8

Current ratio

Current ratio (liquidité générale) = Current assets / Current liabilities

Atelier Boréal: 16 / 8 = 2.0. The assets that will turn into money within the year cover the debts payable within the year twice over. Rule of thumb: above 1 is reassuring; below, you need to understand why. It is the same message as the positive working capital in lesson 12, expressed as a ratio.

Quick ratio

Problem: inventory does not always turn into money quickly (you have to sell it first, then get paid). So it is removed for a stricter test.

Quick ratio (liquidité réduite) = (Current assets − Inventory) / Current liabilities

Atelier Boréal: (16 − 6) / 8 = 1.25. Even without selling a single extra bike, the company can pay its short-term debts by collecting from its customers. In English it is called the quick ratio or acid test.

Cash ratio

Cash ratio (liquidité immédiate) = Cash / Current liabilities

Atelier Boréal: 2 / 8 = 0.25. This ratio is almost always well below 1, and that is normal: keeping a mountain of cash that earns nothing is expensive. It becomes interesting when it drops sharply from one year to the next.

Mind the sector

These thresholds ("above 1") are not laws. A supermarket often has a current ratio below 1 without being in danger: its customers pay immediately, its stock turns over in a few weeks, and it pays its suppliers later. That is the negative WCR from lesson 12: the operating cycle brings in cash. Conversely, a machine manufacturer with a current ratio of 1.2 but idle stock can be in trouble. As always: compare with the sector and look at the trend.

Solvency ratios

Here we look at the weight of debt over time. Useful Atelier Boréal data: equity 20, balance sheet total 38, financial debts 12, cash 2, EBE 7.5, EBIT 5, net financial expenses 0.5, net profit 3.375, depreciation 2.5.

Equity ratio (financial independence)

Equity ratio (autonomie financière) = Equity / Balance sheet total

Atelier Boréal: 20 / 38 = 52.6%. More than half the assets are financed by shareholders. Below about 20%, banks start to worry about an SME, but here again it depends heavily on the sector.

Gearing (net debt)

Gearing = Net debt / Equity, with Net debt = Financial debts − Cash

Atelier Boréal: (12 − 2) / 20 = 10 / 20 = 50%. For €1 contributed by shareholders, the company owes €0.50 net to lenders. Gearing above 100% signals heavy debt for a conventional industrial company. Negative gearing means the company has more cash than debt (a "net cash" position).

Leverage: Net debt / EBE

Leverage = Net debt / EBE (in English net debt / EBITDA)

Atelier Boréal: 10 / 7.5 = 1.33. A very concrete reading: it would take about 1.3 years of EBE to repay all the net debt (if all the EBE went to it, which is theoretical). It is the favourite ratio of banks and rating agencies, because it compares debt with the company's ability to generate cash (the EBE from lesson 10). As a rough guide, below 2 is comfortable, between 2 and 3.5 is watched, above that is heavy (except for specific structures such as LBOs, lesson 37).

Interest cover

Interest cover = EBIT / Financial expenses

Atelier Boréal: 5 / 0.5 = 10. Operating profit covers interest ten times: the burden of debt is very bearable. Below 2 or 3, the slightest downturn in business can make interest hard to pay.

Repayment capacity

Repayment capacity = Financial debts / CAF

CAF (capacité d'autofinancement, self-financing capacity) is, simplifying, net profit plus non-cash expenses such as depreciation. Atelier Boréal: CAF ≈ 3.375 + 2.5 = 5.875, so 12 / 5.875 = 2.0 years. French banks often have a threshold of around 3 to 4 years for an SME.

Covenants: when ratios become contracts

These ratios are not just academic. In many loan agreements, the bank imposes covenants (financial clauses): for example "net debt must not exceed 3 times EBE". If the ratio is breached, the bank can demand early repayment or renegotiate on tougher terms.

Stress test: imagine Atelier Boréal's EBE is halved (crisis, rise in battery prices), to €3.75m, with the same net debt. Leverage rises to 10 / 3.75 = 2.67. Still under a covenant of 3, but the safety margin has melted away. That is what a good analyst does: they don't just look at the ratio, they ask what it would become in a bad year.

Summary for Atelier Boréal

RatioValueDiagnosis
Current ratio2.0Comfortable
Quick ratio1.25Good
Cash ratio0.25Normal
Equity ratio52.6%Solid
Gearing50%Moderate
Net debt / EBE1.33Comfortable
Interest cover10Very good

Verdict: Atelier Boréal is both profitable (lessons 13 and 14) and solid. It even has room to borrow more if a good project comes along, which is handy: you will see in lesson 17 that debt can boost ROE.

Key takeaways

  • Liquidity looks at the short term (paying within the year), solvency at the long term (repaying all debts).
  • Current ratio = Current assets / Current liabilities; the quick version removes inventory.
  • Gearing = Net debt / Equity; Equity ratio = Equity / Balance sheet total.
  • Net debt / EBE: the number of years of EBE needed to repay the debt, a key bank ratio.
  • EBIT / Financial expenses: the ability to pay interest.
  • Thresholds are guides, not laws: compare with the sector, look at the trend and test a bad year.

Exercise

Transports Vidal (fictional), in €m. Assets: fixed assets 14.5, inventory 1, receivables 4, cash 0.5 (total 20). Liabilities: equity 6, financial debts 9 (of which 1.5 due within one year), trade payables 3, tax and social liabilities 2 (total 20). EBE 3, EBIT 1.5, financial expenses 0.45.

  1. Calculate the current, quick and cash ratios.
  2. Calculate the equity ratio and gearing.
  3. Calculate the Net debt / EBE leverage and interest cover.
  4. The bank has imposed a covenant "Net debt / EBE below 3.5". By how much can EBE fall before the covenant is breached (with constant net debt)?
  5. Food for thought: a hypermarket shows a current ratio of 0.8, Transports Vidal a ratio of about 0.85. Why will the banker probably be more worried about Transports Vidal?
Answers (try first!)
  1. Current assets = 1 + 4 + 0.5 = 5.5. Current liabilities = 3 + 2 + 1.5 = 6.5. Current ratio = 5.5 / 6.5 = 0.85. Quick = 4.5 / 6.5 = 0.69. Cash = 0.5 / 6.5 = 0.08.
  2. Equity ratio = 6 / 20 = 30%. Net debt = 9 − 0.5 = 8.5. Gearing = 8.5 / 6 = 142%.
  3. Leverage = 8.5 / 3 = 2.83. Cover = 1.5 / 0.45 = 3.3.
  4. The covenant is breached if EBE < 8.5 / 3.5 = €2.43m. EBE can therefore fall by about €0.57m, i.e. only 19%. The safety margin is small.
  5. For the hypermarket, a ratio below 1 is structural: customers pay immediately, stock sells within a few weeks and suppliers are paid later, so operations continuously generate cash (negative WCR). At Transports Vidal, current assets are mainly trade receivables that take time to come in, cash is very low and the company is already indebted (gearing of 142%, covenant close). The same figure does not mean the same thing at all.

Next lesson: customer, supplier and inventory periods. How many days does your money stay stuck in operations?

16.html:
Why it matters

Picture Atelier Boréal, our fictional electric bike maker. It buys batteries and frames, stores them, assembles the bikes, stores them again, sells them to shops... which pay at 45 or 60 days. All that time, the company has advanced money. And its own suppliers are also waiting to be paid, which gives it a bit of breathing space.

This back-and-forth creates the working capital requirement you met in lesson 12. Today we measure it in days rather than euros. Why? Because days are easy to compare from one year to the next and from one company to another, and because they speak to operational staff: a salesperson understands "our customers pay at 49 days", much less "our trade receivables are €8m".

Gaining a few days on this cycle can free up millions of euros, without borrowing a cent. It is often a company's cheapest source of cash.

The three periods

Customer payment period (DSO)

Customer period (in days) = Trade receivables / Revenue incl. VAT × 365

It is the average number of days between the sale and the cash receipt. In English: days sales outstanding (DSO). Why revenue including VAT (TTC)? Because trade receivables on the balance sheet include VAT (the customer owes you the price including tax), whereas revenue in the income statement is excluding tax (HT). To compare like with like, you put VAT back into the denominator.

Atelier Boréal: trade receivables €8m, revenue excl. VAT €50m, so revenue incl. VAT (VAT at 20%) = €60m.

Customer period = 8 / 60 × 365 = 48.7 days.

Inventory period (DIO)

Inventory period (in days) = Inventory / Cost of goods sold (or materials consumed) excl. VAT × 365

It is the average time goods sit in the warehouse. In English: days inventory outstanding (DIO). Here everything is excluding VAT: inventory is valued excluding tax, at cost. Atelier Boréal consumes €30m of purchases excl. VAT a year.

Inventory period = 6 / 30 × 365 = 73 days.

For a detailed analysis, you distinguish raw materials, work in progress and finished goods, but the principle stays the same.

Supplier payment period (DPO)

Supplier period (in days) = Trade payables / Purchases incl. VAT × 365

It is the average time the company takes to pay its suppliers. In English: days payables outstanding (DPO). Same logic as for customers: trade payables include VAT. Atelier Boréal's purchases incl. VAT = 30 × 1.2 = €36m.

Supplier period = 5 / 36 × 365 = 50.7 days.

The cash conversion cycle

Put the three periods together:

Cash conversion cycle = Inventory period + Customer period − Supplier period

Atelier Boréal: 73 + 48.7 − 50.7 = 71 days (approximately).

Reading: between the moment the company pays its suppliers and the moment its customers pay it, 71 days go by on average. For 71 days, it is Atelier Boréal that finances operations. In practice, the timeline looks like this:

  • Day 0: batteries and frames are received.
  • Day 51: Atelier Boréal pays its supplier. Money goes out.
  • Day 73: the bike is sold to a shop.
  • Day 122 (73 + 49): the shop pays. Money comes in.

Between day 51 and day 122, about 71 days, the money is "stuck". It is this gap that has to be financed, with equity, debt or an overdraft.

The magic case: a negative cycle. If the company collects from its customers before paying its suppliers, the cycle becomes negative: operations generate cash instead of consuming it. This is typically the case in mass retail (customers pay at the till, stock turns over in a few weeks, suppliers are paid later) and for some online retailers. It is the negative WCR from lesson 12, and the explanation for supermarkets' current ratio below 1 seen yesterday.

What a few days are worth

Each day of payment period has a value in euros. For Atelier Boréal:

  • One day of revenue incl. VAT = 60 / 365 = €0.164m, about €164,000.
  • One day of materials consumed excl. VAT = 30 / 365 = €0.082m, about €82,000.
ActionDays gainedCash released
Chase customers: period from 48.7 to 38.7 days10 days of revenue incl. VAT60 × 10 / 365 = €1.64m
Better stock management: from 73 to 58 days15 days of purchases30 × 15 / 365 = €1.23m
Total€2.87m

Nearly €2.9m recovered, when the company's annual net profit is €3.4m! And this cash is released once, but for good, as long as the new periods are maintained. You can see why CFOs talk so much about "hunting down WCR".

The growth trap

The flip side: if Atelier Boréal grows by 20% with the same periods, its inventory, receivables and payables also grow by 20%. Its WCR (€8m in lesson 13) rises to 8 × 1.2 = €9.6m: growth consumes €1.6m of cash. That is why a fast-growing company, even a profitable one, can run short of cash. You saw this mechanism in the cash flow statement in lesson 11: the change in WCR is deducted from the cash generated by operations.

Levers for action, and their limits

  • Customer side: invoice quickly, chase systematically, offer a discount for early payment, or sell your invoices to a specialist firm (factoring), which advances the money in return for a fee.
  • Inventory side: produce to order, reduce the number of product lines, forecast sales better. But careful: too little stock means the risk of running out and losing customers.
  • Supplier side: negotiate longer terms. But the law regulates these periods. In France, the general rule is a maximum of 60 days from the invoice date (or 45 days end of month if the contract provides for it), with specific rules for some sectors. These rules change: always check the current framework. Late payment is penalised, and checks are real.

Remember the idea of a zero-sum game: when a large company lengthens its supplier payment terms, it gains cash... which its suppliers lose. Late payment is regularly cited as a major cause of SME failures.

Key takeaways

  • Customer period = Trade receivables / Revenue incl. VAT × 365.
  • Inventory period = Inventory / Materials consumed (or cost of sales) excl. VAT × 365.
  • Supplier period = Trade payables / Purchases incl. VAT × 365.
  • Cash conversion cycle = Inventory + Customers − Suppliers (in days): the time during which the company finances its operations.
  • One day gained is worth about one day of revenue (or purchases) in cash released.
  • Growth, with constant periods, consumes cash; a negative cycle generates it.

Exercise

La Fromagerie des Aravis (fictional). To keep it simple, everything is excluding VAT. Annual revenue €3,650k, materials consumed €2,190k. On the balance sheet: inventory €360k, trade receivables €450k, trade payables €240k.

  1. Calculate the customer period, inventory period and supplier period (in days, 365-day basis).
  2. Calculate the cash conversion cycle.
  3. The cheese maker cuts its customer period to 30 days. How much cash does it release?
  4. Its revenue rises by 10% next year, with unchanged periods (those in question 1). By how much will its WCR (inventory + customers − suppliers) increase?
  5. Food for thought: a large group proudly announces it has "released €500m of cash" by moving its supplier terms from 45 to 75 days. Is this real value creation? What risks is it taking?
Answers (try first!)
  1. Customers: 450 / 3,650 × 365 = 45 days. Inventory: 360 / 2,190 × 365 = 60 days. Suppliers: 240 / 2,190 × 365 = 40 days.
  2. Cycle = 60 + 45 − 40 = 65 days. (Note: WCR in euros, 360 + 450 − 240 = €570k, represents 57 days of revenue. The two figures differ because the periods are not calculated on the same base: revenue for customers, purchases for inventory and suppliers. The two measures complement each other.)
  3. One day of revenue = 3,650 / 365 = €10k. Gain of 15 days: 15 × 10 = €150k released.
  4. Inventory, customers and suppliers all rise by 10%: WCR goes from €570k to €627k, i.e. + €57k of cash to find. Growth costs cash before it brings any in.
  5. It is mainly a transfer of cash: the group gains €500m that its suppliers must finance in its place. There is a real gain for the group (less debt to carry), but the risks are many: weakened or failing suppliers (supply disruption), price increases to compensate, a poorer relationship, legal risk if terms exceed the legal cap, and a damaged image. A supplier period that lengthens a lot is also a signal the analyst must watch: is it a successful negotiation, or a company struggling to pay?

Next lesson: financial leverage. How debt can boost shareholders' returns... or crush them.

17.html:
Why it matters

In lesson 13 you noticed an oddity: Atelier Boréal's ROE (16.9%) is higher than its ROCE (12.5%). Shareholders earn more than the business itself brings in. How is that possible? Thanks to debt. The company borrows at a cost lower than what its business earns, and the difference goes to the shareholders.

This is financial leverage. It explains why people buy a flat with a mortgage, why LBO funds borrow massively (lesson 37), and why so many heavily indebted companies collapse as soon as business slows. Leverage is an amplifier: it amplifies the good years, and it amplifies the bad ones too.

An intuition with a flat

You buy a studio flat for €100,000 that brings in €6,000 of net rent a year, i.e. 6%. (We ignore taxes for now.)

  • Without a loan: you put in €100,000 of your own money and earn €6,000. Return on your contribution: 6%.
  • With a loan of €80,000 at 4%: you pay €3,200 of interest, leaving €2,800 for a contribution of €20,000. Return on your contribution: 2,800 / 20,000 = 14%.

The property still returns 6%, but your contribution returns 14%. Why? Because you borrow at 4% to invest in something that returns 6%. On each euro borrowed you gain 2 cents, and you have borrowed 4 times your contribution.

The leverage formula

In a company, you reason the same way with ROCE (the return on the business, lesson 13) and the cost of debt. With tax, the formula becomes:

ROE = ROCE + (ROCE − i × (1 − t)) × D / CP

  • ROCE: return on capital employed, after tax.
  • i: interest rate on the debt. i × (1 − t) is its after-tax cost, because interest is deductible from taxable profit.
  • D / CP: net debt over equity (capitaux propres; the gearing from lesson 15).
  • (ROCE − i × (1 − t)) × D / CP: this is the leverage effect, what debt adds to (or takes away from) ROE.

Let's check with Atelier Boréal: ROCE 12.5%, debt at 5% so 3.75% after tax (corporation tax at 25%), D / CP = 10 / 20 = 0.5.

ROE = 12.5% + (12.5% − 3.75%) × 0.5 = 12.5% + 4.375% = 16.875%. Exactly the 16.9% found in lesson 13. Leverage adds 4.4 points of ROE.

The golden rule: leverage is favourable as long as the economic return (after-tax ROCE) exceeds the after-tax cost of debt.

Three structures, one company

Take Solaria (fictional), which installs solar panels. Its capital employed is €100m and its operating profit (EBIT) €12m: ROCE of 12% before tax, so 9% after tax. It can borrow at 5% (3.75% after tax). Tax at 25%. Three ways to finance its €100m:

No debtDebt €50mDebt €75m
Equity1005025
EBIT121212
Interest (5%)0− 2.5− 3.75
Profit before tax129.58.25
Tax (25%)− 3− 2.375− 2.0625
Net profit97.1256.1875
ROE9%14.25%24.75%

Net profit falls with debt (interest must be paid), but it is shared among much less equity: ROE shoots up. Check with the formula for the "€75m" column: 9% + (9% − 3.75%) × 75 / 25 = 9% + 5.25% × 3 = 24.75%.

The club effect: when leverage turns

Now a bad year: Chinese competition drives prices down, and Solaria's EBIT falls to €3m. ROCE of 3% before tax, 2.25% after tax, below the after-tax cost of debt (3.75%). To keep it simple, we assume a loss also gives a 25% tax saving (thanks to carrying losses forward to later years).

No debtDebt €50mDebt €75m
EBIT333
Interest0− 2.5− 3.75
Profit before tax30.5− 0.75
Net profit2.250.375− 0.5625
ROE2.25%0.75%− 2.25%

The roles are reversed: the more debt, the more ROE collapses. Interest, meanwhile, is due whatever happens. This is the club effect (effet massue).

Compare the gap between the good and bad year:

  • No debt: ROE ranges from 9% to 2.25%, a gap of 6.75 points.
  • With €75m of debt: from 24.75% to −2.25%, a gap of 27 points, four times as much.

Debt has not changed Solaria's business, but it has made the shareholder's return much more volatile, and therefore riskier. Leverage does not create free returns: it trades expected return for risk. And that risk has a price: shareholders of an indebted company demand a higher return (you will see this with the CAPM in lesson 27 and the cost of capital in lesson 31).

Why not borrow without limit?

If ROCE exceeds the cost of debt, the formula seems to say: "borrow as much as possible". In practice, several brakes appear:

  • The cost of debt rises with indebtedness: banks lend more expensively to a company that is already heavily indebted. The gap between ROCE and the cost of debt narrows.
  • The risk of bankruptcy increases: one or two bad years can be enough to be unable to pay the interest (remember interest cover and covenants from lesson 15).
  • Shareholders demand more to compensate for volatility: a higher ROE is not necessarily a better deal if it is much riskier.
  • Flexibility disappears: a heavily indebted company can no longer borrow to seize an opportunity.

The question of the "right" amount of debt is one of the big debates in corporate finance. You will meet it again in lesson 32 with the Modigliani-Miller theorem, which shows, in plain language, that in a perfect world debt does not create value by itself: it merely redistributes return and risk.

DuPont leverage and financial leverage

Don't confuse this with the "accounting" leverage from lesson 14 (Total assets / Equity). Both say the same thing in spirit (the more external financing, the more ROE is amplified), but today's formula is more precise: it isolates net financial debt and its cost, and it shows the condition for leverage to work in the right direction.

Key takeaways

  • ROE = ROCE + (ROCE − i × (1 − t)) × D / CP, with ROCE after tax.
  • Leverage is favourable if after-tax ROCE exceeds the after-tax cost of debt, unfavourable otherwise (club effect).
  • The higher the D / CP ratio, the more the effect (positive or negative) is amplified.
  • Debt increases expected ROE and its volatility: it is a trade of return for risk, not a gift.
  • Deductible interest makes debt cheaper after tax (i × (1 − t)).
  • The cost of debt, the risk of bankruptcy and shareholders' requirements all rise with indebtedness.

Exercise

A fictional company has €40m of capital employed and a pre-tax ROCE of 10%. Tax at 25%. It can borrow at 6%.

  1. What is its ROE if it is financed entirely by equity?
  2. It finances itself with €20m of debt and €20m of equity. Calculate ROE with the formula, then check by building the income statement (EBIT, interest, tax, net profit).
  3. Bad year: pre-tax ROCE falls to 4%. What happens to ROE with the structure from question 2? Does leverage work for or against the shareholder?
  4. With a pre-tax ROCE of 10%, what D / CP ratio would be needed to reach an ROE of 15%?
  5. Food for thought: from what pre-tax ROCE does leverage become unfavourable for this company? Why does a prudent CEO not look only at the current year's ROCE when deciding to borrow?
Answers (try first!)
  1. Without debt, ROE = after-tax ROCE = 10% × 0.75 = 7.5%.
  2. After-tax cost of debt = 6% × 0.75 = 4.5%. D / CP = 1. ROE = 7.5% + (7.5% − 4.5%) × 1 = 10.5%. Check: EBIT = €4m, interest = 20 × 6% = €1.2m, profit before tax = €2.8m, tax = €0.7m, net profit = €2.1m, ROE = 2.1 / 20 = 10.5%.
  3. After-tax ROCE = 4% × 0.75 = 3%. ROE = 3% + (3% − 4.5%) × 1 = 1.5%. Check: EBIT 1.6, interest 1.2, profit before tax 0.4, net profit 0.3, ROE = 0.3 / 20 = 1.5%. Without debt, ROE would have been 3%: leverage works against the shareholder.
  4. 15% = 7.5% + 3% × D / CP, so D / CP = 7.5 / 3 = 2.5 (for example €28.6m of debt and €11.4m of equity).
  5. Leverage becomes unfavourable when after-tax ROCE falls below 4.5%, i.e. a pre-tax ROCE below 6%, the interest rate on the debt. A prudent CEO knows that ROCE varies with the economic cycle, whereas interest and repayments are fixed and last for years. So they should borrow based on a plausible bad year, not a good one, and keep a safety margin on their solvency ratios.

Next lesson: case study. We put all the module 3 tools to work analysing a real CAC 40 company.

18.html:
From theory to the real world

Since the start of module 3 you have put into your toolbox ROE, ROA and ROCE (lesson 13), the DuPont decomposition (lesson 14), liquidity and solvency ratios (lesson 15), payment periods and the cash conversion cycle (lesson 16) and leverage (lesson 17). Today we use them all together on a real CAC 40 company: L'Oréal, the world's number one in cosmetics.

Why L'Oréal? Because it is a company everyone knows (you probably have one of its products in your bathroom, under one of its many brands), and because its financial profile is very easy to read. The aim is not to say whether you should buy the share (this course gives no investment recommendations), but to learn a method you can apply to any company.

Important: the figures below are rounded orders of magnitude, inspired by the accounts published for the 2023 financial year and simplified for the exercise. They do not replace the official accounts, which change every year. For a real analysis, always go to the source: the universal registration document (document d'enregistrement universel) published by the group on its website, also available via the AMF (France's financial markets regulator).

The six-step method

  1. Understand the business: what does the company sell, to whom, how does it make money?
  2. Read growth and margins: the income statement over several years.
  3. Measure profitability: ROE, ROCE, DuPont.
  4. Check soundness: liquidity, debt.
  5. Look at cash: WCR, investment, conversion of profit into cash.
  6. Conclude and compare: strengths, weaknesses, points to watch, against competitors.

Step 1: the business

L'Oréal designs, manufactures and sells beauty products (skincare, make-up, hair colour and haircare, fragrances) all over the world, through a portfolio of brands ranging from mass market to luxury, and even dermocosmetics sold in pharmacies. The group also grows through acquisitions, for example the Australian brand Aesop in 2023.

What to take away for finance: the product costs relatively little to make, but the company spends enormously on advertising, marketing and research. What creates value is the brands, which allow it to sell at high prices. So we expect high margins and assets that are relatively "light" in factories, but heavy in intangible assets (brands and goodwill bought in acquisitions).

Steps 2 and 3: margins and profitability

Here are our working figures, rounded (in billions of euros):

ItemOrder of magnitude
Revenueabout 41
EBE (EBITDA)about 10
Operating profitabout 8
Net profit attributable to the groupabout 6
Equityabout 29
Balance sheet totalabout 48
Net debtabout 3

Margins

  • Operating margin = 8 / 41 = 19.5%: nearly 20 cents of operating profit per euro sold. For a conventional manufacturer, 5 to 10% is already decent. It is the signature of strong pricing power (lesson 14).
  • Net margin = 6 / 41 = 14.6%.

A real analyst would also look at the trend over 5 years, and distinguish reported growth from organic growth (also called "like-for-like", i.e. excluding acquisitions and currency effects). Growth driven only by acquisitions or a weak euro is not of the same quality as growth coming from sales themselves.

Profitability ratios

  • ROE = 6 / 29 = 20.7%.
  • ROA = 6 / 48 = 12.5%.
  • Capital employed (approximated via financing) = equity + net debt = 29 + 3 = 32. With tax at 25% for simplicity, ROCE = 8 × 0.75 / 32 = 18.75%.

A ROCE close to 19%, well above a cost of capital that can be put at roughly 7 to 9% for a large group of this kind: L'Oréal creates value (lesson 13).

A real analyst's subtlety: L'Oréal holds a stake of about 9% in Sanofi. This stake inflates equity and assets, but does not contribute to operating profit (it brings in dividends, counted lower down the income statement). By including it in capital employed, you underestimate the ROCE of the cosmetics business. A rigorous analyst would take it out. Moral: always ask whether all the assets on the balance sheet really serve the business.

DuPont

FactorCalculationValue
Net margin6 / 4114.6%
Asset turnover41 / 480.85
Accounting leverage48 / 291.66
ROE14.6% × 0.85 × 1.6620.7%

The diagnosis is crystal clear: ROE comes from the margin. Turnover is low (lots of intangible and financial assets relative to revenue) and leverage is moderate. It is exactly the "luxury and cosmetics" profile seen in lesson 14.

Step 4: soundness

  • Gearing = 3 / 29 ≈ 10%: very little debt.
  • Net debt / EBE = 3 / 10 = 0.3: about four months of EBE would be enough to repay the net debt. Very far from the warning thresholds in lesson 15.
  • Equity ratio = 29 / 48 ≈ 60%.

Consequence for leverage (lesson 17): with so little debt, it barely plays a role. L'Oréal's ROE is almost entirely economic in origin, not financial. It is "good quality" profitability: it does not depend on debt that could turn against the shareholder.

Step 5: cash

Without going into the details of the cash flow statement (lesson 11), an analyst would check three things:

  • Conversion of profit into cash: is operating cash flow close to net profit plus depreciation, or much lower? A persistent gap is a warning sign (lesson 11: profit ≠ cash).
  • WCR (lesson 16): in cosmetics, inventory is large (many product lines, seasons, countries) but retailer customers pay within regulated terms. Above all, watch the trend in inventory and customer periods, in days.
  • Investment: it remains moderate relative to revenue, which leaves plenty of free cash for dividends, share buybacks and acquisitions (lesson 33).

Step 6: conclude

StrengthsPoints to watch
Very high margins, pricing powerDependence on global consumption (China, United States)
ROCE well above the cost of capitalGrowth through acquisitions: prices paid, goodwill on the balance sheet
Very low debtCurrency effects on a very international group
Profitability that does not depend on debtCompetition and the cost of marketing to defend the brands

And the last, essential step: compare. A ratio on its own means nothing. Compare it with the company's history over 5 years, then with its direct competitors in the sector. That is what turns a list of figures into a judgement.

Key takeaways

  • An analysis always follows the same logic: business, growth and margins, profitability, soundness, cash, conclusion.
  • Start by understanding how the company makes money: the ratios then confirm or qualify it.
  • DuPont reveals the engine of ROE: at L'Oréal, the margin, not debt.
  • A high ROE with little debt is better quality profitability than an ROE boosted by leverage.
  • Check that all assets serve the business (example: a financial stake).
  • The real figures are in the universal registration document; always compare over time and against competitors.

Exercise

Groupe Vitalis (fictional), a European food retailer, in billions of euros: revenue 80, EBE 4, operating profit 2, net profit 1.3, balance sheet total 50, equity 12, net debt 6. Tax at 25%.

  1. Calculate the operating margin, net margin and the three DuPont factors. What is the ROE?
  2. Calculate after-tax ROCE (capital employed = equity + net debt).
  3. Calculate gearing and the net debt / EBE ratio.
  4. Compare Vitalis's profile with L'Oréal's: where does ROE come from in each case?
  5. Food for thought: a company has excellent ratios. Is that enough to say its share is a good investment? What is missing from the analysis?
Answers (try first!)
  1. Operating margin = 2 / 80 = 2.5%. Net margin = 1.3 / 80 = 1.6%. Turnover = 80 / 50 = 1.6. Leverage = 50 / 12 = 4.17. ROE = 1.625% × 1.6 × 4.17 = 10.8% (check: 1.3 / 12 = 10.8%).
  2. Capital employed = 12 + 6 = 18. ROCE = 2 × 0.75 / 18 = 8.3%.
  3. Gearing = 6 / 12 = 50%. Net debt / EBE = 6 / 4 = 1.5.
  4. L'Oréal: very high margin, low turnover, moderate leverage, ROE mainly economic in origin. Vitalis: very low margin, high turnover and high accounting leverage (lots of trade payables, typical of retail). Its ROE (10.8%) exceeds its ROCE (8.3%) thanks to the leverage effect of debt. Two businesses, two signatures, and Vitalis's ROE is more sensitive to a fall in margin.
  5. No. Ratios describe the past and the quality of the company. At least these are missing: the outlook (future growth, competition, risks), the quality of management and governance, non-financial issues, and above all the price: an excellent company can be a bad investment if its share is already very expensive. That is the question of valuation, which you will tackle with the P/E ratio (lesson 29) and the DCF method (module 7).

Next lesson: we open module 4, "Deciding to invest". First step: identifying the cash flows of an investment project.

19.html:
Why it matters

Welcome to module 4. So far you have learnt to analyse a company that exists. Now we move on to question no. 1 from lesson 1: where to invest? Should we buy this machine, open this shop, launch this product?

To answer, you already know the tool: discount future cash flows and add them up (lesson 3). But a calculation tool is only as good as the numbers you give it. If the cash flows are wrong, the decision will be wrong, however precise the formula. In practice, mistakes rarely come from the NPV calculation: they come from the cash flows. Today you learn to build them properly.

The five golden rules

1. Think in cash, not profit

A project creates value if it brings in more money than it costs. Not more accounting profit: cash. Remember lesson 11: profit ≠ cash. Depreciation, for example, is an expense but not a cash outflow. The real cash outflow is buying the machine, on the day you pay for it.

2. Keep only incremental cash flows

The only question: what changes in the company's cash flows if it does the project, compared with if it doesn't? You compare "with" and "without". Anything that would exist anyway is irrelevant.

3. Forget sunk costs

A market study already paid for, research costs already incurred: these sums are spent whether or not the project goes ahead. They are sunk costs (coûts irrécupérables). They must not enter the calculation. It is counter-intuitive ("we've already put in €30,000, we can't give up now!"), but it is one of the most frequent decision errors, in business as in life.

4. Add the hidden costs: opportunity and cannibalisation

  • Opportunity cost: if the project uses a warehouse the company already owns but could have rented out for €20,000 a year, that lost rent is a cost of the project, even though there is no invoice.
  • Cannibalisation: if the new product takes sales from an existing product of the company, only the net additional sales count.

5. Separate investment and financing

Remove neither interest nor loan repayments from the project's cash flows. The cost of financing is already taken into account in the discount rate (the cost of capital, lesson 31). Counting it in the cash flows too would mean paying it twice. First judge whether the project is good in itself; how to finance it is a separate decision.

The project cash flow formula

Each year, the project's free cash flow is calculated as follows:

Cash flow = EBIT × (1 − t) + Depreciation − Investment − Change in WCR

  • EBIT × (1 − t): operating profit after tax, the NOPAT from lesson 13. Tax is calculated as if the project had no debt (rule 5).
  • + Depreciation: added back, because it is not a cash outflow. It was only used to calculate tax.
  • − Investment (capex): buying the machines, the buildings, when you pay for them.
  • − Change in WCR: when the business starts or grows, inventory and trade receivables have to be financed (lesson 16). This is cash tied up. At the end of the project, the WCR is recovered (stock is sold off, the last receivables collected): it comes back as a positive.

The depreciation tax shield

The same formula can be rewritten another way, which sheds light on the role of depreciation:

Operating cash flow = EBE × (1 − t) + t × Depreciation

The term t × Depreciation is the tax saving (tax shield) provided by depreciation. Depreciation takes no money out, but it reduces taxable profit, and therefore the tax paid. With €200,000 of depreciation and tax at 25%, the company pays €50,000 less tax each year.

A complete example: the brewery's new line

Brasserie du Mont-Aiguille (fictional), near Grenoble, is considering a production line for alcohol-free beer. We will follow it throughout module 4. The data (in thousands of euros, €k):

  • Investment: €1,000k at the start (year 0), depreciated on a straight-line basis over 5 years, i.e. €200k a year.
  • Revenue: €700k in year 1, then €900k a year from year 2 to year 5.
  • Variable costs: 40% of revenue. Fixed cash costs: €200k a year.
  • WCR: 10% of the year's revenue, built up during the year, fully recovered at the end of year 5.
  • Sale of the line at the end of year 5: €100k. As it is fully depreciated, the gain (€100k) is taxed: 100 × (1 − 0.25) = €75k is left.
  • A market study has already cost €30k: sunk cost, ignore it.
  • Corporation tax: 25% (in line with the standard rate in France, to be checked as it changes).
€kYr 0Yr 1Yr 2Yr 3Yr 4Yr 5
Revenue700900900900900
Variable costs (40%)− 280− 360− 360− 360− 360
Fixed costs− 200− 200− 200− 200− 200
EBE220340340340340
Depreciation− 200− 200− 200− 200− 200
EBIT20140140140140
Tax (25%)− 5− 35− 35− 35− 35
NOPAT15105105105105
+ Depreciation200200200200200

Sale after tax75
Project cash flow− 1,000145285305305470

A few points to understand properly:

  • WCR: it rises to €70k in year 1 (10% of 700), then to €90k in year 2 (10% of 900). Only the change is deducted: 70, then 20, then nothing. In year 5, the €90k is recovered.
  • Year 1 is weak: profit is almost zero and the WCR absorbs €70k. Typical of a start-up phase.
  • Check with the other formula, in year 3: 340 × 0.75 + 0.25 × 200 = 255 + 50 = 305. We get the same cash flow.
  • Sum of cash flows: − 1,000 + 145 + 285 + 305 + 305 + 470 = + €510k. But careful: we are adding euros from different dates, which is forbidden (lesson 3). To know whether the project really creates value, they need to be discounted. That is the subject of tomorrow's lesson.

The most frequent traps

  • Forgetting WCR: a project that increases sales ties up cash. Forgetting it makes the project artificially attractive.
  • Forgetting tax on the gain on resale, or conversely applying it to the whole sale price instead of just the gain (sale price − net book value).
  • Counting existing overheads (the CEO's salary, head office rent) if they do not change with the project.
  • Subtracting interest on the loan that finances the project (rule 5).
  • Mixing nominal cash flows and a real rate, or vice versa (lesson 4): if you forecast prices rising with inflation, discount with a nominal rate.
  • Being too optimistic: project sponsors often overestimate sales and underestimate delays. A good finance person always tests a cautious scenario.

Key takeaways

  • A project is assessed on cash flows, not accounting profit.
  • Keep only incremental cash flows: "with the project" minus "without the project".
  • Ignore sunk costs; include opportunity costs and cannibalisation.
  • Cash flow = EBIT × (1 − t) + Depreciation − Investment − Change in WCR.
  • Depreciation provides a tax saving of t × Depreciation.
  • Remove neither interest nor repayments: financing is in the discount rate.
  • WCR is invested at the start and recovered at the end; resale counts after tax.

Exercise

Lina wants to launch a food truck (fictional) alongside her restaurant. Investment: €60k, depreciated on a straight-line basis over 3 years. Expected additional EBE: €30k a year for 3 years. WCR of €5k built up in year 0 and recovered in year 3. The truck will be sold for €6k at the end of year 3 (net book value zero). Tax: 25%. She has already paid €2k to a consultant to study the idea.

  1. Should the consultant's €2k enter the calculation? Why?
  2. Calculate EBIT, tax and the annual operating cash flow (NOPAT + depreciation). Check with the formula EBE × (1 − t) + t × Depreciation.
  3. Build the table of project cash flows from year 0 to year 3.
  4. Lina realises the food truck will draw some customers away from the restaurant: the restaurant's EBE will fall by €8k a year. What is the project's new annual operating cash flow?
  5. Food for thought: Lina finances the truck with a bank loan at 5%. Her accountant wants to deduct the interest from the project's cash flows. What do you tell him?
Answers (try first!)
  1. No: it is a sunk cost. The €2k is spent whether or not the project goes ahead, so it must not influence the decision.
  2. Depreciation = 60 / 3 = €20k a year. EBIT = 30 − 20 = €10k. Tax = €2.5k. NOPAT = €7.5k. Operating cash flow = 7.5 + 20 = €27.5k. Check: 30 × 0.75 + 0.25 × 20 = 22.5 + 5 = €27.5k.
  3. Year 0: − 60 − 5 = − €65k. Years 1 and 2: + €27.5k. Year 3: 27.5 + 5 (WCR recovered) + 6 × 0.75 (sale after tax, i.e. 4.5) = + €37k.
  4. Incremental EBE is now only 30 − 8 = €22k. EBIT = 22 − 20 = €2k, NOPAT = €1.5k, operating cash flow = 1.5 + 20 = €21.5k a year. Cannibalisation sharply reduces the appeal of the project.
  5. Interest must not be deducted from the cash flows: the cost of financing is taken into account in the discount rate. Otherwise it would be counted twice and the project unfairly penalised. First judge whether the project is good in itself, by discounting its cash flows at the cost of capital; the financing question (loan, personal contribution) is a separate decision.

Next lesson: NPV, net present value. We discount the brewery's cash flows to find out, at last, whether the project creates value.

20.html:
The king of investment criteria

Yesterday you built the cash flows for the new line at Brasserie du Mont-Aiguille (fictional): we spend €1,000k today, and get back 145, 285, 305, 305 then €470k over five years. In total, €1,510k received for €1,000k invested. So, do we go for it?

Not so fast. You have known since lesson 3 that you never compare euros from different dates. The €470k in year 5 is worth much less than €470k today. Everything must be brought back to the same date, then compared. That is exactly what NPV, net present value (VAN, valeur actuelle nette), does: the most widely used (and most robust) decision criterion in corporate finance.

The definition

VAN = − I₀ + F₁ / (1 + k) + F₂ / (1 + k)² + … + Fₙ / (1 + k)ⁿ

  • I₀: the initial investment (year 0), which is not discounted since it happens today.
  • F₁ … Fₙ: the project's cash flows, built as in lesson 19.
  • k: the discount rate, i.e. the project's cost of capital, the minimum return required by those who finance it.

In one sentence: NPV is the sum of all the project's cash flows, discounted at the cost of capital. It is the technique from lesson 3 (the footballer's transfer in three instalments), plus the initial investment.

Decision rule: NPV > 0 → invest. NPV < 0 → walk away. Between several mutually exclusive projects, choose the highest NPV.

Application to the brewery

The brewery estimates that its providers of finance (shareholders and bank) require on average 8% a year for a project with this risk. You will learn to calculate this rate in lesson 31 (the WACC); for now, take it as given.

YearCash flow (€k)Discount factor at 8%Discounted cash flow (€k)
0− 1,0001− 1,000.00
11451 / 1.08 = 0.9259134.26
22851 / 1.08² = 0.8573244.34
33051 / 1.08³ = 0.7938242.12
43051 / 1.08⁴ = 0.7350224.18
54701 / 1.08⁵ = 0.6806319.87
NPV164.78

NPV is + €164.8k: the project is accepted.
