What exactly does this figure mean?

This is the most important point of the lesson. An NPV of €164.8k does not mean the project "earns €164.8k". It means:

  • The project pays back the €1,000k investment;
  • it rewards all providers of finance at 8% a year, exactly what they require;
  • and on top of that, it generates a surplus worth €164.8k today.

That surplus is the value created for shareholders. If the market fully believed the forecasts, the brewery's value should rise by about €164.8k on the day it announces the project. It is the concrete translation of the idea from lesson 1: creating value means earning more than the opportunity cost. A zero NPV is not a failure: the project rewards providers of finance exactly, but creates nothing extra.

The rate changes everything

As in lesson 3, value depends heavily on the discount rate. Here is the brewery's NPV at different rates:

Rate0%4%8%12%14%16%20%
NPV (€k)510.0321.1164.834.3− 23.0− 75.6− 168.8

At 0%, you get the simple sum of cash flows (€510k). The higher the rate, the lower the NPV, because distant cash flows weigh less and less. Somewhere between 12% and 14%, NPV crosses zero. That precise rate has a name: the IRR, and it is tomorrow's topic.

Practical consequence: choosing the right rate is as important as estimating the cash flows well. A project riskier than the company's usual business (a new country, a new technology) should be discounted at a higher rate.

Sensitivity: what if sales disappoint?

Cash flows are forecasts. A good finance person always asks: "what if I'm wrong?". Let's redo the calculation with revenue 10% lower every year (€630k then €810k), all other assumptions unchanged. The cash flows become − 1,000, 120.5, 246.5, 264.5, 264.5 and €420.5k.

NPV at 8%: only + €13.5k.

A 10% fall in sales wipes out more than 90% of the NPV! Why such an effect? Because the fixed costs (€200k) and the investment don't move: any fall in sales lands almost directly on the cash flows. The project remains acceptable, but the safety margin is thin. This sensitivity analysis is essential: it shows which assumptions to check first. You will take it further in the lesson 23 case study.

Comparing projects

The brewery has an alternative: use the same building to expand its lager line (project B, also fictional). Investment of €400k, then €150k a year for 4 years. The two projects are mutually exclusive: the building can only house one of them.

  • NPV of project A (alcohol-free beer) at 8%: €164.8k.
  • NPV of project B (lager) at 8%: − 400 + 150 / 1.08 + 150 / 1.08² + 150 / 1.08³ + 150 / 1.08⁴ = €96.8k.

Both create value, but A creates more: choose A. Keep this example in mind: tomorrow you will see that another criterion, the IRR, gives the opposite answer. And it is NPV that is right.

Another useful property: NPVs add up. If two projects are independent (not exclusive) and both have a positive NPV, the company can do both and create 164.8 + 96.8 = €261.6k of value.

NPV in Excel

Excel's =VAN(taux;valeurs) function (=NPV(rate,values) in English Excel) hides a famous trap: it assumes the first cash flow in the list arrives in one year, and so discounts it. If you put the year-0 investment in it, it will be wrongly discounted.

The right formula: =VAN(8%;B2:F2)+A2 (=NPV(8%,B2:F2)+A2), where A2 contains − 1,000 (year 0) and B2 to F2 the cash flows for years 1 to 5. Result: 164.78. If you get 152.57 (i.e. 164.78 / 1.08), you have put everything inside the function.

Key takeaways

  • NPV = sum of cash flows discounted at the cost of capital, investment included.
  • NPV > 0: the project pays back the investment, rewards providers of finance at the required rate, and creates additional value on top.
  • Between exclusive projects, keep the highest NPV; NPVs of independent projects add up.
  • NPV falls when the discount rate rises; a riskier project deserves a higher rate.
  • A sensitivity analysis shows which assumptions really matter.
  • In Excel: =VAN(taux;cash flows years 1 to n) + cash flow year 0 (=NPV(...) in English Excel).

Exercise

Back to Lina's food truck (lesson 19): cash flows of − €65k (year 0), €27.5k (year 1), €27.5k (year 2) and €37k (year 3).

  1. Calculate the NPV at 10%. Should Lina go ahead?
  2. Calculate the NPV at 6%. Why is it higher?
  3. With the cannibalisation from lesson 19, the cash flows become − 65, 21.5, 21.5 and €31k. What is the NPV at 10%? Conclusion?
  4. Two exclusive projects: X gives − 100 then 60 and 60; Y gives − 100 then 0 and 125. Calculate their NPVs at 8%, then at 12%. Which do you choose in each case?
  5. Food for thought: a project has an NPV of + €2k for an investment of €5m. The CFO hesitates. Why might they be right to be cautious, when the rule says "NPV > 0, invest"?
Answers (try first!)
  1. NPV = − 65 + 27.5 / 1.1 + 27.5 / 1.1² + 37 / 1.1³ = − 65 + 25.00 + 22.73 + 27.80 = + €10.5k. Positive NPV: yes, the project creates value.
  2. NPV at 6% = + €16.5k. With a lower rate, future cash flows are "penalised" less by discounting, so NPV rises.
  3. NPV = − 65 + 21.5 / 1.1 + 21.5 / 1.1² + 31 / 1.1³ = − €4.4k. Once cannibalisation is taken into account, the project destroys value: Lina should walk away (or find a way to limit cannibalisation, for example by parking the truck far from the restaurant).
  4. At 8%: NPV(X) = 7.00, NPV(Y) = 7.17: choose Y, narrowly. At 12%: NPV(X) = 1.40, NPV(Y) = − 0.35: choose X. Y has later cash flows, so it is more sensitive to the rate. The ranking of two projects can flip depending on the discount rate.
  5. Because an NPV of €2k on €5m is practically zero: the slightest forecasting error (slightly lower sales, slightly higher costs, a slightly higher rate) would make it negative. NPV is never more reliable than the assumptions that produce it. Before deciding, you need a sensitivity analysis, scenarios, and to ask whether the rate properly reflects the risk. There may also be unquantified constraints (team capacity, strategic risk) or other, more attractive projects for the same money.

Next lesson: the IRR and its pitfalls. Executives' favourite criterion... and why it can mislead you.

21.html:
Executives' favourite criterion

Yesterday you saw that the brewery's NPV goes from positive to negative somewhere between 12% and 14%. This tipping-point rate is very telling: it is the project's "intrinsic" return. It is called the IRR, internal rate of return (TRI, taux de rendement interne in French).

Executives love the IRR: a percentage is understood instantly ("this project returns 13% a year"), whereas an NPV of €164.8k needs explaining. In investment committees as in private equity, people talk IRR constantly. The problem: this very intuitive figure can lead to bad decisions. Today you learn to calculate it, to use it, and above all to spot its pitfalls.

The definition

The IRR is the discount rate that makes NPV equal to zero:

0 = − I₀ + F₁ / (1 + IRR) + F₂ / (1 + IRR)² + … + Fₙ / (1 + IRR)ⁿ

Decision rule: IRR > cost of capital → invest. IRR < cost of capital → walk away.

The intuition: the IRR is the interest rate the project "pays" on the money that stays invested in it. If this rate exceeds what money costs (the cost of capital), the project creates value. It is the same logic as ROCE compared with the cost of capital in lesson 13, but applied to a project over its whole life.

Simple one-period example: you invest €200 and get back €230 in a year. 0 = − 200 + 230 / (1 + IRR), so 1 + IRR = 230 / 200 = 1.15, i.e. an IRR of 15%. Easy. As soon as there are several cash flows, however, there is no direct formula: you have to use trial and error.

Calculating the brewery's IRR

The brewery's cash flows (lessons 19 and 20): − 1,000, 145, 285, 305, 305, €470k. We already know a few points of the NPV profile:

RateNPV (€k)
8%+ 164.8
12%+ 34.3
14%− 23.0

The IRR is between 12% and 14%. A linear interpolation gives a good approximation:

IRR ≈ 12% + 2% × 34.3 / (34.3 + 23.0) = 12% + 2% × 0.598 ≈ 13.2%

The exact calculation (by computer) gives 13.18%. In Excel: =TRI(A2:F2) (=IRR(A2:F2) in English Excel), this time with all the cash flows, year 0 included (unlike the NPV function, the IRR function does not have this trap).

With a cost of capital of 8%, the IRR of 13.2% clears the hurdle: invest. Same conclusion as with NPV. For a standalone "conventional" project (an outlay at the start, then inflows), NPV and IRR always give the same answer to the question "yes or no?". The problems start elsewhere.

Pitfall no. 1: comparing projects of different sizes

Remember yesterday's alternative: project B (expanding the lager line), mutually exclusive with project A (alcohol-free beer).

InvestmentNPV at 8%IRR
A: alcohol-free beer€1,000k€164.8k13.2%
B: lager€400k€96.8k18.5%

IRR prefers B, NPV prefers A. Which is right? NPV. IRR is a percentage: it says nothing about the size of the value created. Better to earn 13% on €1,000k than 18.5% on €400k, if money costs 8%. What makes shareholders richer is euros of value created, not percentages.

A simple picture: would you rather earn 50% on €10 (€5 gain) or 20% on €1,000 (€200 gain)?

The Fisher rate (crossover rate). The ranking between A and B depends on the cost of capital. By calculating the IRR of the difference cash flows (A − B), you find about 11%: this is the rate at which the two projects have the same NPV (about €65.6k each). Below 11%, A has the better NPV; above, B does. IRR, however, always says "B", whatever the cost of capital: it cannot see this switch.

Pitfall no. 2: several IRRs (or none)

Some projects have "non-conventional" cash flows: outflows after the inflows. Example: a stone quarry that will have to be restored at the end of operations. Cash flows (fictional): − 100 today, + 230 in one year, − 132 in two years (the restoration).

Try calculating the NPV at 10%: − 100 + 230 / 1.1 − 132 / 1.1² = − 100 + 209.09 − 109.09 = 0. And at 20%: − 100 + 191.67 − 91.67 = 0 too!

This project has two IRRs: 10% and 20%. Which one do you compare with the cost of capital? Neither makes sense. Mathematically, each change of sign in the sequence of cash flows can create one more IRR; some projects have none at all. NPV, on the other hand, always gives a single answer for a given rate. Here, at a 15% cost of capital, NPV is slightly positive; at 8% or 25%, it is negative.

Pitfall no. 3: lending or borrowing?

Compare two transactions: (a) you lend €100 and get back €120 in a year; (b) you borrow €100 and repay €120 in a year. In both cases, the IRR is 20%. But in (a) it is a return (the higher the better), in (b) it is a cost (the higher the worse). The rule "IRR > cost of capital" only works for a conventional investment project, where money goes out first and comes in later. Always look at the direction of the cash flows before interpreting an IRR.

Pitfall no. 4: the reinvestment assumption

IRR implicitly assumes that cash received along the way can be reinvested at the IRR itself. For a 13% project, fair enough; but for a project showing 40%, it is unrealistic to believe that every euro recovered will find another investment at 40%. Result: high IRRs are often too flattering.

A correction exists: the modified IRR (MIRR, TRIM in French). You compound all the positive cash flows to the end of the project at the cost of capital (a more realistic assumption), then find the rate linking the initial investment to this final value (with the lesson 3 formula: i = (VF / VA)^(1/n) − 1).

For the brewery, at an 8% reinvestment rate: final value of the cash flows in year 5 = 145 × 1.08⁴ + 285 × 1.08³ + 305 × 1.08² + 305 × 1.08 + 470 = €1,711.4k. MIRR = (1,711.4 / 1,000)^(1/5) − 1 = 11.3%, compared with 13.2% for the conventional IRR. In Excel: =TRIM(A2:F2;8%;8%) (=MIRR(A2:F2,8%,8%) in English Excel).

So, NPV or IRR?

NPVIRR
UnitEuros of value createdPercentage
Size of the projectTaken into accountIgnored
Non-conventional cash flowsAlways one answerSeveral IRRs possible, or none
Implicit reinvestmentAt the cost of capital (realistic)At the IRR (often too optimistic)
ReadabilityNeeds explainingVery intuitive

Finance people's answer: NPV decides, IRR communicates. You calculate both, you often present the IRR because it speaks to people, but in case of conflict (exclusive projects, odd cash flows), NPV has the final word. IRR remains very useful as a "safety margin": a project with a 13.2% IRR for an 8% cost of capital can absorb a rise of 5 points in the rate before becoming bad.

Key takeaways

  • The IRR is the rate that sets NPV to zero; invest if IRR > cost of capital.
  • For a standalone conventional project, NPV and IRR give the same decision.
  • Between exclusive projects of different sizes, IRR can be wrong: follow NPV.
  • Cash flows that change sign several times can give several IRRs (or none).
  • IRR assumes reinvestment at the IRR; the MIRR corrects this by reinvesting at the cost of capital.
  • In Excel: =TRI(cash flows year 0 to n) and =TRIM(cash flows;finance rate;reinvestment rate) (=IRR and =MIRR in English Excel).

Exercise

  1. You invest €500 and get back €560 in a year. What is the IRR? If your cost of capital is 10%, do you invest?
  2. Lina's food truck (lessons 19 and 20) has cash flows of − 65, 27.5, 27.5 and €37k. Its NPV at 10% is €10.5k. Without calculating, is its IRR above or below 10%? The exact calculation gives 18.5%: is that consistent?
  3. Two exclusive one-year projects, cost of capital 10%. C: − €10k then + €15k. D: − €100k then + €130k. Calculate the IRR and NPV of each. Which do you choose?
  4. A project has cash flows of − 1,000, + 2,500, − 1,540. Check that 10% and 40% are both IRRs. Calculate the NPV at 20%, then at 8%. Is the project attractive if the cost of capital is 8%?
  5. Food for thought: an investment fund reports an IRR of 35% on a deal sold after one year, having invested €2m. Another fund reports an IRR of 18% on a €200m deal held for six years. Why is the first, more impressive, figure not necessarily a sign of better performance?
Answers (try first!)
  1. 1 + IRR = 560 / 500 = 1.12, so IRR = 12%. 12% > 10%: yes, you invest (NPV = − 500 + 560 / 1.1 = + €9.09).
  2. NPV at 10% is positive, and NPV falls as the rate rises: so you need to go above 10% to bring it to zero. The IRR is above 10%. An IRR of 18.5% is consistent.
  3. C: IRR = 15 / 10 − 1 = 50%, NPV = − 10 + 15 / 1.1 = €3.64k. D: IRR = 130 / 100 − 1 = 30%, NPV = − 100 + 130 / 1.1 = €18.18k. IRR prefers C, but D creates five times more value: choose D (the size pitfall).
  4. At 10%: − 1,000 + 2,500 / 1.1 − 1,540 / 1.21 = − 1,000 + 2,272.73 − 1,272.73 = 0. At 40%: − 1,000 + 2,500 / 1.4 − 1,540 / 1.96 = − 1,000 + 1,785.71 − 785.71 = 0. NPV at 20% = − 1,000 + 2,083.33 − 1,069.44 = + 13.89. NPV at 8% = − 1,000 + 2,314.81 − 1,320.30 = − 5.49. With an 8% cost of capital, the project destroys value, even though both its IRRs (10% and 40%) exceed 8%! Only NPV gives the right answer.
  5. Several reasons: (1) size: 35% on €2m in one year is a gain of about €0.7m, far less than €200m earns at 18% a year for six years (several hundred million euros); (2) duration: a high IRR over a short period doesn't tell you whether the money recovered could then be reinvested as well (reinvestment assumption); (3) an IRR on a single deal may be down to luck, and says nothing about the risk taken. That is why investors also look at the multiple on invested money and the amounts at stake, not just the IRR.

Next lesson: the payback period and the profitability index. How long does the project take to pay back its stake, and how much value does each euro invested create?

22.html:
Why it matters

For two lessons you have had two powerful tools: NPV (lesson 20) and IRR (lesson 21). Yet if you ask an SME boss, they will often answer something else: "How long until I get my money back?". That is the payback period, the most widely used criterion in business... and also the one most criticised by finance people.

Today we complete the investment toolbox with two complementary criteria: the payback period, which is about speed and risk, and the profitability index, which is about the efficiency of each euro invested. You will see when they help, and when they mislead.

The simple payback period

The payback period (délai de récupération) is the time needed for the project's cumulative cash flows to pay back the initial investment.

Payback period = the date at which the sum of cumulative cash flows becomes positive (or zero)

Take two (fictional) projects at an SME in Lyon that is torn between two new machines. Each costs €100,000. The annual cash flows (calculated as in lesson 19) are as follows:

YearProject A: cash flowA: cumulativeProject B: cash flowB: cumulative
0− €100,000− €100,000− €100,000− €100,000
1€40,000− €60,000€10,000− €90,000
2€40,000− €20,000€30,000− €60,000
3€40,000€20,000€50,000− €10,000
4€10,000€30,000€70,000€60,000

For A, the cumulative figure turns positive during year 3. At the end of year 2, €20,000 is still missing, and year 3 brings in €40,000. Assuming cash flows arrive evenly through the year:

Payback of A = 2 + 20,000 / 40,000 = 2.5 years (2 years and 6 months).

For B, €10,000 is missing at the end of year 3, and year 4 brings in €70,000:

Payback of B = 3 + 10,000 / 70,000 = 3.14 years (about 3 years and 2 months).

On this criterion, A is better: you get your money back faster. Many companies set themselves a maximum period ("no more than 3 years") and reject any slower project. With this rule, B would be rejected.

The flaws of simple payback

This criterion has two big flaws, and you need to know them by heart.

  1. It ignores the time value of money. A euro received in year 3 counts as much as a euro received in year 1. You have known since lesson 3 that this is wrong.
  2. It ignores everything that happens after the payback period. B's €70,000 in year 4 barely counts, even though that is precisely when B becomes very profitable. A project that earns enormous amounts for 15 years can be rejected in favour of a quick project that stops just afterwards.

Look at the NPV of the two projects at an 8% discount rate:

CriterionProject AProject BBetter
Simple payback2.5 years3.14 yearsA
NPV at 8%€10,434€26,123B

The two criteria contradict each other. And it is NPV that is right about value creation: B makes the company richer by more than €26,000 (in today's money), A by only €10,000.

The discounted payback period

To correct the first flaw, you calculate the period using discounted cash flows rather than raw cash flows. That is the discounted payback period.

For project A, at 8%:

YearCash flowDiscounted cash flowDiscounted cumulative
0− €100,000− €100,000.00− €100,000.00
1€40,000€37,037.04− €62,962.96
2€40,000€34,293.55− €28,669.41
3€40,000€31,753.29€3,083.88
4€10,000€7,350.30€10,434.18

Discounted payback of A = 2 + 28,669.41 / 31,753.29 = 2.90 years (about 2 years and 11 months). Note: the last cumulative figure, €10,434.18, is exactly the NPV. Logical: NPV is the sum of all the discounted cash flows.

Same calculation for B: discounted payback = 3.49 years (about 3 years and 6 months).

The discounted payback is always longer than the simple payback, since each future cash flow weighs less. It corrects the first flaw, but not the second: it still ignores what happens after payback.

So why does everyone use it?

Because it answers a real question: how long is my money exposed? For an SME short of cash, or for a project in a sector where technology changes fast (a mobile app, electronic equipment), distant cash flows are very uncertain. A short payback is then a form of prudence. It is also an easy criterion to explain to a management committee.

Good practice: use payback as a complementary criterion (an indicator of risk and liquidity), never as the only criterion.

The profitability index

Second tool of the day. The profitability index (PI, indice de profitabilité, IP) relates the value created to the money invested:

PI = present value of future cash flows / initial investment = 1 + NPV / investment

It reads like this: "each euro invested brings in PI euros in present value".

  • PI > 1: the project creates value (positive NPV).
  • PI = 1: the project neither creates nor destroys value (zero NPV).
  • PI < 1: the project destroys value (negative NPV).

For our two machines: PI of A = 110,434 / 100,000 = 1.10; PI of B = 126,123 / 100,000 = 1.26. Each euro invested in B brings in €1.26 in today's value.

For a standalone project, the PI gives exactly the same decision as NPV (accept if PI > 1 ⇔ NPV > 0). Its value shows up in a very common situation: when money is limited.

When the budget is limited: capital rationing

In theory, a company should launch every project with a positive NPV. In practice, it often has a capped investment budget (the bank won't lend more, shareholders don't want to put in more money). This is called capital rationing.

Fictional example: a company has €450,000 this year and is choosing between four projects.

ProjectInvestmentNPVPI
P1€200,000€60,0001.30
P2€150,000€30,0001.20
P3€100,000€35,0001.35
P4€250,000€50,0001.20

Naive method: pick the biggest NPVs. P1 (€60,000) then P4 (€50,000): €450,000 spent, budget used up. Total NPV: €110,000.

PI method: rank by decreasing PI and take the projects in order while the budget allows. P3 (1.35), P1 (1.30), then P2 (1.20): 100,000 + 200,000 + 150,000 = €450,000. Total NPV: 35,000 + 60,000 + 30,000 = €125,000.

The PI does better, because it selects the projects that create the most value per scarce euro. Be careful though: this method works well when projects are divisible or of comparable sizes. With very different projects, it is better to test all the possible combinations that fit in the budget (here, none exceeds €125,000).

Summary of the four criteria

CriterionQuestion askedStrengthWeakness
NPVHow much value do I create?The reference criterionDepends on the rate chosen
IRRWhat return does the project offer?Easy to grasp (a %)Pitfalls seen in lesson 21
PaybackHow long until I get my money back?Measures risk, simpleIgnores what follows
PIHow much does each euro invested bring in?Useful if budget is limitedIgnores project size

In case of conflict between criteria, remember finance people's rule: NPV decides, except under a budget constraint (then PI helps to rank).

Key takeaways

  • The payback period measures the time needed for cumulative cash flows to pay back the investment.
  • Simple payback ignores the time value of money; discounted payback takes it into account and is always longer.
  • Both ignore cash flows after payback: they can lead you to reject an excellent long-term project.
  • Payback remains useful as an indicator of risk and liquidity, alongside NPV.
  • PI = PV of future cash flows / investment = 1 + NPV / investment. Accept if PI > 1.
  • Under capital rationing, ranking projects by decreasing PI often maximises total NPV.
  • In case of conflict, NPV has the last word.

Exercise

A project costs €60,000 and brings in €15,000, €20,000, €25,000 then €20,000 over four years. The discount rate is 10%.

  1. Calculate the simple payback period.
  2. Calculate the discounted cash flows and the discounted payback period.
  3. Calculate the NPV and the profitability index. Does the project create value?
  4. The company requires a discounted payback of at most 3 years. Is the project accepted? What do you think in light of question 3?
  5. Food for thought: why can a start-up with only six months of cash left legitimately give more weight to the payback period than a large group such as TotalEnergies?
Answers (try first!)
  1. Cumulative: − €45,000, − €25,000, then €0 at the end of year 3. The simple payback is exactly 3 years.
  2. Discounted cash flows: 15,000 / 1.1 = €13,636.36; 20,000 / 1.1² = €16,528.93; 25,000 / 1.1³ = €18,782.87; 20,000 / 1.1⁴ = €13,660.27. Cumulative: − €46,363.64, − €29,834.71, − €11,051.84, then €2,608.43. Discounted payback = 3 + 11,051.84 / 13,660.27 = 3.81 years (about 3 years and 10 months).
  3. NPV = sum of discounted cash flows − 60,000 = 62,608.43 − 60,000 = €2,608.43. PI = 62,608.43 / 60,000 = 1.04. Yes, the project creates value, but not much: each euro invested brings in €1.04 in present value.
  4. No: 3.81 years > 3 years, the project is rejected. Yet its NPV is positive. The payback rule makes you give up a value-creating project. That said, the NPV is small: a small forecasting error would be enough to make it negative. Here the payback rule plays its role as a safeguard against risk.
  5. For the start-up, the main risk is running out of cash before the project pays off: a magnificent NPV is useless if the company has gone bankrupt in the meantime. A large group, with easy access to debt and the markets, can wait for distant cash flows. The payback period measures precisely this liquidity exposure (remember lesson 15 on liquidity).

Next lesson: a big case study. Should we open a new factory? We bring all the module 4 tools to bear on a single file.

23.titre: Étude de cas : la nouvelle usine
23.html:
The file on the table

You have just been hired as a financial analyst at Verdalis, a (fictional) company that makes compostable food packaging. The CEO wants to open a new factory in Normandy. The investment committee meets in a week and the CFO hands you the file: "Tell us whether we go ahead. With the numbers to back it up."

Step 1: gather the assumptions

After several meetings with the sales team and the plant, you have the following assumptions (all fictional):

  • Investment: €10m up front (building and machines), depreciated on a straight-line basis over 5 years, i.e. €2m a year.
  • Analysis period: 5 years.
  • Revenue: €6m in the first year (ramp-up), €9m in the second, then €10m a year.
  • Variable costs (materials, energy, transport): 45% of revenue.
  • Fixed costs (wages, maintenance, insurance): €1.5m a year.
  • Corporation tax: 25% (the standard rate in France is around this level today, but always check the current rate).
  • WCR: 15% of the year's revenue, fully recovered at the end.
  • Resale value of the factory after 5 years: €2m.
  • Discount rate: 9%, Verdalis's cost of capital (you will see how it is calculated in lesson 31).

Two more pieces of information are lying around in the file:

  • A market study was already paid for last year: €200,000.
  • The factory will be partly financed by a loan at 4%.

Remember lesson 19: the market study is a sunk cost. Whether or not the factory opens, the money is spent: it must not enter the calculation. As for the loan interest, you don't deduct it from the cash flows: the cost of financing is already in the discount rate. Counting it twice would be a classic mistake.

Step 2: build the cash flows

You know how to do all of this: cash flows (lesson 19), NPV (lesson 20), IRR (lesson 21), payback and PI (lesson 22). Let's put it together. Amounts in thousands of euros (€k).

Year012345
Revenue6,0009,00010,00010,00010,000
Variable costs (45%)− 2,700− 4,050− 4,500− 4,500− 4,500
Fixed costs− 1,500− 1,500− 1,500− 1,500− 1,500
EBE1,8003,4504,0004,0004,000
Depreciation− 2,000− 2,000− 2,000− 2,000− 2,000
Operating profit− 2001,4502,0002,0002,000
Tax (25%)+ 50− 362.5− 500− 500− 500
Net operating profit− 1501,087.51,5001,5001,500
+ Depreciation2,0002,0002,0002,0002,000
− Change in WCR− 900− 450− 15000
Investment, then WCR recovered and net resale− 10,000+ 3,000
Cash flow− 10,0009502,637.53,3503,5006,500

A few points to understand properly:

  • Positive tax in year 1: the project loses €200k, which reduces the tax Verdalis pays on its other, profitable activities. This tax saving of €50k is a real cash flow for the company.
  • Depreciation does not leave the till: it is deducted to calculate tax, then added back (lesson 11: profit ≠ cash).
  • WCR: €900k of WCR is needed in year 1 (15% of 6,000), €1,350k in year 2, then €1,500k. Only the changes consume cash.
  • The + €3,000k in year 5: the €1,500k of WCR is recovered, and the factory is sold for €2,000k. As it is fully depreciated, the gain is taxed: 2,000 × (1 − 25%) = €1,500k net.

Step 3: calculate the four criteria

NPV

Each cash flow is discounted at 9%:

YearCash flowDiscounted cash flowDiscounted cumulative
0− 10,000− 10,000.0− 10,000.0
1950871.6− 9,128.4
22,637.52,219.9− 6,908.5
33,3502,586.8− 4,321.7
43,5002,479.5− 1,842.2
56,5004,224.62,382.3

NPV = €2,382k, i.e. about €2.4m of value created.

IRR, payback and PI

  • IRR: the rate that sets NPV to zero is about 15.8%, well above the 9% cost of capital.
  • Simple payback: at the end of year 3, the cumulative figure is − €3,062.5k; year 4 brings in €3,500k. Payback = 3 + 3,062.5 / 3,500 = 3.9 years.
  • Discounted payback: 4 + 1,842.2 / 4,224.6 = 4.4 years. That is long: the money remains exposed for almost the whole life of the project.
  • Profitability index: 12,382.3 / 10,000 = 1.24. Each euro invested brings in €1.24 in present value.

Step 4: test how robust the result is

A positive NPV calculated on forecasts proves nothing until you have looked at what happens if you are wrong. That is sensitivity analysis: change one assumption at a time and recalculate.

ScenarioNPVIRR
Central scenario€2,382k15.8%
Revenue − 10% every year€998k12.0%
Variable costs at 50% of revenue (dearer energy)€1,093k12.2%
Failed start: revenue of €3m in year 1€1,281k12.6%
Discount rate at 11%€1,609k15.8%
Factory unsaleable after 5 years€1,407k13.3%

This table tells you several things:

  • The project withstands each shock taken individually: NPV stays positive everywhere.
  • The most sensitive variable is revenue: 10% fewer sales wipes out nearly 60% of the NPV. That is the effect of fixed costs, an operating leverage that amplifies differences.
  • Looking for the break-even point, you find that NPV becomes zero if revenue is about 17% below forecast every year. That is the project's safety margin.

In practice, you also build scenarios combining several shocks (a pessimistic scenario with falling sales and dear energy), because bad news rarely comes alone.

Step 5: the recommendation

Here is what you might write at the top of your memo to the committee:

Recommendation: launch the project. NPV of €2.4m, IRR of 15.8% for a 9% cost of capital, PI of 1.24. The project remains value-creating as long as sales are no more than 17% below forecast. Point to watch: a discounted payback of 4.4 years, and high sensitivity to revenue.

And you add the qualitative elements the numbers don't capture:

  • Commercial risk: are the sales forecasts based on signed contracts or on hopes? A customer accounting for 40% of volumes is a major risk.
  • Options: a factory in Normandy may open the door to the British market, or be expanded if it is a success. This flexibility has value, even if conventional NPV does not measure it.

Your role: give the committee a reliable figure, then show them what could change it.

Key takeaways

  • An investment study has five steps: assumptions, cash flows, criteria, sensitivity, recommendation.
  • Exclude sunk costs and financing costs (already in the discount rate).
  • Don't forget the tax saving in loss-making years, WCR and its recovery, and the after-tax residual value.
  • NPV is the main criterion; IRR, payback and PI complete the diagnosis.
  • Sensitivity analysis identifies the assumptions that matter most, and the break-even point gives the safety margin.
  • A good recommendation combines numbers and qualitative risks.

Exercise

  1. A committee member wants to add the €200,000 market study to the project's cost "to be prudent". What do you tell them?
  2. The plant director points out that the site will need decontaminating at the end. How would you include this cost in the cash flows?
  3. Redo the cash flow calculation if WCR represents 25% of revenue instead of 15%. What is the new NPV at 9%?
  4. The NPV with an unsaleable factory is €1,407k. Derive this figure from the central NPV.
  5. Food for thought: the CEO, enthusiastic, asks you to "lower the discount rate so the project gets through more easily". Why is this dangerous, and what do you suggest instead?
Answers (try first!)
  1. That it is a sunk cost: it has already been paid, whatever the decision. Including it does not make the analysis more prudent, it makes it wrong. You could wrongly reject a value-creating project. The only relevant question: what additional cash flows does the project generate from today?
  2. As a cash outflow in the final year (or the year it occurs), net of the tax saving if the expense is deductible. It reduces NPV all the more the larger it is, and all the less the further away it is (discounting).
  3. WCR: €1,500k in year 1, 2,250 in year 2, then 2,500. Changes: 1,500, 750, 250, 0, 0. Cash flows: year 1 = 1,850 − 1,500 = 350; year 2 = 3,087.5 − 750 = 2,337.5; year 3 = 3,500 − 250 = 3,250; year 4 = 3,500; year 5 = 3,500 + 2,500 (WCR recovered) + 1,500 (net resale) = 7,500. NPV at 9% ≈ €2,152k. It falls by about €230k: the WCR is recovered, but late, and the money tied up in the meantime has a cost.
  4. Without a resale, the €1,500k net in year 5 is lost. Its present value: 1,500 / 1.09⁵ = €974.9k. So 2,382.3 − 974.9 = €1,407.4k. We get the same figure.
  5. Because the discount rate is not chosen to get the result you want: it reflects the return required by providers of finance for that level of risk (lesson 31). Lowering it artificially makes value-destroying projects look profitable. What you can suggest: present the NPV at several rates, show that the IRR (15.8%) comfortably exceeds the cost of capital, and work instead on reducing risks (customer contracts, hedging energy prices).

Next lesson: we open module 5 on risk and financial markets. Shares, bonds: who does what on the markets?

24.html:
Why it matters

In module 4 you learnt to decide whether a project is worth it. But one question stayed in the shadows: where does the discount rate come from? Why 9% for Verdalis's factory, and not 5% or 15%? The answer lies in the financial markets. That is where the price of money and of risk is set.

This module 5 will give you the tools to measure risk and the return investors require. We start today with the setting: who sells what, to whom, and where.

What are financial markets for?

On one side, there are agents who need money: companies wanting to invest, States running a deficit. On the other, agents who have savings: households, pension funds, insurers. The financial system brings them together. There are two main channels:

  • Intermediated finance: the saver deposits money at the bank, and the bank lends to the company. The lender does not know the borrower.
  • Market finance (or direct finance): the company issues securities (shares, bonds) that investors buy directly.

In Europe, companies, especially SMEs, still rely heavily on bank loans, whereas in the United States market financing dominates. But large French companies make extensive use of both.

Shares: becoming a co-owner

A share (action) is a title of ownership: it represents a fraction of a company's capital. If a company has 1 million shares and you own 1,000, you hold 0.1% of the company.

Being a shareholder gives three main rights:

  • A right to profits: the dividend, if voted by the general meeting. It is never guaranteed.
  • A voting right at the general meeting (appointing directors, approving the accounts).
  • A right to what is left in a liquidation, after all creditors have been paid. Often, nothing is left.

That is why the shareholder is called a residual claimant: paid last, with whatever is left. In exchange for that risk, they enjoy all the upside if the company succeeds.

Market capitalisation = share price × number of shares

Fictional example: a company has 50 million shares trading at €80. Its market capitalisation is 50m × 80 = €4 billion. That is what the market thinks its equity is worth. The largest French companies, such as LVMH or TotalEnergies, are each worth several hundred billion euros (the exact figure changes every day).

A share's return comes from two sources: the dividend and the change in price (capital gain or loss).

Return on a share over a period = (dividend + closing price − opening price) / opening price

You buy a share for €50, receive a €2 dividend, and sell it for €55 a year later: return = (2 + 55 − 50) / 50 = 14%. If it had fallen to €45, your return would have been (2 − 5) / 50 = −6%.

Bonds: lending money

A bond (obligation) is a debt security: by buying it, you lend money to the issuer. In return, the issuer undertakes to pay you:

  • coupons (the interest), usually every year, calculated on the face value (nominal);
  • repayment of the face value at maturity.

Fictional example: a bond with a face value of €1,000, a 3.5% coupon and a 5-year maturity. You receive €35 a year for 5 years, plus €1,000 at the end.

The main issuers are:

  • States: in France, these are OATs (obligations assimilables du Trésor, French government bonds). The French State's debt is largely financed this way.
  • Companies: these are called corporate bonds. Only companies of a certain size have access to them.

The main risk is that the issuer doesn't pay: that is default risk. Rating agencies (S&P, Moody's, Fitch) assess it with grades from AAA (very safe) to C or D (default). A distinction is drawn between investment grade (AAA to BBB−) and speculative grade (high yield, below that). The lower the rating, the higher the rate the issuer must offer.

A bond's price also varies over time, in the opposite direction to interest rates (remember lesson 3?). We will see the precise calculation in lesson 28.

Shares and bonds side by side

ShareBond
NatureTitle of ownershipDebt security
IncomeVariable dividend, not guaranteedCoupon fixed in advance
RepaymentNever (you sell on the market)At maturity
Voting rightYesNo
Ranking in bankruptcyLastBefore shareholders
Risk and expected returnHighLower

Remember the last row: it is at the heart of the coming lessons. The more risk you take, the more return you require. That is why equity costs the company more than debt (lesson 1, and we will put a number on it in lesson 31).

Primary market, secondary market

This is a fundamental distinction, and often misunderstood.

  • The primary market is for new securities. The company issues shares (stock market flotation, capital increase) or bonds, and receives the money. This is where it raises finance.
  • The secondary market is for second-hand securities. One investor sells their securities to another. The company receives not a single euro from these trades.

When you buy a TotalEnergies share on the stock exchange, you buy it from another investor, not from TotalEnergies. So why is the secondary market useful to the company? Because it provides liquidity: an investor is more willing to buy new securities if they know they can sell them at any time. Without an active secondary market, the primary market would be much more expensive.

Who does what?

Issuers

Companies, States, local authorities, public bodies. They are looking for funds.

Investors

  • Individuals, directly or via their assurance-vie (French life-insurance savings wrapper), their PEA (plan d'épargne en actions, a French tax-advantaged share account) or employee savings schemes.
  • Institutional investors: insurers, pension funds, asset management companies (which manage funds such as UCITS (OPCVM) and ETFs), sovereign wealth funds. They hold most of the securities.

Intermediaries and infrastructure

  • Investment banks advise issuers (preparing a flotation, placing a bond issue).
  • Brokers pass on buy and sell orders.
  • Stock exchanges match orders. In Paris, it is Euronext Paris.
  • Clearing houses and custodians make sure trades settle properly (the securities and the money really do change hands).

Regulators

In France, the AMF (Autorité des marchés financiers, the financial markets authority) ensures investors are properly informed and punishes abuses (insider dealing, market manipulation). At European level, ESMA coordinates national regulators, and the ECB supervises the large banks of the euro area.

Indices: the market's thermometer

A stock market index summarises the performance of a basket of shares. The best known in France is the CAC 40, made up of 40 large companies listed in Paris (you analysed one in lesson 18). People also follow the Euro Stoxx 50 (large euro-area companies) or the S&P 500 (United States). When people say "the market rose 1% today", they usually mean an index. These indices will serve as the benchmark for measuring "market risk" in lessons 26 and 27.

Key takeaways

  • Financial markets bring together those who need financing and those who have savings, through direct finance, alongside intermediated bank finance.
  • A share is a title of ownership: uncertain dividend, voting right, paid last. Market cap = price × number of shares.
  • A bond is a debt security: coupons and repayment of face value, with a default risk measured by ratings.
  • More risk = more required return: shares cost the company more than debt.
  • The primary market finances the company; the secondary market gives it liquidity, without fresh money.
  • Key players: issuers, investors (mainly institutional), intermediaries, Euronext, and the regulator, the AMF.

Exercise

  1. A company has 120 million shares, trading at €35.50. What is its market capitalisation?
  2. You buy a share for €42, receive a €1.50 dividend and sell it for €39. What is your return?
  3. A bond has a face value of €1,000, a 4.25% coupon and a 7-year maturity. How much do you receive each year, and in total if you hold it to the end?
  4. Primary or secondary market? (a) A start-up floats on the stock market. (b) Your aunt sells her Orange shares. (c) The State issues a new 10-year OAT. (d) A fund buys Airbus bonds from another fund.
  5. Food for thought: can a profitable company have an interest in watching its share price, even though it receives nothing from stock market trades?
Answers (try first!)
  1. 120,000,000 × 35.50 = €4,260,000,000, i.e. €4.26 billion.
  2. (1.50 + 39 − 42) / 42 = − 1.50 / 42 = −3.57%. The dividend does not make up for the fall in price.
  3. Annual coupon: 1,000 × 4.25% = €42.50. Total: 7 × 42.50 + 1,000 = €1,297.50 (in undiscounted euros, of course).
  4. (a) Primary: the start-up receives the money. (b) Secondary: Orange receives nothing. (c) Primary: the State raises finance. (d) Secondary: a trade between two investors.
  5. Yes, for several reasons. If it ever wants to raise new funds (capital increase), a high share price lets it raise more while giving up fewer shares. A high price also makes acquisitions paid in shares easier and protects against a hostile takeover. Finally, executives are often paid partly in shares, and the price reflects investors' judgement of the strategy.

Next lesson: return and risk. How to measure the risk of an investment with expected value, variance and standard deviation.

25.html:
Why it matters

Yesterday we saw that a share earns more on average than a bond, but is riskier. Fine. But "riskier" by how much? To decide, you need to measure risk with a number, just as you measure return.

Today you will learn the three statistical tools that underpin all of market finance: expected value (the average expected return), variance and standard deviation (the spread around that average). Don't panic: they are averages, and you can calculate them in a few lines.

Expected return

The future is uncertain. To reason about it, you imagine several scenarios, with a probability for each, and the investment's return in each case.

Fictional example: you are torn between two shares for next year. Solaria, a solar panel maker highly dependent on the economic cycle, and Eau du Sud, a water distributor with stable business.

ScenarioProbabilitySolaria returnEau du Sud return
Recession25%−10%2%
Normal growth50%8%5%
Strong growth25%25%7%

The expected return is the average of the returns, weighted by the probabilities:

E(R) = sum of (probability × return) over all scenarios

  • Solaria: 0.25 × (−10) + 0.5 × 8 + 0.25 × 25 = −2.5 + 4 + 6.25 = 7.75%
  • Eau du Sud: 0.25 × 2 + 0.5 × 5 + 0.25 × 7 = 0.5 + 2.5 + 1.75 = 4.75%

Careful: the expected value is not what you will get. With Solaria, you will never get 7.75%: you will get −10%, 8% or 25%. It is what you would get on average if you could replay the year thousands of times.

Measuring spread: variance and standard deviation

Solaria earns more on average, but its outcomes are very spread out. To measure this spread, you take each scenario's deviation from the average, square it (so negative deviations don't cancel out positive ones), and take the weighted average.

Variance: σ² = sum of [probability × (return − E(R))²]

Standard deviation: σ = √variance

For Solaria (returns in %):

ScenarioDeviation from meanSquared deviation× probability
Recession−10 − 7.75 = −17.75315.0678.77
Normal8 − 7.75 = 0.250.060.03
Strong growth25 − 7.75 = 17.25297.5674.39
Variance153.19

Solaria's standard deviation: √153.19 = 12.38%. Same calculation for Eau du Sud: variance of 3.19, standard deviation of 1.79%.

Why two measures? Variance is expressed in "percent squared", a unit that means nothing to anyone. Standard deviation, on the other hand, is expressed in the same unit as the return: you can say "Solaria returns 7.75% on average, with a typical deviation of about 12 points around that average". That is why standard deviation is the most widely used measure. On the markets, it is called volatility.

With historical data

In real life, nobody knows the scenario probabilities. So you often use the past: take the observed returns and calculate their average and standard deviation.

Fictional example: a share returned 12%, −8%, 20%, 5% and 1% over five years.

  • Average: (12 − 8 + 20 + 5 + 1) / 5 = 30 / 5 = 6%.
  • Deviations from the average: 6, −14, 14, −1, −5. Squared: 36, 196, 196, 1, 25. Sum: 454.
  • Variance: 454 / (5 − 1) = 113.5. Standard deviation: √113.5 = 10.65%.

Did you notice we divide by n − 1 (4) and not by n (5)? With a sample from the past, this corrects a slight statistical bias. Excel does it for you: =MOYENNE(...), =VAR.S(...) and =ECARTYPE.STANDARD(...) (=AVERAGE, =VAR.S and =STDEV.S in English Excel).

Interpreting standard deviation

If returns roughly follow a normal distribution (the famous bell curve), you have two useful benchmarks:

  • about 2 years out of 3 (68%), the return falls between average − σ and average + σ;
  • about 19 years out of 20 (95%), it falls between average − 2σ and average + 2σ.

For our share: two years out of three between −4.65% and 16.65%, and 95% of the time between −15.31% and 27.31%. That gives a much more concrete idea of the risk than a simple "it's risky".

An important caveat: real markets experience more extreme crashes than the normal distribution predicts (2008, March 2020). These benchmarks are orders of magnitude, not guarantees.

Going from monthly to annual volatility

Return accumulates over time, but risk grows more slowly: it increases with the square root of time (assuming independent months).

Annual σ ≈ monthly σ × √12

A share with monthly volatility of 4% has annual volatility of about 4 × 3.46 = 13.9%.

The risk-return pair

An investment is often summed up by two figures: its expected return and its standard deviation. To give you an idea, here are long-run historical orders of magnitude (they vary by country and period):

InvestmentAverage annual returnAnnual volatility
Savings account or money marketLowAlmost zero
Government bondsModerateA few %
Broad equity indexHigherAbout 15 to 20%
Individual shareVariableOften 25 to 40%

Notice that the individual share is riskier than the index that contains it. That is the effect of diversification, tomorrow's topic.

Comparing two investments

A rational investor prefers, for equal risk, the higher return, and for equal return, the lower risk. But between Solaria (7.75%; 12.38%) and Eau du Sud (4.75%; 1.79%), neither dominates the other: the choice depends on your risk aversion.

One tool helps compare: the Sharpe ratio, which measures the return earned above the risk-free rate per unit of risk.

Sharpe ratio = (E(R) − risk-free rate) / σ

With a risk-free rate of 3%: Solaria = (7.75 − 3) / 12.38 = 0.38; Eau du Sud = (4.75 − 3) / 1.79 = 0.98. Eau du Sud rewards each unit of risk taken much better.

Key takeaways

  • Expected return is the average of returns weighted by probabilities: E(R) = Σ p × R.
  • Variance measures spread: σ² = Σ p × (R − E(R))². Standard deviation σ, its square root, is expressed in %: it is volatility.
  • With historical data, divide the sum of squared deviations by n − 1.
  • Normal distribution: about 68% of cases within average ± σ, 95% within average ± 2σ (but crashes are more frequent than expected).
  • Risk grows with the square root of time: annual σ ≈ monthly σ × √12.
  • The Sharpe ratio compares excess return per unit of risk.

Exercise

  1. An investment returns −5% with a probability of 30%, 6% with 40% and 15% with 30%. Calculate its expected return, variance and standard deviation.
  2. A share returned 4%, −2%, 10% and 8% over four years. Calculate the historical average and standard deviation.
  3. A fund has monthly volatility of 2.5%. What is its approximate annual volatility?
  4. Three funds: A (expected return 6%, σ 10%), B (6%; 15%), C (9%; 15%). Which one would no rational investor buy? Can the other two be separated?
  5. Food for thought: standard deviation counts very good surprises as "risk" just as much as very bad ones. Why is that debatable, and what other limitations do you see in this measure?
Answers (try first!)
  1. E(R) = 0.3 × (−5) + 0.4 × 6 + 0.3 × 15 = −1.5 + 2.4 + 4.5 = 5.4%. Deviations: −10.4; 0.6; 9.6. Variance = 0.3 × 108.16 + 0.4 × 0.36 + 0.3 × 92.16 = 32.448 + 0.144 + 27.648 = 60.24. Standard deviation = √60.24 = 7.76%.
  2. Average = (4 − 2 + 10 + 8) / 4 = 5%. Deviations: −1, −7, 5, 3; squared: 1, 49, 25, 9; sum: 84. Variance = 84 / 3 = 28. Standard deviation = √28 = 5.29%.
  3. 2.5 × √12 = 2.5 × 3.46 = about 8.66%.
  4. B is dominated: A offers the same return with less risk, and C more return for the same risk. Between A and C, there is no universal answer: C earns more but is riskier. A cautious investor may prefer A, another C. With a risk-free rate of 2%, the Sharpe ratios are 0.40 for A and 0.47 for C: C rewards risk slightly better.
  5. An investor doesn't complain about a surprise rise: what they fear is losses. Measures such as downside risk alone or maximum drawdown capture this better. Other limitations: historical standard deviation assumes the past resembles the future, it underestimates extreme events, and it depends heavily on the period chosen. It is an excellent starting point, not an absolute truth.

Next lesson: diversification and Markowitz's portfolio theory, or why you can reduce risk without reducing return.

26.html:
The only free lunch in finance

"Don't put all your eggs in one basket." Everyone knows the proverb. In 1952, a young American economist, Harry Markowitz, turned it into precise mathematics, which much later earned him the Nobel prize. His discovery: by combining investments intelligently, you can reduce risk without sacrificing return. Diversification is often called "the only free lunch in finance".

Yesterday you learnt to measure the return and risk of a single investment. Today we move on to the portfolio: what happens when you hold several?

The return of a portfolio: a simple average

Take two fictional shares:

  • A, a technology company: expected return 10%, standard deviation 25%.
  • B, a consumer goods company: expected return 6%, standard deviation 15%.

You invest a proportion w of your money in A and the rest (1 − w) in B. The portfolio's expected return is the weighted average:

E(Rp) = w × E(RA) + (1 − w) × E(RB)

Half and half: 0.5 × 10 + 0.5 × 6 = 8%. Nothing magic so far.

The risk of a portfolio: where it all happens

For risk, it is not an average. Everything depends on how the two shares move together. This is measured with the correlation coefficient ρ (the Greek letter "rho"), between −1 and +1:

  • ρ = +1: the two shares always rise and fall together, in the same proportions.
  • ρ = 0: their movements are unrelated.
  • ρ = −1: when one rises, the other always falls.

Covariance combines correlation and volatilities: Cov(A, B) = ρ × σA × σB. And the formula for the risk of a two-asset portfolio is:

σp² = w² × σA² + (1 − w)² × σB² + 2 × w × (1 − w) × Cov(A, B)

The last term is the key. If the correlation is low or negative, it is small or negative, and it reduces total risk.

The effect of correlation

Portfolio of 50% A and 50% B, with different correlations:

Correlation ρExpected returnPortfolio standard deviation
+18%20.0%
+0.38%16.4%
08%14.6%
−18%5.0%

Return stays at 8% in every case. But risk melts away as correlation falls. With ρ = +1, there is no benefit: risk is the simple average (0.5 × 25 + 0.5 × 15 = 20%). As soon as ρ < 1, the portfolio is less risky than the average of its components. That is diversification.

Calculation details for ρ = 0.3: Cov = 0.3 × 25 × 15 = 112.5. σp² = 0.25 × 625 + 0.25 × 225 + 2 × 0.25 × 112.5 = 156.25 + 56.25 + 56.25 = 268.75. σp = √268.75 = 16.4%.

Varying the weights

Keep ρ = 0.3 and change the allocation:

Share of AShare of BExpected returnStandard deviation
0%100%6.0%15.0%
25%75%7.0%14.4%
50%50%8.0%16.4%
75%25%9.0%20.2%
100%0%10.0%25.0%

Look at the second row: by replacing a quarter of B with A, the riskier share, you get more return (7% against 6%) and less risk (14.4% against 15%). Adding a risky asset reduced risk! It is counter-intuitive, and it is Markowitz's whole contribution.

The least risky portfolio possible (the minimum variance portfolio) here contains about 18% of A: return 6.72%, standard deviation 14.3%.

The efficient frontier

If you plot all these portfolios on a graph (risk on the horizontal axis, return on the vertical), you get a curve shaped like a "nose" lying on its side. With dozens of assets, you get a whole area of possible portfolios.

Markowitz shows that a rational investor should only consider portfolios on the upper edge of this area: for each level of risk, those offering the maximum return. That is the efficient frontier.

  • A portfolio below the frontier is inefficient: another offers more return for the same risk. In our table, 100% B (6%; 15%) is inefficient, because 25% A + 75% B does better on both counts.
  • On the frontier, the choice between portfolios depends on your risk aversion: the theory does not choose for you.

How many securities do you need?

Imagine shares that all have a volatility of 30% and a correlation of 0.3 with each other (realistic orders of magnitude for European shares). If you hold n of them in equal parts:

Number of securitiesPortfolio standard deviation
130.0%
224.2%
519.9%
1018.2%
2017.4%
5016.8%
Infinity16.4%

Two lessons:

  1. The first securities added reduce risk a lot. Beyond 20 to 30 securities, the gain becomes small.
  2. Risk never falls to zero. It levels off at 16.4% (√0.3 × 30%).

Specific risk and systematic risk

This observation splits a share's total risk into two pieces:

  • Specific risk (or diversifiable risk): particular to the company. A product recall, a lawsuit, a CEO resigning. In a broad portfolio, these bad surprises are offset by other companies' good surprises. It disappears with diversification.
  • Systematic risk (or market risk): it affects all companies at the same time. A recession, an ECB rate rise, a pandemic. No diversification eliminates it.

Total risk = systematic risk + specific risk. Only systematic risk cannot be eliminated by diversification.

This distinction has a huge consequence, which you will see tomorrow: since anyone can eliminate specific risk for free by diversifying, the market does not reward it. Only systematic risk earns an extra return. That is the starting point of the CAPM.

A limitation to keep in mind

Correlations are not stable. In a crisis (2008, March 2020), almost all shares fall together: correlations climb towards 1, and diversification protects less just when you need it most. That is why fund managers also diversify across asset classes (shares, bonds, property) and geographical regions.

Key takeaways

  • A portfolio's return is the weighted average of returns.
  • Its risk is not an average: σp² = w²σA² + (1 − w)²σB² + 2w(1 − w)Cov(A, B), with Cov = ρ × σA × σB.
  • As soon as correlation is below 1, diversification reduces risk without reducing return.
  • The efficient frontier groups the portfolios offering the best return for each level of risk.
  • Specific risk is eliminated by diversification; systematic risk remains.
  • Correlations rise in a crisis: diversification is not absolute protection.

Exercise

Two assets: X (expected return 12%, standard deviation 30%) and Y (expected return 4%, standard deviation 10%). Their correlation is 0.2.

  1. Calculate the covariance between X and Y.
  2. For a portfolio of 60% X and 40% Y, calculate the expected return and standard deviation.
  3. Recalculate the standard deviation if the correlation were −0.5. Comment.
  4. With shares of 30% volatility and a correlation of 0.3 with each other, what is the standard deviation of an equally weighted portfolio of 4 securities? Of 25 securities? (Formula: σp² = σ²/n + (1 − 1/n) × ρ × σ².)
  5. Food for thought: an employee puts all their savings into shares of the company that employs them, "because they know it well". What would Markowitz say?
Answers (try first!)
  1. Cov = 0.2 × 30 × 10 = 60 (in %²).
  2. Return: 0.6 × 12 + 0.4 × 4 = 8.8%. Variance: 0.36 × 900 + 0.16 × 100 + 2 × 0.6 × 0.4 × 60 = 324 + 16 + 28.8 = 368.8. Standard deviation: √368.8 = 19.2%. The weighted average of standard deviations would have given 22%: diversification saves nearly 3 points of risk.
  3. Cov = −0.5 × 30 × 10 = −150. Variance: 324 + 16 + 0.48 × (−150) = 268. Standard deviation: √268 = 16.4%. Same return, less risk: a negative correlation makes diversification even more effective, because the two assets offset each other.
  4. n = 4: 900 / 4 + 0.75 × 0.3 × 900 = 225 + 202.5 = 427.5, i.e. σ = 20.7%. n = 25: 36 + 0.96 × 270 = 295.2, i.e. σ = 17.2%. We are approaching the floor of 16.4% (systematic risk).
  5. That it is the opposite of diversification, and even worse: their salary and their savings depend on the same company. If it struggles, they risk losing their job and their savings at the same time (correlation close to 1). Knowing a company well does not reduce its specific risk. This is what happened to many Enron employees in the United States in 2001.

Next lesson: the CAPM (MEDAF in French) and beta, or how to calculate the return shareholders require from a share.

27.html:
The price of risk

Since the start of the course, one question keeps coming back: which discount rate should you use? For Verdalis's factory (lesson 23), we took 9% without much justification. It is time to answer seriously, at least for shareholders.

Yesterday you saw that diversification eliminates specific risk, but not systematic risk. The CAPM (Capital Asset Pricing Model; in French MEDAF, modèle d'évaluation des actifs financiers) draws the logical conclusion: only systematic risk is rewarded. And it gives a simple formula to calculate the return shareholders require. This model, developed in the 1960s notably by William Sharpe, is used every day in banks, audit firms and finance departments.

Beta: measuring systematic risk

A share's beta (β) measures its sensitivity to market movements. It answers the question: when the market rises or falls by 1%, how much does this share move on average?

  • β = 1: the share follows the market. The market by definition has a beta of 1.
  • β > 1: the share amplifies movements. With β = 1.5, a 10% market fall brings the share down by about 15% on average.
  • β < 1: the share is calmer than the market. With β = 0.6, a 10% market fall brings the share down by about 6%.
  • β close to 0: the share does not depend on the market.

β = Cov(R share, R market) / Var(R market)

By sector, you generally see low betas for businesses not very sensitive to the economic cycle (water or electricity distribution, basic food, healthcare), and high betas for cyclical businesses (cars, construction, luxury, banks, semiconductors). People still buy water in a recession, far fewer new cars.

Calculating a beta from data

Fictional example: over five years, the market (an index such as the CAC 40) and a share had the following returns.

YearMarketShareMarket deviationShare deviationProduct of deviationsMarket deviation²
110%14%472816
2−5%−9%−11−16176121
315%20%91311781
42%1%−4−62416
58%9%2244
Totalavg 6%avg 7%349238

Covariance = 349 / 4 = 87.25. Market variance = 238 / 4 = 59.5. So β = 87.25 / 59.5 = 1.47. (You can also divide 349 by 238 directly: the "/ 4" cancel out.)

This share amplifies market movements by about 50%. In practice, you would rather use 2 to 5 years of monthly or weekly returns, and Excel does the calculation (=PENTE(share returns ; market returns), =SLOPE(...) in English Excel). Financial data providers also publish the betas of listed companies.

The CAPM formula

E(Ri) = rf + βi × [E(Rm) − rf]

  • rf: the risk-free rate. In practice, the yield on long-term government bonds (for France, the 10-year OAT, around 3% in recent years; check the current level).
  • E(Rm) − rf: the market risk premium, the extra return investors require to hold shares rather than risk-free securities. Estimates vary, often between 5 and 7% for European markets.
  • βi: the share's beta.

The logic is crystal clear: required return = reward for time (rf) + reward for systematic risk (β × premium). Specific risk appears nowhere: the market does not pay for it, since you can get rid of it for free by diversifying.

Example

With a risk-free rate of 3% and a risk premium of 6%:

Company (fictional)BetaCalculationRequired return
Water distributor0.63 + 0.6 × 66.6%
Large diversified group1.03 + 1.0 × 69.0%
Car parts supplier1.43 + 1.4 × 611.4%
Share from the previous table1.473 + 1.47 × 611.8%

This required return is the cost of equity, often written ke. It is what the company must earn for its shareholders for them to stay. You will reuse it to calculate the cost of capital in lesson 31.

The security market line and alpha

If you plot the formula on a graph, with beta on the horizontal axis and required return on the vertical, you get a straight line: the Security Market Line. It starts at rf (for β = 0) and passes through the market return (for β = 1).

According to the CAPM, every correctly priced share lies on this line. If an analyst thinks a share will earn more than the CAPM requires, the difference is called alpha:

Alpha = expected return (according to the analyst) − required return (according to the CAPM)

Example: a share with a beta of 1.2 requires 3 + 1.2 × 6 = 10.2%. An analyst forecasts 12%. Alpha = +1.8%: in their view, the share is undervalued (it is above the line). Fund managers spend their lives looking for positive alpha. Studies show that after fees, most don't find it consistently, which explains the success of index funds.

The beta of a portfolio

Good news: unlike standard deviation (lesson 26), a portfolio's beta is a simple weighted average.

βp = sum of (weight × beta of each security)

A portfolio of 50% shares with beta 1.4, 30% with beta 0.6 and 20% with beta 1.0 has a beta of 0.5 × 1.4 + 0.3 × 0.6 + 0.2 × 1.0 = 1.08. A manager who expects the market to fall can reduce their portfolio's beta by selling the most cyclical securities.

The model's limitations

The CAPM is a model, and therefore a simplification:

  • Beta is estimated from the past and changes over time. A company that transforms itself (new business, more debt) sees its beta move.
  • The choice of data changes the result: monthly or weekly returns, 2 or 5 years, CAC 40 or a European index.
  • The risk premium cannot be observed: everyone estimates it their own way.
  • A single risk factor is not much. Researchers (Fama and French) have shown that company size and other factors also explain returns.

Despite everything, it remains the benchmark for estimating the cost of equity, because it is simple, logical, and nobody has found a replacement everyone agrees on.

Key takeaways

  • Only systematic risk is rewarded, because specific risk is eliminated by diversification.
  • Beta measures a share's sensitivity to the market: β = Cov(Ri, Rm) / Var(Rm). The market has a beta of 1.
  • CAPM: E(Ri) = rf + β × (E(Rm) − rf). It gives the cost of equity ke.
  • The market risk premium is often estimated at 5 to 7%; the risk-free rate is that of long-term government bonds.
  • Alpha is the gap between the expected return and the return required by the CAPM.
  • A portfolio's beta is the weighted average of the betas.

Exercise

  1. Risk-free rate: 2.5%. Market risk premium: 5.5%. What is the required return on a share with a beta of 1.3?
  2. Your portfolio contains 40% of a share with beta 0.9 and 60% of a share with beta 1.5. What is its beta? If the market falls by 10%, how much does your portfolio fall on average?
  3. The covariance between a share and the market is 180 (in %²), and the market's standard deviation is 20%. Calculate the beta, then the required return with rf = 3% and a 6% premium.
  4. With rf = 3% and a 6% premium, an analyst forecasts a 10% return for a share with a beta of 1.5. Calculate alpha. What does the analyst conclude?
  5. Food for thought: a small biotech company has enormous volatility (60% a year) but a beta of only 0.5. How is that possible? Why does the CAPM assign it a lower required return than a large carmaker that is much less volatile?
Answers (try first!)
  1. 2.5 + 1.3 × 5.5 = 2.5 + 7.15 = 9.65%.
  2. βp = 0.4 × 0.9 + 0.6 × 1.5 = 0.36 + 0.9 = 1.26. If the market falls by 10%, the portfolio falls by about 12.6% on average.
  3. Var(Rm) = 20² = 400. β = 180 / 400 = 0.45. Required return = 3 + 0.45 × 6 = 5.7%.
  4. Required return = 3 + 1.5 × 6 = 12%. Alpha = 10 − 12 = −2%. The share lies below the security market line: it doesn't earn enough for its risk. According to the analyst, it is overvalued and should be avoided (or sold).
  5. Beta only measures risk linked to the market. The biotech's success depends mainly on its clinical trials, not on the economy: its enormous volatility is almost entirely specific risk. In a diversified portfolio, this risk is diluted (a failed trial at one, a success at another). The carmaker, on the other hand, suffers in every recession, at the same time as the rest of the portfolio: that is the risk investors cannot avoid, and they charge for it.

Next lesson: valuing bonds. Price, yield and duration, or why bonds fall when rates rise.

28.html:
Why it matters

Bonds have a reputation as "quiet" investments. Yet in 2022, when the ECB raised its rates at high speed to fight inflation, euro-area government bond indices lost around 15 to 20% (and much more for the longest bonds). Insurers, pension funds and banks saw the value of their portfolios melt. In the United States, the failure of Silicon Valley Bank in 2023 partly stems from this.

How can a "safe" investment lose so much? You have had the answer since lesson 3: when the rate rises, present value falls. Today we apply this idea to bonds (introduced in lesson 24) and learn to measure their sensitivity to rates with duration.

The price of a bond

A bond is a series of cash flows known in advance: coupons each year, then repayment of the face value at maturity. Its price is quite simply the present value of these cash flows, discounted at the market rate (the return required today for this type of issuer and this maturity).

Price = C / (1 + y) + C / (1 + y)² + … + (C + N) / (1 + y)^n

where C is the coupon, N the face value, n the number of years remaining and y the market rate.

Fictional example: a government bond with a face value of €1,000, a 3% coupon (€30 a year), maturity 5 years. If the 5-year market rate is 4%:

YearCash flowCash flow discounted at 4%
1€30€28.85
2€30€27.74
3€30€26.67
4€30€25.64
5€1,030€846.58
Price€955.48

On the markets, the price is expressed as a percentage of face value: here 95.55%.

The inverse price-rate relationship

Let's calculate the price of the same bond for different market rates:

Market ratePriceThe bond is said to trade...
2%€1,047.13above par
3%€1,000.00at par
4%€955.48below par
5%€913.41below par

The logic is intuitive. If new bonds pay 4%, nobody will pay €1,000 for an old bond that only pays 3%. Its price falls until it too gives its buyer 4%. Remember the rule:

Market rate = coupon: price at par. Market rate > coupon: price below par. Market rate < coupon: price above par.

Important: if you hold the bond to maturity and the issuer doesn't default, you do receive all your coupons and your €1,000. The loss is only real if you have to sell early, or if you have to value your portfolio at market price (the case for banks and funds).

The yield to maturity

Often you go the other way: you know the price on the market and are looking for the rate. The yield to maturity (YTM, taux de rendement actuariel) is the rate that makes the price equal to the present value of the cash flows. Recognise the idea? It is exactly the IRR from lesson 21, applied to a bond.

Example: our 3% bond trades at €950. What return does a buyer who holds it to the end get? You need to find y such that the calculated price equals €950. By trial and error (or with =TAUX(5;30;-950;1000) in Excel, =RATE(5,30,-950,1000) in English Excel), you find y ≈ 4.13%.

This return comes from two sources: the coupons (€30 a year, i.e. 3.16% of the price paid) and the €50 gain at maturity, when you get €1,000 back for a security bought at €950.

The credit spread

The required rate depends on the issuer. A company must offer more than the State, because it can default. The gap is called the spread (or credit premium):

Yield on a corporate bond = risk-free rate of the same maturity + credit spread

The spread widens as the rating falls (lesson 24). It is also what the press measures when comparing the French OAT with the German Bund: the gap between the two reflects the perceived risk of each State.

Zero-coupon bonds

Some bonds pay no coupon: you buy them for less than face value and receive the face value at maturity. Their price is a simple discounting calculation (lesson 3):

Price of a zero-coupon bond = N / (1 + y)^n

A €1,000 10-year zero-coupon bond is worth 1,000 / 1.03¹⁰ = €744.09 if the rate is 3%, and €675.56 if the rate rises to 4%. Just one extra point on the rate wipes out 9.2% of its value.

Duration: measuring sensitivity to rates

Not all bonds react in the same way to a rise in rates. The more distant the cash flows, the more discounting crushes them, and the more sensitive the price. Duration measures this distance.

Macaulay duration

It is the average life of the cash flows, weighted by their present value:

D = Σ [t × discounted cash flow in year t] / price

For our bond at a 4% rate: multiply each discounted cash flow by its year, i.e. 28.85 × 1 + 27.74 × 2 + 26.67 × 3 + 25.64 × 4 + 846.58 × 5 = 4,499.83. Divide by the price: D = 4,499.83 / 955.48 = 4.71 years.

Duration is slightly shorter than maturity (5 years), because the coupons arrive earlier. For a zero-coupon bond, duration and maturity are equal.

Modified duration

To get to price sensitivity, you use modified duration:

Dmod = D / (1 + y)

Change in price (in %) ≈ − Dmod × change in rate

Here, Dmod = 4.71 / 1.04 = 4.53. If the rate goes from 4% to 5%, the price falls by about 4.53%, i.e. 4.53% × 955.48 = €43.27. The exact calculation gives 955.48 − 913.41 = €42.07: the approximation is very good for small rate changes.

The 2022 case

Imagine a fictional 30-year bond, issued with a 1% coupon when long-term rates were at 1%. If long-term rates rise to 3.5% (a move of this size happened between 2021 and 2023), its price goes from €1,000 to about €540: a 46% loss on a perfectly solvent government security. That is why fund managers watch the duration of their portfolios like a hawk.

Key takeaways

  • The price of a bond is the present value of its coupons and face value, at the market rate.
  • Rates and prices move in opposite directions. Coupon above the rate: price above par; coupon below: price below par.
  • The yield to maturity is the bond's IRR for a buyer who holds it to maturity.
  • Yield on a corporate bond = risk-free rate + credit spread.
  • Duration (Macaulay) measures the average life of the cash flows; modified duration gives the sensitivity: ΔP/P ≈ − Dmod × Δy.
  • The longer a bond and the lower its coupon, the more sensitive it is to rates.

Exercise

  1. A bond with a face value of €1,000 pays a 5% coupon and matures in 3 years. The market rate is 4%. Calculate its price. Is it above or below par? Why?
  2. What is the price of a zero-coupon bond with a face value of €1,000, maturing in 8 years, if the market rate is 3.5%?
  3. Calculate the Macaulay duration and modified duration of the bond in question 1. Estimate the change in its price if rates rise by 0.5 points.
  4. A bond has a Macaulay duration of 7 years and a yield of 3%. By how much (approximately) does its price change if rates rise by 0.5 points?
  5. Food for thought: you think the ECB will cut its rates in the coming months. Do you prefer to hold short or long bonds? And if you need your money back in a year to buy property?
Answers (try first!)
  1. Price = 50 / 1.04 + 50 / 1.04² + 1,050 / 1.04³ = 48.08 + 46.23 + 933.45 = €1,027.75. It trades above par, because its coupon (5%) is higher than the market rate (4%): buyers are willing to pay more for a security that pays more than new issues.
  2. 1,000 / 1.035⁸ = €759.41.
  3. D = (1 × 48.08 + 2 × 46.23 + 3 × 933.45) / 1,027.75 = (48.08 + 92.46 + 2,800.35) / 1,027.75 = 2.86 years. Dmod = 2.86 / 1.04 = 2.75. Estimated change: − 2.75 × 0.5% = −1.38%, i.e. about 1.38% × 1,027.75 ≈ − €14.1 (the exact calculation at 4.5% gives − €14.01).
  4. Dmod = 7 / 1.03 = 6.80. Change: − 6.80 × 0.5% ≈ −3.4%.
  5. If rates fall, bond prices rise, and all the more so the longer the duration: to benefit from the fall, you prefer long bonds. But it is a bet: if you are wrong, you lose a lot. If you need your money in a year, the right choice is a bond (or investment) whose maturity matches your horizon: you know exactly what you will receive, whatever happens to rates. Matching duration with your investment horizon is called immunisation, and it is what insurers do.

Next lesson: valuing shares. The Gordon-Shapiro model and the P/E ratio, or how to put a price on a share.

29.html:
What is a share worth?

Yesterday, valuing a bond was almost easy: its cash flows are written into the contract. For a share, it is another story. Dividends are not guaranteed, they can rise or disappear, and the share has no maturity. Yet every day, millions of investors put a price on it.

Today you will discover the two main approaches: the "fundamental" method, which discounts future dividends (the Gordon-Shapiro model, also known as the Gordon growth model), and the "comparison" method, which uses a multiple, the P/E ratio (PER in French). The first forces you to think about what creates value; the second is the one you hear about everywhere in the financial press.

The principle: discount what the shareholder receives

If you buy a share and hold it for a year, you receive a dividend D1 and sell the share at price P1. With a required return k (calculated by the CAPM, lesson 27), the fair price today is:

P0 = (D1 + P1) / (1 + k)

But P1 itself depends on the year-2 dividend and the year-2 price, and so on. Repeating the reasoning to infinity leads to a fundamental idea:

The value of a share is the present value of all future dividends.

The resale price disappears, because it merely reflects the dividends the next buyer will receive. One practical problem remains: it is impossible to forecast dividends to infinity. Hence a simplifying assumption.

The Gordon-Shapiro model

Myron Gordon and Eli Shapiro assumed that the dividend grows at a constant rate g for ever. In that case, the infinite sum simplifies into a very short formula:

P0 = D1 / (k − g)

with D1 the dividend expected in one year, k the return required by shareholders and g the annual growth rate of dividends (you need k > g).

Fictional example: Moreau SA, a listed regional bakery chain, has just paid a dividend of €2 per share. This dividend is expected to grow by 3% a year. With a risk-free rate of 3%, a risk premium of 5% and a beta of 1, the CAPM gives k = 3 + 1 × 5 = 8%.

  • Dividend expected in one year: D1 = 2 × 1.03 = €2.06.
  • Value of the share: P0 = 2.06 / (0.08 − 0.03) = 2.06 / 0.05 = €41.20.

Beware the classic trap: the formula uses D1, next year's dividend, and not the dividend just paid (D0).

A very sensitive formula

The denominator k − g is a small number: the slightest change in k or g changes the result a lot.

AssumptionsCalculationValue
k = 8%, g = 2%2.04 / 0.06€34.00
k = 8%, g = 3%2.06 / 0.05€41.20
k = 8%, g = 4%2.08 / 0.04€52.00
k = 9%, g = 3%2.06 / 0.06€34.33

Just one extra point of growth adds 26% of value. That is why share prices move so much when growth prospects change, and fall when interest rates rise (k increases). Also keep in mind that g is perpetual growth: it cannot exceed the growth of the economy for long (a few % a year in nominal terms). If g gets close to k, the formula explodes and no longer makes sense.

Where does growth come from?

A company grows because it reinvests part of its profits. If it keeps a proportion b of its profit (the retention rate) and these funds earn its ROE (lesson 13), then:

g = b × ROE

A company with an ROE of 12% that distributes 60% of its profit (keeping 40%) can grow its dividends by about 0.4 × 12 = 4.8% a year. It is a way of checking that a growth assumption is realistic.

Reversing the formula: the implied return

Rearranging the formula gives the return the market expects from a share based on its price:

k = D1 / P0 + g (dividend yield + growth)

A share priced at €50, which will pay a €2 dividend and whose dividend grows by 4% a year, offers an implied return of 2 / 50 + 4% = 4% + 4% = 8%. Analysts use this formula to estimate the cost of equity, alongside the CAPM.

The P/E ratio: the most famous multiple

In practice, many investors reason by comparison. The P/E ratio (Price Earnings Ratio, PER in French), or earnings multiple, is the ratio of the share price to earnings per share (EPS, BPA in French):

P/E = share price / earnings per share = market capitalisation / net profit

It reads: "the market pays x years of earnings to buy the share". For Moreau SA, if the company distributes 60% of its profit, expected EPS is 2.06 / 0.6 = €3.43, and the P/E is 41.20 / 3.43 = 12.

What a P/E tells you

Combining Gordon-Shapiro and the definition of P/E gives: P/E = payout ratio / (k − g). Here: 0.6 / 0.05 = 12. This relationship explains what makes a P/E high:

  • Strong expected growth (high g): technology or luxury companies often have P/Es well above average.
  • Low risk (low k): investors pay more for stable earnings.
